https://www.rfa.org/english/china/2025/0.body: A human rights group is urging Kazakhstan not to deport to China a 23-year-old ethnic Kazakh man who fled from Xinjiang several weeks ago, warning he could face persecution and internment there. Atajurt, a volunteer group that campaigns for Kazakh victims of oppression in Xinjiang, said Friday it had confirmed that the man, Yerzhanat Abai, has been detained by Kazakh police. Serikzhan Bilash, who heads the group, said Yerzhanat Abai, a Chinese national, is being held in the Panfilov City Detention Center in Zharkent county, Almaty province, which is about 40 kilometers (25 miles) from the border with China. “He could be secretly escorted to China by Xinjiang’s national security or Kazakhstan’s National Security Bureau at any time, and no one knows his specific situation. Only if this matter is made public to the world will the Kazakh government be unable to repatriate him,” said Serikzhan. Serikzhan, who lives in exile in the United States, has been a vocal campaigner for the release of fellow ethnic Kazakhs from Chinese camps, where the ruling Chinese Communist Party held an estimated 1.8 million ethnic minority Uyghurs, Kazakhs, and other Muslims in mass incarceration centers after 2017. Beijing denies the allegations. “Many young people in Xinjiang are often summoned by the police, or sent to learning centers under various pretexts, saying they are providing employment opportunities. In fact, they are arranged to work in factories in the mainland, most of which are chemical factories that are harmful to health, and the wages are even lower than in Xinjiang,” Serikzhan said. According to Atajurt, Yerzhanat Abai entered Kazakhstan on March 27 and sought help from the group in the Kazakh city of Almaty four days later. He said he was from Gongliu county, Yili prefecture in Xinjiang, China. The circumstances of his leaving China and why he was detained in Kazakhstan weren’t immediately clear. RFA sought comment without success from the Kazakhstan Interior Ministry and the Chinese Consulate General in Almaty. Edited by Mat Pennington.

https://www.rfa.org/english/uyghur/2025/.body: BANGKOK – A Thai court slashed the number of prosecution witnesses for the long-stalled trial of two Uyghur men incarcerated for a decade following the retaliatory bombing of a Bangkok shrine popular with Chinese visitors. Adem Karadag and Yusufu Mieraili, both handcuffed and shackled, appeared Thursday at a Bangkok criminal court for a fresh arraignment aimed at speeding up proceedings in the politically sensitive case. “I still have hope for freedom,” Karadag told Radio Free Asia through a courtroom interpreter. “I want to go anywhere but not to be sent back to China like others.” Both men smiled and hugged their Thai lawyer and Uyghur interpreter. “I exercised. I can eat well,” Mieraili said in Thai. Both men deny they triggered the Erawan Shrine bomb in the Aug. 17, 2015 attack that was apparent retaliation for Thailand’s repatriation of dozens of Uyghur migrants to China, where they face high risk of persecution. Twenty people died in the bombing of the Hindu shrine in downtown Bangkok and more than 120 more injured. The trial has languished due to jurisdiction changing between civilian and military courts amid regime changes in Thailand. Lack of qualified courtroom interpreters also has caused delays. The criminal court on Thursday cut the number of prosecution witnesses to 20 from 55 to shorten the trial. It has set 11 court dates from September to December. The pair are charged with first-degree murder and could face execution if found guilty. Police arrested Karadag and Mieraili shortly after the bombing based on CCTV footage, but failed to find dozens of other alleged perpetrators. The trial is expected to finish next year, said Chuchart Gunpai, a lawyer for the defendants. Uyghur exodus through Southeast Asia Uyghurs are Turkic-speaking Muslims who mostly live in the Xinjiang region of China but are also spread across Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Uzbekistan and Turkey. They have been fleeing China in large numbers to escape what they describe as persecution and repression by Chinese authorities – allegations that Beijing denies. Before the bombing, nearly 400 Uyghurs who fled China were arrested in Thailand in 2014, according to the Thai foreign ministry. The fleeing Uyghurs were hoping for resettlement in Turkey via Malaysia, right advocates and other lawyers said. Others likely slipped through the Thai-Malaysian border without detection by authorities. In June 2015, Thailand allowed 172 Uyghur women and children to leave for Turkey, but two weeks later appeared to bow to pressure from Beijing and put 109 Uyghur men, blindfolded, on a plane back to China, provoking international condemnation. The Thai foreign ministry said at that time the men “have been verified as Chinese and evidence of their involvement in criminal activities has been sent by the Government of China.” The decision drew condemnation from the World Uyghur Congress, an exiled Uyghur group, which claimed 25 Uyghurs were killed resisting the forced deportation. Thailand denied any deaths. “Had Thailand followed the principle of not sending people into harm’s way, these mishaps could have been avoided,” Chalida Tarjaroensuk, the director of the People’s Empowerment Foundation, who assisted the Uyghurs, told RFA. Related Stories Previous Lack of Interpreter Stalls Uyghur Suspects’ Trial in 2015 Bangkok Bombing 2 Uyghur suspects in Bangkok bombing return to court after 9-month delay US condemns Thailand’s deportation of 40 Uyghurs to China Next Poor conditions Following the deportations and the arrests of Karadag and Mieraili in 2015, more than 50 Uyghurs remained in Thai immigration prison until earlier this year. Some said they were denied proper lawyer visits and kept in cramped unhygienic cells without adequate medical care. Thai officials said three detainees died during their imprisonment. Some 40 of the imprisoned Uyghurs were deported to China in the dead of night on Feb. 27. Reporters who traveled with Thai officials to China to check on conditions for the deported men said they were subjected to Chinese surveillance. Another three Uyghur men, who held Kyrgyzstan passports, were resettled in Canada. Five Uyghurs are continuing to serve sentences for jailbreaking, according to Chalida, who fears they will also face deportation to China after their release in the next year or two. Edited by Stephen Wright and Taejun Kang.

https://www.rfa.org/english/china/2026/0.body: Taiwan’s plan to open a second trade office in the Philippines is an example of Manila and Taipei accelerating cooperation in response to Chinese pressure in the South China Sea, analysts told Radio Free Asia. During a radio interview on Sept. 15, Taiwan’s Foreign Minister Lin Chia-lung said that Taipei’s plan to open a second representative office in Cebu, the Philippines’ second largest city, was going smoothly. Taipei’s trade offices serve as de facto embassies and consulates in countries that officially recognize China, but maintain unofficial relations with Taiwan, which Beijing considers to be a rogue province. Foreign Minister Lin said that the additional trade office would serve travelers and businesses in the central Philippines, and would be an integral part of a proposed Taiwan-Philippines Economic Corridor. Days later, Taiwan confirmed that it had donated a decommissioned patrol vessel to the Philippines for use in its coast guard. These developments are directly related to Beijing’s hostile tactics in the South China Sea, Ray Powell, executive director of Stanford University’s SeaLight maritime transparency project, told RFA. Beijing claims the entirety of the sea as its territory, including the area within the Philippines’ exclusive economic zone, which Manila calls the West Philippine Sea. china and philippines claims The overlapping claims of China and the Philippines in the South China Sea. (AFP) “Of course China’s aggression in the West Philippine Sea is a central part of this story,” said Powell. “It has made Manila less willing to grant Beijing the kind of deference that other countries like Malaysia or Papua New Guinea have recently been so eager to show on Taiwan policy.” Papua New Guinea announced in July that it would close the Taiwan trade office in Port Moresby, and Malaysia’s Prime Minister Ibrahim Anwar in August controversially stated in an interview with Al Jazeera that he sees “Taiwan as part of China, period.” The trend of smaller countries showing deference to China “has conditioned Beijing to expect that its coercive methods will always produce compliance eventually,” Powell said. “For now at least it has not produced that kind of result in the Philippines.” Defining “one China” As a condition of entering into official relations with China, countries must affirm that there is one China and recognize Beijing as the sole legal government of China. China’s official stance, the one-China principle, states that Taiwan is an inalienable part of China. Many countries maintain their own one-China policies that stop short of the principle to allow unofficial ties with Taipei. When Taiwan announced the plan to open a new trade office in Cebu, Beijing protested, with Chinese Foreign Ministry spokesperson Guo Jiakun urging the Philippines to uphold the one-China Principle through “concrete actions” and refrain from taking steps that could damage relations with China. “No matter how the DPP authorities collude with external forces or in what form they seek so-called ‘diplomatic breakthroughs,’ their efforts to serve the goal of ‘Taiwan independence’ are doomed to be futile,” Guo said, referring to Taiwan’s ruling Democratic Progressive Party. The Philippine Department of Foreign Affairs responded that Manila’s one-China policy remained unchanged but did not prevent economic, cultural and functional cooperation with Taiwan. Philippine Defense Secretary Gilberto Teodoro Jr. was more direct, telling local media: “We define the one-China policy. We define it. Not them.” The exchange highlights a widening difference between Manila and Beijing over what the Philippines’ one-China policy allows. The Taiwan trade office in Cebu should not be interpreted as a change in Manila’s formal position, Joseph Kristanto, a research analyst at Singapore’s S. Rajaratnam School of International Studies, told RFA. “Rather, I think it reflects the ongoing expansion and institutionalization of the Philippines’ unofficial and functional relationship with Taiwan,” he said. “This distinction is important: Manila continues to recognize Beijing as the sole legal government of China under its one-China Policy, yet it does not view this policy as precluding economic, cultural, or other practical forms of engagement with Taiwan.” That relationship had already begun expanding before the latest dispute. In April 2025, Philippines President Ferdinand Marcos Jr.’s administration relaxed decades-old restrictions on engagement with Taiwan. Most Philippine officials may now travel there for economic, trade and investment purposes if they use ordinary passports and do not use their official titles. The restrictions continue to apply to the president, vice president, foreign secretary and defense secretary, illustrating the line Manila is trying to maintain between functional engagement and steps that might resemble formal diplomatic recognition. “Currently, Manila appears intent on maintaining a distinction between expanding functional ties and taking actions that could be construed as formal diplomatic recognition,” Kristanto said. “The 2025 guidelines are particularly illustrative: they facilitate interactions with Taiwan for economic and investment purposes while retaining restrictions on contacts involving the Philippines’ most senior officials.” Economic interdependence Practical interests are also driving the relationship. More than 200,000 Filipinos work in Taiwan, and the two sides offer visa-free entry to each other’s citizens. Taipei has also placed greater emphasis on trade, investment, tourism and supply-chain cooperation with the Philippines. Foreign Minister Lin said the proposed Taiwan-Philippines Economic Corridor would connect with the U.S.-Japan-Philippines-backed Luzon Economic Corridor, an initiative aimed at strengthening infrastructure and supply chains. Kristanto cautioned against explaining the closer relationship entirely through the South China Sea dispute. “The deterioration in Manila-Beijing relations has certainly made Taiwan more strategically relevant to the Philippines, and we have seen indications of expanding practical cooperation in areas such as maritime security,” he said. “But many drivers of closer Philippines-Taiwan relations – economic links, labor, geographical proximity, and supply-chain cooperation – exist independently of the South China Sea dispute. I therefore see pressure from China more as an accelerant to an existing trend than as its sole cause.” Powell said the Philippines increasingly viewed China’s treatment of Taiwan as part of a wider effort to pressure smaller countries that resisted Beijing’s preferred regional order. “There’s an active attempt by China, very obvious now, to make a more Sinocentric world and to put down others who do not agree with them – particularly when these others are smaller countries,” Powell said, quoting from a recent SeaLight podcast interview with Teodoro. Kristanto said the significance of the Cebu office lay less in the facility itself than in Manila’s growing confidence in defining its relationship with Taipei on its own terms. “Manila appears increasingly willing to insist that maintaining a one-China policy does not give Beijing a veto over its unofficial relationship with Taiwan,” Kristanto said. “So, in my view, the significance of the Cebu office lies less in the office itself than in what it tells us about how much more comfortable Manila has become in expanding ties with Taiwan while arguing that its formal diplomatic position remains unchanged.” Edited by Eugene Whong.

https://www.rfa.org/english/uyghur/2026/.body: Read RFA coverage of this story in Uyghur Chinese authorities in Xinjiang’s regional capital Urumqi on July 4 arrested two Uyghur sisters and their mother for sending goods to their eldest sister in Turkey, and a third sister was arrested a week later, the eldest told Radio Free Asia. Guzelnur Kamil said her family had been shipping ordinary household goods, including clothing, footwear, hats, daily necessities, seasonings, and packaged food items to support her business in Turkey. “They were simply miscellaneous everyday items,” she told RFA. “My mother said, ‘Even if we cannot send you cash, let us send you goods so you can do business, my child, and provide for your children,’” she said. Guzelnur, who moved to Turkey in 2016, said the shipments were assembled by her sister, Guljennet Kamil, who from 2018-2020 was detained in an internment camp . Guljennet also suffers from partial paralysis following an accident and was helped by her sister with a share of the profits from her business. However, according to Guzelnur, the police used this communication as a pretext to target the family. Investigation Guzelnur said the police interrogation of her family began on July 1, and explained that her mother, Bahargul Tohti, along with her sisters Guljennet and Gulzeper Hekim, were interrogated several times. Police used Guljennet’s shipping of goods to Turkey as a pretext, alleging suspicion of “supporting terrorists,” she said, adding that her mother and sisters were ordered to lead police to the exact shops where they purchased the goods and the logistics companies they used to ship them. “On the 4th, they spoke very politely, asking my mother to come to the police station at 9:00 AM,” she said. “After taking her in, they also brought in my sisters. They took their blood samples and photographed them from the front, back, and sides. After that, they just took them away without saying a word.” Turkey is one of 26 countries that China considers “sensitive,” along with primarily Muslim-majority nations such as Indonesia, Saudi Arabia, Egypt and Kazakhstan according to Human Rights Watch . Under China’s “ Strike Hard Campaign ,” those who have been to these countries, have families, or otherwise communicate with people there, have been questioned, detained, and even imprisoned. Guzelnur said her family in Urumqi has not sent her any goods for more than a year. Instead, she has been importing merchandise from Central Asian countries. The shipments from her family had already ceased long before her family was arrested by police. “We have documentation for everything—from where it was shipped, and even who received the goods,” Guzelnur said. “We provided those files, and my mother and sisters provided everything to the police. Yet the police still told them, ‘We will investigate you; there are also things going on over there in Turkey.’ What things could be going on here? We have nothing going on here. We can even present clean records from here.” According to Guzelnur, her mother and sisters were taken to the Nanjiao Police Station in Urumqi. “One is an orphan girl, one is my mother, and one is my disabled sister... What am I supposed to do now?!” she told RFA, referring to her adopted sister Gulzeper. RFA confirmed that Guljennet was moved from the police station and is currently being held at the Tianshan District Detention Center. Ethnic unity law The arrests came just days after China’s new ethnic unity law went into effect. On July 10, Norway-based Uyghur activist Abduweli Ayup posted on X , “Three Uyghurs detained in Urumqi. The National Security police didn’t tell the reasons, they put them in detention on July 4th. They are the first target we learned after China enacted the ethnic unity promotion law.” Critics of China’s ethnic unity law warn that the law brings accelerated forced assimilation and cultural erasure of Uyghurs and Tibetans . It also raises fears of Beijing’s increasing transnational repression and its ability to stifle dissident voices overseas. Guzelnur told RFA that her third sister, Gulmire Kamil, who remained at home after her mother and two sisters were arrested on July 4, was arrested by police a week later. Gulmire previously served 10 years in prison for her connection with the July 5, 2009 unrest in Urumqi. Translated by Tahir Izgil. Edited by Charlie Dharapak and Eugene Whong.

https://www.rferl.org/a/kyrgyz-activist-.body: News Kyrgyz Activist Gets 2 Years For Criticizing Growing Chinese Presence By RFE/RL's Kyrgyz Service and Zamira Eshanova October 01, 2026 18:08 CET Kyrgyz Activist Gets 2 Years For Criticizing Growing Chinese Presence Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Kyrgyz activist Mavlyan Askarbekov was detained in June after criticizing the growing presence of Chinese citizens in Kyrgyzstan, including their involvement in small and midsize businesses. (file photo) The Lenin District Court in Bishkek found activist and politician Mavlyan Askarbekov guilty and sentenced him to two years in prison on offenses related to a law on incitement of racial, ethnic, national, religious, or interregional hatred, a verdict he called "absurd." Askarbekov was detained in June after criticizing the growing presence of Chinese citizens in Kyrgyzstan, including their involvement in small and midsize businesses. Prosecutors said Askarbekov's Facebook posts contained explicit calls to incite interethnic discord. "When does incitement to hatred occur? When someone writes something against a particular ethnic group and calls for some kind of action against them. Expressing criticism alone does not constitute incitement to hatred," lawyer and human rights defender Klara Sooronkulova told RFE/RL. SEE ALSO: China's Growing Footprint In Kyrgyzstan Fuels Concerns Over Resources, Sovereignty "No one in those posts called for action against the Chinese. People everywhere are saying, ‘'There are too many Chinese.' Are they going to imprison everyone for that?" she added. China's expanding role in Kyrgyzstan has become increasingly hard to ignore. During the first half of 2026, Kyrgyzstan issued some 61,000 work visas, according to the Foreign Ministry's Consular Department, with about 60 percent going to Chinese citizens. That influx of Chinese workers is part of a wider economic expansion and also hard to miss on city streets. In a country of just more than 7 million people -- where hundreds of thousands leave to work abroad, mainly in Russia, and remittances sustain many households -- the arrival of so many Chinese workers has been difficult to accept for many Kyrgyz. Kyrgyz officials have defended Chinese involvement as necessary for development and have tried to keep a lid on the government for failing to provide clear information about Chinese migration and employment. In battling online criticism, the state has turned to what it calls "forensic linguistic examination" to determine whether social media posts break the law. Joomart Karabaev, a former researcher at the Kyrgyz National Academy of Sciences, said the practice has been entirely weaponized. He knows that firsthand. Karabaev was arrested and given a three-year probationary sentence after publicly exposing how state security forces dictate expert findings. "They have started playing the role of a court, effectively becoming an institution that rubber-stamps the guilt established by the investigation and prosecution," he said. "It has become common to dig up someone's old and new opinions when their political position is disliked, find an article under which they can be charged, and then imprison them based on the conclusions of a linguistic examination," Karabaev added. In Askarbekov's case, he criticized the growing number of Chinese citizens involved in Kyrgyzstan's small and medium-sized businesses, arguing they were displacing local entrepreneurs. SEE ALSO: As Trump Courts Xi, Pressure Mounts To Confront China Over Support For Iran He publicly called on the prime minister to discuss the issue in a live debate. Instead of public dialogue, the initiative ended in Askarbekov's prosecution and imprisonment. The case comes as China's economic clout in Central Asia continues to grow. As of June, Kyrgyzstan owed about $1.4 billion to China, according to the Kyrgyz Finance Ministry. China remained the country's largest external creditor, accounting for 28.1 percent of total external debt at the end of 2025, according to the International Monetary Fund. This deep economic reliance has made public criticism of Chinese influence a highly sensitive political issue across the region. In 2019, Kyrgyz activist Guljamila Saparalieva was arrested and charged with inciting ethnic hatred after participating in a protest against Beijing's treatment of Muslims in Xinjiang and the influx of Chinese migrants. SEE ALSO: In US-China AI Race, Kazakhstan Faces Pressure To Pick A Side In neighboring Uzbekistan, farmers in several regions accused local authorities of pressuring them to surrender farmland that was subsequently leased or earmarked for Chinese investors between late 2024 and early 2026. Beijing is reported to closely monitor such developments and has shown a willingness to deploy diplomatic pressure when public demonstrations affect its strategic interests. In November 2025, members of the Nagyz Atajurt movement in Kazakhstan protested near the border with China, demonstrating against Beijing's treatment of ethnic Kazakhs in Xinjiang and demanding the release of a Kazakh citizen detained there. The activists also raised broader alarms about China's growing leverage over Astana. The demonstration prompted China's Consulate General in Almaty to issue a sharp diplomatic note to Kazakhstan's Foreign Ministry. The note, obtained and reviewed by RFE/RL's Kazakh Service, called the protest "an open provocation against the dignity of the People's Republic of China" and an insult to the Chinese Communist Party and its leadership, urging Kazakh authorities to "seriously investigate" the incident. Kazakh court documents reveal that investigators placed the diplomatic note directly into the case file. The prosecution cited China's formal objections as evidence that the protest damaged bilateral relations. The activists were subsequently convicted of inciting ethnic discord and each received a five-year prison sentence. https://www.rfa.org/english/china/2025/0.body: Online censorship in China by some regional governments is even more aggressive than enforcement of the national-level ‘Great Firewall’ by the central government, according to a recent study and local sources. The Great Firewall Report (GFW Report) highlights how the central Chinese province of Henan has adopted its own provincial firewall which is less sophisticated and robust than the central government’s but more volatile and aggressive, blocking significantly more websites than the national-level censorship system. Local sources told Radio Free Asia that the heightened restrictions at the provincial government level may reflect uncertainty about instructions from higher authorities, leading to “excessive blocking” to avoid blame for failing to carry out their duties. GFW Report is a censorship monitoring platform, primarily focused on China. During one experiment its researchers ran between Dec. 26, 2023 and March 31, 2025, they found that the Henan Firewall blocked 4.2 million domains, about six times that of the 741,542 at the national level. Since 2023, netizens in Henan had reported a rise in the number of websites that were inaccessible in the region but accessible elsewhere in China, the study found. “This localized censorship suggests a departure from China’s centralized censorship apparatus, enabling local authorities to exert a greater degree of control within their respective regions,” researchers Mingshi Wu at GFW, Ali Zohaib and Amir Houmansadr at University of Massachusetts Amherst, Zakir Durumeric at Stanford University, and Eric Wustrow at the University of Colorado Boulder wrote in the GFW Report published in May, “A Wall Behind A Wall: Emerging Regional Censorship in China.” But the phenomenon extends beyond Henan, sources inside China told RFA. Local governments in neighboring Hebei, another central Chinese province, as well as those in Tibet and Xinjiang have been operating similar censorship systems as the one reported in Henan for at least four years, Zhao Yuan, a network engineer based in Hebei, said. “In the past, we could access overseas websites that were not blocked by the national firewall,” Zhao said. “Now, even virtual private networks (VPNs) in Henan and Hubei don’t work.” While the national-level firewall, known as the Great Firewall, targets more news and media sites, in line with China’s long-standing policy of censoring politically sensitive information, the provincial-level firewall systems, like the one in Henan, blocks domains focusing on topics like the economy, technology, and business, GFW Report researchers found. The Chinese Communist Party has, in recent years, emphasized a multi-pronged approach to censorship , including the management of all types of propaganda at the domestic and international level through a framework known as “territorial management” and implementation of “digital stability maintenance” measures, such as policing of sensitive content online on dates deemed politically sensitive by the government. “Local governments have taken the initiative to establish local blocking systems, indicating that the top leaders are increasingly vigilant about the flow of information,” Wei Sicong, a Beijing-based political observer, said. china-regional-censorship-firewall-local-province Commuters wearing face masks to help curb the spread of the coronavirus browse their smartphones inside a subway train in Beijing Wednesday, Feb. 10, 2021. China's internet watchdog cracked down on online speech and issued a new requirement that bloggers and influencers have a license before they can publish on certain topics. (Andy Wong/AP) ‘Turning off the whole world’ Researchers at GFW found that the Henan firewall monitors and blocks traffic leaving and entering the province, as opposed to the national-level censorship system that is focused on traffic entering and exiting the country. Other sources in the region told RFA that the heightened restrictions at the provincial government level suggest lack of clear legal know-how about how to enforce instructions from higher-ups. “Officials would rather block more and more than take responsibility. So the result you see is ‘turning off the whole world’,” network engineer Zhang Jianan said. GFW Report researchers said their analysis showed no regional censorship in other areas they studied, such as Beijing, Guangdong, Shanghai, and Jiangsu. In Henan and Hebei, however, local residents told RFA that even the websites of some foreign universities are inaccessible, as a result of which they turn to VPNs and other circumvention tools to bypass government censorship and surveillance. “Some classmates can connect in Beijing and Shanghai, but we can’t in Zhengzhou and can only rely on circumvention software,” Zhang, a student at Henan’s Zhengzhou University, said. Hebei-based network engineer Zhao said, “The censorship is getting stricter and stricter. We can’t even connect to some foreign university websites.” RFA found that as early as December 2023, a university in Henan province sought to purchase a “public opinion monitoring system,” specifically aimed at international students, students and dissidents, and had conducted an open bidding process. Henan University of Science and Technology had laid out a 2024-2025 budget of 120,000 yuan (or US$16,657) for the public opinion monitoring service system to provide 24/7 real-time monitoring, early warning analysis and crisis response of public opinion information on the entire network, covering news websites and social media platforms such as Weibo and Douyin, the university’s website showed. When RFA contacted the university, a teacher confirmed they are using an old monitoring system and that they have now started a bidding process for a new one. Edited by Mat Pennington.

https://www.rferl.org/a/politkovskaya-ru.body: Russia Two Decades On, Politkovskaya's Daughter Says Little Has Changed In Russia Since Her Mother's Murder By RFE/RL October 07, 2026 12:45 CET Two Decades On, Politkovskaya's Daughter Says Little Has Changed In Russia Since Her Mother's Murder Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Activists attend a rally in honor of slain journalist Anna Politkovskaya in Moscow. (file photo) Two decades after the murder of Anna Politkovskaya, a tenacious investigative reporter who exposed the brutality of Russia's war in Chechnya and documented how President Vladimir Putin curtailed democracy in Russia, her daughter, Vera, says little has changed in the country's political climate. People told her, “You’re exaggerating. You see everything through a dark lens,” she told RFE/RL's Russian Service in an interview ahead of the 20th anniversary of Politkovskaya's brutal killing on October 7, 2006. "And now it’s the same thing, except that the divide has deepened so much. Everything has become so stark, even compared with what she predicted more than 20 years ago". Politkovskaya, who worked for the independent newspaper Novaya Gazeta, was gunned down in her Moscow apartment. The shooting occurred on President Vladimir Putin's birthday, prompting speculation that it was meant as a "gift" to the president. Embed share 20 Years Since The Death Of Russian Journalist Anna Politkovskaya by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:02:29 0:00 Direct link 240p | 4.6MB 360p | 6.2MB 480p | 8.9MB 720p | 14.7MB 1080p | 25.1MB Former Russian police officer Sergei Khadzhikurbanov -- who denied the charges -- was sentenced to 20 years in prison for his role in organizing the assassination but received a pardon from Putin in 2023 after taking part in Moscow's ongoing full-scale invasion of Ukraine. Two natives of Russia's North Caucasus region of Chechnya, Rustam Makhmudov and Lom-Ali Gaitukayev, were subsequently handed life sentences after a jury found Makhmudov guilty of shooting Politkovskaya, while Gaitukayev was convicted of organizing the assassination. Gaitukayev later died in prison. Another defendant in the case, former Moscow police officer Denis Pavlyuchenkov, was sentenced to 11 years in prison after he confessed to organizing the surveillance of Politkovskaya before she was murdered. Six Novaya Gazeta journalists and contributors -- Igor Domnikov (2000), Yury Shchekochikhin (2003), Politkovskaya (2006), Anastasia Baburova (2009), Stanislav Markelov (2009), and Natalya Estimirova (2009) -- have been killed in attacks that the newspaper and human rights activists say were retribution for their work. SEE ALSO: Daughter Blames 'System' Built By Putin, Kadyrov For Rights Activist Estemirova’s Death Since Politkovskaya's death, Russian authorities have gradually expanded the legal toolbox used to punish dissent, censor independent media, shutter civil society groups, and silence opposition lawmakers. This includes measures such as the "foreign agent" law, which punishes individuals and groups that receive foreign funding, and the "undesirables" law, which bans foreign organizations deemed a threat to national security and criminalizes people who work for, associate with, or donate money to such organizations. Such moves are exactly what her mother's reporting was aimed at exposing, said Vera Politkovskaya, who now lives abroad at an undisclosed location. "Essentially, the main theme of my mother's work was telling the stories of ordinary people," she said. "And how that everyday person was run over by the political and military system...That's what my mom witnessed and talked about back then. She saw, so to speak, further ahead than many other people did. And people didn't believe her." SEE ALSO: The List Is Long: Russians Who Have Died After Running Afoul Of The Kremlin Anna Politkovskaya was born in New York in 1958, the daughter of a Soviet diplomat from Ukraine. She was won numerous Russian and international awards, including an Amnesty International Global Award for Human Rights Journalism in 2001, a PEN Freedom to Write award in 2002, and an Olaf Palme Prize in 2004. In 2007, she became the first person ever to receive a posthumous UNESCO/Guillermo Cano World Press Freedom Prize. https://www.rferl.org/a/russia-mobilizat.body: Russia Invades Ukraine From Central Asia To Russia For Work -- And Into The Military By RFE/RL's Kazakh Service and RFE/RL's Russian Service October 05, 2026 21:29 CET From Central Asia To Russia For Work -- And Into The Military Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Miras Tasharghanov, pictured here with his mother, Gulzhan Tasharghanova, thought he was going to be working in a Russian meat-processing plant. Instead he ended up in Ukraine with the Russian Army. Listen to this article 5 min This audio is automated Learn more Miras Taszharghanov traveled to the Russian city of Kursk on August 20 to work at a meat-processing plant, expecting to earn 90,000 rubles (about $1,000) a month. Instead, his family says, the 25-year-old Kazakh national was taken from his workplace directly to a military recruitment center, where he was forced to sign a contract with the Russian Army. “He told me, ‘They throw a contract at you, put a gun to your head, and tell you to sign, and that’s it. They didn’t even ask us whether we wanted to or not,’” said Tashzharghanov’s mother, Gulzhan Taszharghanova, describing a harrowing phone call with her son. Following a brief two-week military training period, Tashzharghanov was transferred to the Voronezh region, which borders Ukraine. Fearing her son would be deployed to the front lines as an assault trooper, Taszharghanova pleaded with authorities in Astana to intervene. In response to his case and others like it, Kazakhstan's Foreign Ministry announced that its embassy in Moscow sent a diplomatic note to the Russian Foreign Ministry on September 18, formally asking for the return of citizens who said they had been coerced into military service. But by early October, geolocation information Taszharghanov had sent to relatives indicated that he was near Bilolutsk in the Russian-occupied Luhansk region of Ukraine, RFE/RL’s Kazakh Service reported . His plight illustrates the risks facing some Central Asian migrants. Millions travel to Russia in search of livelihoods -- working in construction, agriculture, retail, and manufacturing. Uzbek migrant workers plant tomato seedlings in Astrakhan, Russia. (file photo) Rights advocates and migrants interviewed by RFE/RL have described cases in which foreign workers have faced pressure to join the Russian military. They say recruitment has taken place during police raids, workplace sweeps, at migration offices and in detention centers and prisons. Other migrants have been recruited with promises of large cash bonuses and fast-tracked Russian citizenship. Some sign up voluntarily, including for financial reasons, while others have alleged deception, threats, or physical coercion. SEE ALSO: Thousands Of Central Asians Enlisted To Fight Russia's War In Ukraine Through 'Coercion, Enticements' In September, a 44-year-old Uzbek migrant from Samarkand recounted being detained during a police raid in Rostov-on-Don over an expired work permit. He claimed that officers beat and pressured him until he signed a contract. After being deployed to the front line and wounded in the occupied Luhansk region, he spoke to RFE/RL’s Uzbek Service from a military hospital in St. Petersburg, begging the Uzbek government to help him return to his four children. For others, the realization comes too late. In Tajikistan’s northern Sughd region, a family recently buried their 58-year-old father whose body was returned from Ukraine in August, just months after he voluntarily signed a six-month contract. “He had financial issues, and going to Ukraine seemed to be a quick fix,” a source close to the family told RFE/RL on condition of anonymity. Pressure Takes Different Forms According to Russian migration-rights expert Valentina Chupik, recruitment tactics vary wildly: In some cases, she says, contracts are intentionally slipped into piles of routine paperwork that migrants sign at migration offices. In other cases, she alleges, coercion is explicitly violent. “There were mass raids, real torture with electric shocks and beatings,” Chupik told RFE/RL’s Russian Service, describing the measures allegedly used to force compliance. The reports of recruitment pressure come amid a broader, state-driven tightening of migration laws. Russian authorities have expanded workplace bans, stepped up deportations, and enforced stricter entry restrictions even as domestic industries face critical labor shortages. “Russia is not currently a safe country for Central Asian workers, and, naturally, where possible it is better to avoid traveling there,” warned Denis Jivaga, director of the Kazakhstan Bureau for Human Rights. SEE ALSO: Russia’s War Dead In Ukraine Believed To Include Hundreds Of Central Asians The true scale of foreign recruitment remains difficult to establish independently, as Moscow does not disclose comprehensive figures regarding foreign nationals serving in its armed forces. Ukraine's state-run I Want to Live project, which helps Russian soldiers surrender and tracks foreign nationals serving in Moscow’s military, said that as of May 2026, it had identified 12,919 citizens from Central Asian countries who had signed contracts with Russia's Defense Ministry. These figures have not been independently verified by RFE/RL. (Written and reported by Farangis Najibullah, with additional reporting by RFE/RL’s Azattyq Asia and RFE/RL’s Russian Service) From Central Asia To Russia For Work -- And Into The Military Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Follow us Facebook X (Twitter) Youtube Instagram Follow us Print RFE/RL's Kazakh Service RFE/RL's Kazakh Service offers informed and accurate reporting in the Kazakh and Russian languages about issues that matter in Kazakhstan, while providing a dynamic platform for audience engagement and the free exchange of news and ideas. https://www.rferl.org/a/iran-oil-petrole.body: Iran Tajikistan Begins Receiving Iranian Oil, Testing New Supply Route And Extent Of US Sanctions By Farangis Najibullah and RFE/RL's Tajik Service October 02, 2026 11:12 CET Tajikistan Begins Receiving Iranian Oil, Testing New Supply Route And Extent Of US Sanctions Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Tajikistan has asked Iran to supply up to 2.55 million tons of crude oil and petroleum products annually, including gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel. (file photo) Listen to this article 7 min This audio is automated Learn more Tajikistan announced that it is now receiving oil and petroleum products from Iran, opening a potential new energy source for a country whose fuel supplies have long been dominated by Russia. The deliveries began in late August, Tajikistan's Energy and Water Resources Ministry told the Asia-Plus news agency, following talks between the two countries on expanding cooperation in the oil and gas sector. The ministry has not disclosed the volume of the shipments, their commercial terms, or how the oil and petroleum products were transported to Tajikistan. The move also raises questions about potential US secondary sanctions for doing business with Iran, particularly as Washington has stepped up pressure on Tehran's oil revenues. A US Treasury official, who asked not to be identified, said the department would not comment on specific allegations of sanctions violations but warned that Iran's petroleum and petrochemical sectors are subject to increased sanctions risk. "Anyone operating in that sector incurs that risk themselves should they continue to choose to do so," the official said in an e-mailed response to RFE/RL. SEE ALSO: Amid Setbacks, Putin Looks To Restore Russia's Standing At Bishkek SCO Summit Tajikistan has asked Iran to supply up to 2.55 million tons of crude oil and petroleum products annually, including gasoline, diesel, and jet fuel. But that figure represents a requested or potential volume rather than the amount currently being delivered. The potential shift toward Iranian supplies could give Dushanbe another option, although the economics and logistics of moving large quantities of Iranian oil to landlocked Tajikistan remain unclear. The oil deal comes as Tajikistan faces continued uncertainty over fuel supplies from Russia, which accounted for more than 91 percent of the country's petroleum-product imports in the first half of 2026. Russian fuel shortages and export restrictions, exacerbated by Ukrainian drone strikes on Russian oil refineries, have prompted Tajikistan and other Central Asian countries to seek alternative sources. In July, Tajik authorities said they were in talks with neighboring countries to secure future supplies. Tajik political analyst Parviz Mullojonov said the search for Iranian supplies was being driven in part by Tajikistan's need to secure alternative energy sources. A Tajik delegation that visited Tehran in August held talks with Iranian officials responsible for oil products and railways, with energy supplies and logistics among the issues discussed, according to the Tajik Embassy in Tehran. Warming Relations The Iranian deliveries also come amid a broader warming of relations between Dushanbe and Tehran. "The report that Iran has started to sell oil to Tajikistan comes as the relation between Dushanbe and Tehran is warming and they're becoming closer," said Edward Lemon, president of the Oxus Society for Central Asian Affairs. Tajikistan and Iran, which share close linguistic and historic ties, established diplomatic relations in 1992. Tajikistan's Foreign Ministry says bilateral trade reached $438 million in 2025, up 28 percent from the previous year, and that the countries have signed more than 200 agreements and memorandums. At a meeting of the Tajik-Iranian intergovernmental commission in Dushanbe in May, officials discussed energy, transport, industry, investment, science, and technology. SEE ALSO: Central Asia's Fuel Crisis: The Cost Of Russian Dependence And Short-Term Thinking The two countries also have defense ties. In 2022, Iran and Tajikistan inaugurated a drone-manufacturing facility in Dushanbe, designed to produce Iranian-designed Ababil-2 drones. But relations between the two countries have not always been close. Ties deteriorated sharply in the mid-2010s, with Dushanbe wary of Tehran's alleged support for Tajikistan's banned Islamic Renaissance Party. In 2017, Dushanbe also accused Tehran of involvement in a series of political killings in Tajikistan in the 1990s, allegations that Tehran denied. The relationship began to thaw in the early 2020s. In 2022, Tajik President Emomali Rahmon visited Tehran, and the two sides pledged to strengthen diplomatic, trade, and security ties. The Sanctions Question A Tajik delegation that visited Tehran in August held talks with Iranian officials responsible for oil products and railways, with energy supplies and logistics among the issues discussed, according to the Tajik Embassy in Tehran. But closer energy cooperation with Iran could also create complications for Dushanbe as Washington increases pressure on Tehran. Under US Iran sanctions authorities, foreign companies and financial institutions can face sanctions for certain significant transactions involving Iranian petroleum and petroleum products. The US Treasury official also emphasized the secondary sanctions exposure for those who continue doing business with the Iranian regime and said any entity facilitating money laundering or sanctions evasion on behalf of Iran risks being cut off from the US financial system. SEE ALSO: Why China Is Unlikely To Pressure Iran Ahead Of Trump-Xi Summit The Treasury Department has repeatedly warned of sanctions exposure linked to Iranian oil and in August announced an expansion of conduct that could trigger secondary sanctions. A State Department spokesperson said in an e-mailed response to RFE/RL that the United States would continue to "disrupt, expose, and dismantle" Iranian military and proliferation activities, procurement schemes, malicious cyberoperations, and illicit oil trade that sustain what Washington calls the Iranian regime's "malign behavior." The spokesperson called on the international community to join the United States in holding those involved accountable. Lemon said the possibility of secondary sanctions should factor into Dushanbe's calculations as it expands purchases from Iran. "Tajikistan could of course become one of those countries," he said. At the same time, Lemon said, the scale of Tajik-Iranian cooperation could be important in determining how seriously Washington views the relationship. "The scale of cooperation is quite low, much in contrast to countries such as Russia or China," he said. Mullojonov said Tajikistan was seeking to balance relations with the United States, Russia, China, Turkey, and other powers while pursuing its own economic interests. "Maintaining a diplomatic balance is incredibly difficult because these global powers often have conflicting agendas," Mullojonov said. For now, it remains unclear whether Iranian oil can become a substantial alternative to Russian supplies. RFE/RL contacted Tajikistan's Energy and Foreign Affairs ministries for comment but has not received a response. https://www.rferl.org/a/rubio-russia-war.body: News Rubio Warns Russia's War Could Spill Beyond Ukraine's Borders By Alex Raufoglu October 08, 2026 18:06 CET Rubio Warns Russia's War Could Spill Beyond Ukraine's Borders Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Portuguese Foreign Minister Paulo Rangel (left) and US Secretary of State Marco Rubio leave after their joint press conference and meeting in Lisbon on October 8. LISBON -- US Secretary of State Marco Rubio warned that Russia's war against Ukraine is at a stalemate but could escalate into a broader regional conflict if the deadlock pushes either side toward increasingly dangerous actions. Speaking in Lisbon on the final stop of a three-country swing through NATO allies Iceland, Greece, and Portugal, Rubio said Washington believes the war ultimately requires a negotiated settlement and remains ready to facilitate diplomacy. His remarks came as a Russian strike on two buses in the Ukrainian city of Kramatorsk killed at least 33 people on October 8, according to local authorities. Embed share Russian Strike On Ukrainian Buses Kills More Than 30 Passengers In Kramatorsk by RFE/RL Embed share The code has been copied to your clipboard. width px height px The URL has been copied to your clipboard No media source currently available 0:00 0:01:28 0:00 Asked by RFE/RL about Russia's attacks on Ukraine and the security of NATO's eastern flank, Rubio called the conflict “a very dangerous war” that has reached reached a stalemate, which generally ends either through negotiations or escalation. The first option requires both sides to make difficult compromises. The second could involve Russia or Ukraine intensifying the conflict in an attempt to change the military balance. “That’s very dangerous,” Rubio said. He warned that escalation could include sabotage in neighboring NATO countries, a strike, or other actions that could rapidly widen the conflict. That could “quickly turn what is a war between two countries to a much broader, far more dangerous regional conflict,” he said. “In the end, we do not believe that there will be military solutions...We think this war needs to end, and the negotiated settlement is sooner and better.” Portugal's foreign minister backed diplomatic efforts to end the war, saying Russia's invasion violates international law and that any settlement should respect Ukraine's sovereignty. SEE ALSO: More Drones, More Missiles, No Air Defenses: Moldova In The Cross Fire Of Russia's War On Ukraine Rubio also recast the debate over NATO defense spending, describing increased military outlays as an investment in defense rather than simply “spending more.” He said stronger individual NATO members would strengthen the alliance and its deterrence. Rubio said NATO is fundamentally a defensive alliance and that its credibility depends on the capabilities of its members. “NATO is important. For NATO to matter, NATO has to be strong,” he said. “For NATO to be strong, NATO's member states need to be strong.” He said NATO members have different circumstances and cannot all contribute in the same way, but each should develop the strongest capabilities it can. “ He also called for greater cooperation on advanced military technology and the next generation of weapons, saying allies need to work together to meet future threats. Asked whether European allies could continue to rely on the US amid possible changes to the American military presence in Europe, Rubio stressed the importance of maintaining strong NATO capabilities and deterrence. He did not provide details on future US troop deployments but said the alliance's members share responsibility for maintaining its strength. Rubio also sharply criticized Iran when asked about concerns surrounding the use of Portugal's Lajes air base and allegations raised by Amnesty International over potential violations of international law. He declined to comment on a Portuguese investigation, saying it was a matter for Portuguese authorities. Rubio instead accused Amnesty International of failing to focus on alleged abuses by Iran's government against protesters, including the "murders in cold blood of tens of thousands of people in the streets.” “Those are war crimes. Those are crimes against humanity. Those are crimes committed against their own people,” Rubio said. https://www.rferl.org/a/ukraine-russia-e.body: Schemes: Investigating Ukraine Exclusive: 'Key Targets': A Russian Blueprint For A Cold, Dark Winter In Ukraine By Olya Ivleva , Kyrylo Ovsyaniy , Kira Tolstyakova , Valeriya Yegoshyna and Schemes October 08, 2026 17:21 CET Exclusive: 'Key Targets': A Russian Blueprint For A Cold, Dark Winter In Ukraine Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Kyiv's Darnytsia Thermal Power Station after a Russian attack in February. KYIV -- Early on September 30, Russia hammered Kyiv and the surrounding region with what Ukrainian Prime Minister Serhiy Koretskiy said was the most massive attack on energy infrastructure in the area since 2025. A child was found dead under the rubble of a home outside the capital – one of five people killed that day, officials said, and one of tens of thousands of civilian casualties in Russian attacks since the start of the full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022. Among the facilities targeted that day were two combined heating and power plants in Kyiv and a thermal power plant outside the city. Those three plants, and dozens of other vital pieces of infrastructure across Ukraine, are featured in a detailed document that sets out a potential blueprint for a campaign by Moscow to inflict enormous suffering on civilians with attacks aimed at sharply cutting supplies of power, heat, and water. Schemes, the investigative unit of RFE/RL’s Ukrainian Service, obtained a copy of the Russian-language document from sources in Ukraine’s defense forces. Emergency workers at a Kyiv aprtment building following a Russian missile strike in August 2025. The content suggested it is the same document that The New York Times , in a report last week that cited unnamed sources, said Ukrainian Energy Minister Denys Shmyhal showed European officials at a September 17 meeting in Paris. “I briefed our partners on Russia's plans to strike energy infrastructure, based on information provided by Ukrainian intelligence,” Shmyhal said in a Telegram post that day. The document obtained by Schemes identifies four “priority goals” -- power generation and supply, water supply, sewage systems, and heating. It contains an analysis of Ukraine's energy infrastructure and detailed calculations of the number of missiles, drones, and bombs Russia would need to cut power in Kyiv, Kharkiv, and Odesa by as much as 90 percent and drastically curtailing supplies of heat and water in those cities, which are Ukraine’s largest. Other "priority cities" include Dnipro, Zaporizhzhya, Mykolayiv, Kherson, Poltava, Chernihiv, Kryviy Rih, Cherkasy, Kropyvnytskiy, Lviv, Vinnytsia, and Ivano-Frankivsk. The Rivne Nuclear Power Plant in western Ukraine (file photo) A list of 60 “key targets” includes the three operating nuclear power plants that are controlled by Ukraine -- the Zaporizhzhya plant is occupied by Russia -- as well as 10 major hydroelectric power plants and dozens of other facilities. In addition to power plants and other infrastructure, the document indicates that one aim would be to disable substations, transmission lines, and interconnectors near the western border through which electricity is imported from Europe and distributed deeper in Ukraine. 'Cold, Precise' Shmyhal gave no details about the intelligence in his September 17 post, but in subsequent comments on national television, he indicated he had shown “two large [Russian] documents” to the Europeans at the meeting. "It shocked our partners, just as it did us, with its cynicism -- that cold, terrorist calculation of how to destroy our energy infrastructure.... The documents are drafted in a very cold, precise manner,” he said, according to RBC-Ukraine. “They include tables and specify the quantity of weaponry needed to destroy each target. The types of weapons range from ballistic missiles to jet-powered and conventional drones.” This description corresponds to the document obtained by Schemes. For example, it states that two Iskander missiles would be needed to take out one high-voltage installation that transmits electricity from a nuclear power plant. The document assesses power plants solely in terms of electricity consumption, making no mention of any potential threat from radiation, for example, but includes a fine-print warning that attacks with certain types of weapons on heating plants close to populated areas could cause civilian casualties. The document is titled Analytical Brief: Analysis Of Ukraine’s Power Generation And Utilities Sector, and is dated August 2026. The authors are not named in the copy obtained by Schemes, which is missing some pages, and the metadata has been altered. It does not indicate whom it was presented to in Russia. However, the brief itself cites sources of its data, including publicly accessible services such as OpenStreetMap and Worldometers as well as the official websites of Ukrainian power companies and the Energy Ministry. It also refers to "technical specifications of generating capacities" and the master plans of Kyiv and other cities. Most references cite assessments by unnamed experts or representatives of the Russian Armed Forces and an analysis by a "working group" whose members and affiliations are not identified. Russian officials have not commented on the document or on Shmyhal’s meeting with European energy officials in Paris last month. However, in early October, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov suggested that Russia would step up strikes on Ukrainian infrastructure, casting Russian attacks as “retribution” for Kyiv’s hits on Russian energy and logistics facilities. A Kyiv resident warms up by a fire in front of a veteran-run food truck during a power blackout following Russian strikes on civil infrastructure in January. Russia has been seeking to turn cold and darkness into weapons since the first year of the full-scale invasion: Attacks on power and energy infrastructure began in the initial weeks. By the autumn of 2022, it became a concerted campaign, and Ukraine’s first big blackout occurred that November. Each autumn has brought an upsurge in attacks. The Ukrainian Prosecutor-General’s Office told Schemes it is investigating 3,374 Russian strikes on 1,177 energy facilities in Ukraine. Ukrainian energy industry experts say that every month this summer and in September, Russia launched about 160 strikes against critical infrastructure outside the frontline zone -- meaning in and around cities far from the fighting on the ground. But analysts and military insiders said that they were familiar with similar documents from previous years and that it fell short of being an actual attack plan. 'Maximum Hardship' Similar documents “have been appearing -- at least to my knowledge -- since 2023,’” Oleksandr Kharchenko, director of the Kyiv-based Energy Industry Research Center, told Schemes. Some of the names of the weapons have changed and there have been “certain distinctions and differences” year to year, Kharchenko said. He added that "the briefing document underwent significant changes in 2024, but since then, I haven't really seen any major alterations." An Iskander missile at an arms show outside Moscow (file photo) Kharchenko also pointed to something that seems evident in the format and wording of the document. "This is not a combat order,” he said. “It is a document designed to demonstrate a concept to high-ranking Russian officials, intended to elicit a reaction like: 'Oh yes, we’ll destroy everything; the plan is excellent.'” Russia, he said, is “attempting to destroy critical infrastructure, cut off heat and electricity to key population centers, and cause us maximum hardship.” A Ukrainian defense industry representative whom Schemes asked to verify the document said he was already familiar with it. Speaking on condition of anonymity for security reasons, he also said it was not an operational combat plan, but a set of calculations. "It is a document used

https://www.rferl.org/a/mecca-alliance-i.body: News Analysis Testing Times For Mecca Alliance Partners As Iran-Aligned Houthis Mount Attacks By Daud Khattak October 07, 2026 15:25 CET Testing Times For Mecca Alliance Partners As Iran-Aligned Houthis Mount Attacks Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Fighters loyal to Iran-aligned Houthi rebels march during a rally last month to recruit more fighters in the Yemeni capital, Sanaa. Saudi Arabian allies Pakistan and Turkey are facing a major test just two months after signing a joint defense agreement as the rise of Iran-aligned Houthi rebels in Yemen test the deal, which says "any armed attack against any one of the three states shall be regarded as an attack against them all." As fighting between the Houthis and Saudi-backed government forces rages in Yemen, experts believe that any active military interference by Pakistan or Turkey -- the other two partners in the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement -- in support of Saudi Arabia, may heighten regional tensions amid the US-Iran conflict. "(The Islamic republic) can still support the Houthis but if Turkey and Pakistan enter (the war), the situation would become complicated," Frankfurt-based Middle East analyst Ali Sadrzadeh told RFE/RL's Radio Farda. SEE ALSO: Yemen Conflict Intensifies, Reverberating Beyond The Region The three sides held an emergency meeting in the Saudi capital, Riyadh, on October 5, the day Saudi-backed Yemeni government forces announced that they had secured effective control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, a claim denied by the Houthis. Last month, the Houthi rebels captured the Red Sea port city of Mocha and other areas around the strait, a key route for Saudi oil exports to Asia that has gained in importance with the disruption of shipments through the Strait of Hormuz because of the Iran war. The Houthis have also warned that Saudi airspace "will be the theatre of operations of our armed forces." The renewed fighting has displaced some 184,000 people and threatened shipping through the vital chokepoint linking the Red Sea and the Gulf of Aden. In an apparent reference to recent Houthi strikes on the Saudi cities of Mecca and Medina, two of Islam's most sacred locations, Saudi Defense Minister Prince Khalid bin Sultan said in a social media post that the alliance meeting "reaffirmed the solidarity and unity of our countries in confronting the heinous attacks against the Kingdom and the holy sites." He added that the three sides agreed to activate collective deterrence measures within the framework of the alliance in response to the attacks and "all those responsible for them." A Festering Conflict The conflict between Saudi Arabia and the Houthis has festered for years. Saudi Arabia launched a military intervention in Yemen in March 2015, after Houthi rebels seized the capital, Sanaa, and forced the internationally recognized government to flee the country. The conflict is widely viewed as part of the broader Saudi-Iranian rivalry, with the two countries backing opposing sides. Major fighting subsided after a UN-brokered truce in 2022, but the conflict was never fully resolved and has escalated again this year. Alarm bells rang when the Houthis last month stepped up attacks against Saudi targets, including a key oil pipeline, and advanced toward the Bab el-Mandeb Strait. A joint statement released after the emergency October 5 meeting stated that it was meant to address the "security developments and threats facing the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia." SEE ALSO: What Houthi Gains In Yemen Mean For The Iran War Experts believe the joint statement of the Mecca alliance, affirming the provision of "agreed military forces and capabilities" and their "rapid deployment in the Kingdom" is a clear declaration of support for Saudi Arabia in the face of increasing attacks from the Houthis. But they say such support also risks triggering another confrontation in the region. Sadrzadeh said that, although there are an estimated 30,000-40,000 Pakistani troops based in Saudi Arabia, he does not think the nuclear-armed country would agree to send forces to Yemen because Pakistan "wants to maintain its relationship with the Islamic republic." Just a day ahead of the emergency meeting, Iran Foreign Ministry spokesman Esmaeil Baqaei warned that any "new intervention" in (Yemen) would further complicate the situation. In a reference to Pakistan's reported deployment of troops in Saudi Arabia to fight the Houthis in Yemen, Baqaei said that "we hope that it is not true and really is just a rumor," adding that "any new intervention in developments related to Yemen would only make the situation more complicated." Rabia Akhtar, a professor of international relations at the University of Lahore, believes that Pakistani forces taking part in strikes against the Houthis could lead to a confrontation with Iran. "Tehran could see that as Pakistan joining a campaign against its regional interests, even if Islamabad insists that its involvement is limited to supporting Saudi Arabia," she told RFE/RL. Walking A Tightrope Nuclear-armed Pakistan shares a roughly 900-kilometer-long border with Iran along its southwestern frontier. Unlike its often-fraught relations with India and Afghanistan, its other two neighbors to the east and west, ties between Islamabad and Tehran are mostly stable. Akhtar said that Saudi Arabia is an important partner for Pakistan, but Iran is a neighbor and Islamabad "will have to live with the consequences of its decisions long after this particular episode ends." SEE ALSO: Saudi Arabia, Pakistan, Turkey Sign Joint Defense Pact Amid US-Iran Tensions Pakistan has been walking a tightrope by not taking sides since the United States and Israel launched air strikes on Iran on February 28. Despite maintaining traditionally close relations with Saudi Arabia and several other oil-rich Gulf countries, Pakistan has restricted itself mostly to statements of condemnation in the face of Iran's drone and missile attacks on its Arab neighbors over the past few months. Islamabad has also presented itself as a mediator and hosted the first-ever face-to-face talks between Iranian and US officials since 1980 in April. While experts see the October 5 emergency meeting of the Mecca alliance as a fresh escalation amid the regional hostilities, Khalid Sultan of the National University of Modern Languages believes that it should not automatically be interpreted as a precursor to a broader ground war in Yemen. "The (Mecca) agreement's significance lies not simply in military cooperation, but in the emergence of a collective regional deterrence mechanism," he told RFE/RL, adding that the success of the Mecca Joint Defense Agreement will ultimately be measured not by how quickly it enters a war, but by how effectively it prevents one. "For Pakistan, in particular, the policy challenge will be to honor its defense commitment to Saudi Arabia while avoiding an open-ended military entanglement in Yemen." Akhtar said any Pakistani participation in attacks on Houthis could undermine its role as a mediator with Tehran. "A clearly limited role in defending Saudi territory could remain compatible with mediation," she said. "Joining an offensive campaign in Yemen would make that position much harder to sustain." https://www.rferl.org/a/belarus-sanction.body: Belarus Sanctioned Belarus Trucks And A Mystery Logo: 'HAL' Vehicles Spotted In Minsk October 07, 2026 17:14 CET By RFE/RL's Belarus Service Photo: threads.com (Courtesy Image) Belarus Sanctioned Belarus Trucks And A Mystery Logo: 'HAL' Vehicles Spotted In Minsk October 07, 2026 17:14 CET By RFE/RL's Belarus Service Sanctioned Belarus Trucks And A Mystery Logo: 'HAL' Vehicles Spotted In Minsk Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Share Copy link Facebook X (Twitter) LinkedIn Email Share Prefer us on Google Fleets of unusual vehicles have been spotted in Minsk in recent days that may be linked to a murky trade deal with Indonesia. Trucks with a military color scheme and nearly identical to the Belarus-made MAZ-5316 have been seen sporting the logo "HAL" in place of the usual MAZ badge. The MAZ-5316 is a heavy-duty 4WD truck produced since the early 2000s by the Minsk Automobile Plant. The vehicles are used for civilian and military purposes, including as troop carriers . A 2016 file image of an MAZ-5316 in service with the Ukrainian military Sightings of HAL-branded vehicles first emerged this summer, when dozens of trucks covered with concealing material were spotted in Indonesia. Reports from the Asian country claimed the partially concealed vehicles were part of an order of some 1,500 Belarusian trucks for Indonesia's Defense Ministry. A screengrab of a video shows concealed trucks with the HAL brand. In May, an Indonesian delegation toured Belarus's MAZ plant as part of a trip to "explore the company's export potential." In July, Belarusian leader Aleksandr Lukashenko visited Indonesia to meet with the country's president, Prabowo Subianto. Belarus declared the primary purpose of the July trip to be "issues of bilateral military-technical cooperation" and "the deepening of industrial cooperation between Minsk and Jakarta." Indonesian Economics Affairs Minister Airlangga Hartarto inspects a MAZ truck during a trip to Belarus in May. So what is HAL, and why would Belarusian trucks sport the unfamiliar logo? Belarusian truck manufacturer MAZ is under EU and US sanctions, a status that blocks many countries from dealing with the company. Indonesia has not imposed sanctions against Belarus but faces the risk of secondary penalties for dealing with entities on Western blacklists. An Indonesian company called PT HAL Teknologi functions as a distributor for supplies of specialized equipment for defense agencies and other entities in the country, but it is unclear if the company has been involved in vehicle imports from Belarus. Uladzimer Zhyhar from BelPol, an organization of former Belarusian security officials, told RFE/RL's Belarus Service there is a history of sanctioned Belarusian businesses creating new branding to minimize the risk that purchasing countries will be stung for dealing with sanctioned entities. "Previously, they tried to organize something similar with [Belarusian heavy transport equipment company] BelAZ deliveries to Poland. They sold entire dump truck assemblies without labels, without the country of origin. And then it was all pieced together [in Poland], but the dump trucks were branded as something else," Zhyhar said. He added that for some militaries, the kinds of hardware produced in Belarus is desirable enough that risky, complex import schemes are deemed worthwhile. Factories such as MAZ, Zhyhar said, "generally produce a product that, I would say, belongs to previous generations. But this is exactly what some countries need, because the types of weapons that they have require exactly the older, 'quasi-Soviet' models," he said. An image shared on social media purporting shows a HAL-branded truck near the MAZ factory in Minsk. In some cases, Zhyhar said, products from sanctioned Belarusian companies have been paid for through bartering to avoid financial services that are closely watched by regulators. Belarusian state-linked brands order commodities up to the value of the products being exported, resulting in "goods, not money going to Belarus," Zhyhar said. The National Statistics Committee of Belarus has not published detailed data on foreign trade since 2021, but in 2020 Indonesia purchased 8 unidentified trucks from Belarus at a cost of $56,138 per vehicle. Recent reports from the Indonesian Statistics Service do not include information on truck deliveries from Belarus, though there is data on small deliveries of parts including brake systems and clutches. The Minsk Automobile Plant did not response to a query from RFE/RL's Belarus Service on whether MAZ was involved the production of trucks with the HAL logo. Amos Chapple contributed to this report.
