Share SGP 001 / 0926 / OBS 044 Criminalisation / Judicial harassment / Obstacles to the right to freedom of peaceful assembly Singapore 22 September 2026 The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership of the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), requests your urgent intervention in the following situation in Singapore . Description of the situation: The Observatory has been informed about the criminalisation and judicial harassment of Mr. Jolovan Wham , a social worker and human rights defender, Elijah Tay , a human rights defender, who identifies as non-binary, affiliated with the Transformative Justice Collective (TJC), a civil society group advocating for human rights and the abolition of the death penalty in Singapore, as well as two other TJC activists, Mses Kirsten Han and Kokila Annamalai . On 3 September 2026, Mr. Jolovan Wham and Elijah Tay received notices to attend court on separate dates in relation to multiple charges brought under the repressive Public Order Act (POA) and the Penal Code arising from their peaceful activism. On 7 September 2026, Mr. Jolovan Wham appeared before the State Court of Singapore, where he was charged under the POA and the Penal Code. Three charges under the POA concerned his participation in candlelight vigils held without permit near Changi Prison on 22 November 2024, 29 November 2024, and 23 January 2025, ahead of the executions of death row prisoners. A fourth charge under the POA concerned his organisation, on 3 February 2025, of a public assembly without a permit in a prohibited area, in relation to an assembly near the State Courts to advocate for the abolition of the death penalty. The fifth charge, brought under Section 179 of the Penal Code, concerned his refusal to answer questions from police during questioning about the vigil conducted on 22 November 2024. These charges followed five additional charges brought against Mr. Jolovan Wham under the POA on 3 February 2025, in connection with his participation in peaceful candlelight vigils held outside Changi Prison ahead of the executions of prisoners sentenced to death for drug trafficking in 2022 and 2023. Two of these charges were dropped. On 13 May 2026, Mr. Jolovan Wham was convicted on the remaining three offences. He was fined SGD 3,500 (approximately 2,379 Euros) per offence, amounting to SGD 10,500 (approximately 7,135 Euros) in total. Mr. Jolovan Wham is currently appealing his conviction. On 9 September 2026, Elijah Tay appeared before the State Court, and was charged on nine counts under the POA and the Penal Code. In addition to Elijah Tay, five other women, including one foreign national, were charged under the POA in relation to their organisation and participation in various public assemblies, including those in relation to the situation in Gaza. Four charges against Elijah Tay under the POA concern their participation in public assemblies without a permit, including a gathering to submit letters opposing the Maintenance of Racial Harmony Bill to the Ministry of Home Affairs in June 2024 and vigils for prisoners sentenced to death on 22 and 29 November 2024 and on 23 January 2025. Another charge under the POA concerns their participation in an assembly in a prohibited area without a permit, in relation to gathering near the State Courts on 3 February 2025 to advocate for the abolition of the death penalty. A further charge under the POA concerns the organisation of a memorial event without a permit in January 2025 featuring over 100 pairs of shoes and a white burial shroud in solidarity with Palestinian students killed in Gaza. Elijah Tay also faces two charges under Section 179 of the Penal Code concerning their refusal to answer questions from police about the vigils, as well as a charge under Section 298A of the Penal Code in relation to their pro-Palestine chant during an indoor Palestine-focused event on 2 February 2024, which was deemed by the authorities to be prejudicial to the maintenance of racial harmony that could disturb "public tranquillity." On 17 September 2026, Mses Kirsten Han and Kokila Annamalai as well as two other individuals were charged under the POA for their participation in a public assembly in a prohibited area. Their charges stemmed from a peaceful gathering on 3 February 2025 outside the State Courts to show support for Mr. Jolovan Wham, who attended a court hearing in relation to the five above-referenced charges brought against him under the POA. The Observatory recalls that Mr. Jolovan Wham has repeatedly faced judicial proceedings in connection with his peaceful human rights activities. In November 2017 , he was charged with three counts of organising public assemblies without a permit, one count of vandalism and three counts of refusing to sign statements, in relation to peaceful gatherings held between November 2016 and July 2017. In January 2019 , Mr. Jolovan Wham was also convicted of organising an illegal assembly without permit in relation to a public discussion on civil disobedience and social movements held in November 2016. His conviction and sentence were upheld on appeal in October 2019, when he was fined SGD 3,200 (approximately 2,070 Euros). Moreover, in March 2020, the Court of Appeal upheld a separate conviction and sentence against Mr. Jolovan Wham of SGD 5,000 (approximately 3,290 Euros) for “scandalising the court” over a Facebook post concerning the Singaporean and Malaysian judiciaries. The Observatory also recalls that the charges against Mr. Jolovan Wham and Elijah Tay took place in a context of extremely limited civic space in Singapore, where human rights defenders and civil society organisations have repeatedly faced restrictions and harassment in relation to the exercise of their rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly. In January 2025 , restrictions were imposed on activists from TJC in relation to their online advocacy against the death penalty. In October 2025 , Ms. Kokila Annamalai and two other TJC activists, Mses Siti Amirah Binte Mohamed Asrori and Sobikun Nahar, faced judicial harassment in connection with the organisation of a peaceful pro-Palestinian protest. The Observatory further recalls that the POA remains the legislative cornerstone of Singapore’s repression of the right to freedom of peaceful assembly, particularly due to its highly restrictive authorisation regime. The POA requires all individuals who seek to organise a public assembly to give advance notice and apply for permission from the Commissioner of Police no less than 14 working days before the planned event. Under the POA, the Minister of Home Affairs can issue orders that prohibit public assemblies or processions in “any public place” (defined as a “prohibited area”), if it is “in the public interest to do so”. The Commissioner of Police may refuse to grant a permit if there are “reasonable ground[s]” to believe that the proposed assembly may result in “public disorder”, “a public nuisance”, “an obstruction in any public road”, or “feelings of enmity, hatred, ill-will or hostility between different groups in Singapore”. All these broadly defined grounds significantly restrict the exercise of freedom of assembly in Singapore and do not appear to be necessary or proportionate, as required by international standards. The Observatory is concerned that the multiple criminal proceedings against Mr. Jolovan Wham, Elijah Tay, Ms. Kirsten Han, and Ms. Kokila Annamalai unduly restrict their rights to freedom of expression and freedom of peaceful assembly and contribute to a chilling effect on other human rights defenders in Singapore. The Observatory calls on the Singaporean authorities to immediately put an end to all acts of judicial harassment against Mr. Jolovan Wham, Elijah Tay, Ms. Kirsten Han, Ms. Kokila Annamalai, and other human rights defenders, and to ensure that they are able to carry out the

Share UGA 004 / 0826 / OBS 039 Arbitrary arrest / Arbitrary detention / Criminalisation / Restriction on freedom of peaceful assembly Uganda 24 August 2026 The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership of the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), requests your urgent intervention in the following situation in Uganda. Description of the situation: The Observatory has been informed about the arbitrary arrest and detention of four young environmental human rights defenders, Mr Ssembalirwa Aniwaly , Mr Mugoya Hassan , Mr Okanya Ivan and Mr Ariong Arone Patrick , members of the youth-led movement Rooted in Resistance , which advocates for greater accountability regarding Uganda's natural resources and for the protection of the environment. On 10 August 2026 at around 9:00 a.m., the four human rights defenders were peacefully marching along King George Way in central Kampala towards Parliament, where they intended to submit a petition calling for a new economic model centred on economic freedom and broad-based prosperity for Ugandans from the country's oil resources. They were reportedly wearing orange T-shirts bearing the words "Rooted in Resistance" and carrying placards stating, among others, "Prioritize other sectors of the economy", "Oil is Temporary, Nature is Permanent" and "Oil Today, Problems Tomorrow". Ugandan police intercepted and arrested the four activists during the peaceful march, after which they were taken to Central Police Station in Kampala. They were subsequently brought before the Buganda Road Chief Magistrate's Court in Kampala, before Grade One Magistrate Rophine Achayo, where they pleaded not guilty to charges of « public/common nuisance for allegedly disrupting traffic and creating road hazards » under the Road Act, Cap. 346 . On 10 August 2026, they were remanded to Luzira Maximum Security Prison, where they remain detained. Their next court hearing is scheduled for 28 August 2026. The arrests took place in the context of ongoing mobilisation by Rooted in Resistance concerning Uganda's oil sector and the environmental and social consequences of oil-related projects, including the East African Crude Oil Pipeline (EACOP) . The movement, formerly known as Students Against EACOP Uganda, has repeatedly organised peaceful protests and petitions concerning the project and the use of Uganda's natural resources. The Observatory recalls that these incidents illustrate a persistent pattern of harassment targeting those opposing EACOP and defending environmental and human rights. Environmental rights defenders in Uganda have, in recent years, repeatedly faced arbitrary arrests, judicial harassment, and torture. For example, on 9 August 2024 , 47 students were arrested in Kampala during a peaceful protest against the EACOP project. Between May and June 2024 , environmental activists like Adriko Sostein , Julius Tumwiine , and Stephen Kwikiriza were arrested and arbitrarily detained, as well as Bob Barigye , Noah Katiiti , Newton Mwesigwa , Julius Byaruhanga , Desire Ndyamwesigwa , Raymond Binntukwanga , and Jealousy Mugisha Mulimbwa . In April 2025, 11 environmental defenders, known as #KCB11 were arbitrarily arrested and detained following a peaceful protest denouncing the Kenyan Commercial Bank’s decision to fund EACOP. In October 2024, the United Nations Special Rapporteur on Human Rights Defenders sent a letter to the Ugandan government, raising concern about the increasing harassment of activists opposing the EACOP, particularly Students for Global Democracy. More recently, in April 2026 , eight young environmental defenders affiliated with Rooted in Resistance were convicted and sentenced to 11 months' imprisonment in connection with their participation in a peaceful protest against EACOP. These cases have occurred against a broader backdrop of increasing restrictions on civic space in Uganda, including in the context of the 2026 elections. Human rights defenders and other civic actors have increasingly faced arrests, judicial proceedings and other forms of intimidation in connection with their legitimate activities. In this context, the use of criminal proceedings and custodial sentences against environmental defenders opposing EACOP further raises concerns about the shrinking space for civic participation in Uganda. The Observatory also recalls that, as a State Party to the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), Uganda must respect and ensure the rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly (Articles 19 and 21), as well as the right to a fair trial (Article 14). The Observatory expresses its utmost concern over the arrest and detention of Mr Ssembalirwa Aniwaly, Mr Mugoya Hassan, Mr Okanya Ivan and Mr Ariong Arone Patrick in connection with their participation in a peaceful march to Parliament. The Observatory is also worried that their prosecution may have a chilling effect on civil society actors advocating for environmental protection and responsible management of Uganda's natural resources. The Observatory condemns the arbitrary arrest and detention and criminalisation of Mr Ssembalirwa Aniwaly, Mr Mugoya Hassan, Mr Okanya Ivan and Mr Ariong Arone Patrick, which appear to be linked to their legitimate activities as environmental human rights defenders. The Observatory urges the Ugandan authorities to immediately and unconditionally release them, drop all charges brought against them and guarantee in all circumstances that environmental human rights defenders are able to peacefully express their opinion and participate in public debate without fear of reprisals or judicial harassment. Actions requested: Please write to the Ugandan authorities urging them to: i. Guarantee in all circumstances the physical integrity and psychological well-being of Mr Ssembalirwa Aniwaly, Mr Mugoya Hassan, Mr Okanya Ivan and Mr Ariong Arone Patrick; as well as all human rights defenders in Uganda; ii. Immediately and unconditionally release Mr Ssembalirwa Aniwaly, Mr Mugoya Hassan, Mr Okanya Ivan and Mr Ariong Arone Patrick and drop all charges against them as their prosecution is solely linked to their legitimate activities and peaceful exercise of their rights; iii. Guarantee that Mr Ssembalirwa Aniwaly, Mr Mugoya Hassan, Mr Okanya Ivan and Mr Ariong Arone Patrick have immediate and unrestricted access to adequate food, healthcare, lawyers and family members, and ensure that their conditions of detention fully comply with international human rights standards; iv. Put an end to all acts of harassment, including judicial harassment against members of Rooted in Resistance and all environmental human rights defenders in Uganda, and guarantee that they are able to carry out their legitimate activities without fear of reprisals or intimidation; v. Ensure strict respect for fundamental freedoms, and in particular guarantee in all circumstances respect for the freedoms of peaceful assembly and expression, as guaranteed by international human rights law, in particular Articles 19 and 21 of the ICCPR, as well as the right to a fair trial, as guaranteed under Article 14 of the ICCPR; Addresses: • Mr Kaguta Yoweri Museveni, President of the Republic of Uganda, E-mail: [email protected] / [email protected] , X: @KagutaMuseveni • Ms Robinah Nabbanja, Prime Minister of the Republic of Uganda, Email: [email protected] , X: @RobinahNabbanja • Mr Adonia Ayebarer, Minister of Foreign Affairs of the Republic of Uganda, Email: [email protected] ; X: @UgandaMFA • Hon. Norbert Mao, Minister of Justice and Constitutional Affairs of Uganda, Email: [email protected] / [email protected] • Hon. Sam Mayanja, Attorney General of Uganda, Email: [email protected] / [email protected] • Ms Jane Frances Abodo, Director of Public Prosecutions, Ministry of Justice and Constitutional Affairs of Uganda, Email: [email protected] • Ms Mariam Fauzat Wangadya, Chairpe

Share BHR 001 / 0926 / OBS 043 Arbitrary arrest Arbitrary detention / Judicial harassment/ Bahrain 15 September 2026 The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership of the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), requests your urgent intervention in the following situation in Bahrain . Description of the situation: The Observatory has been informed of the arbitrary re-arrest of Mr Naji Fateel , a prominent Bahraini human rights defender and co-founder of the Bahrain Youth Society for Human Rights (BYSHR), more than two years after his release under a royal pardon. On 18 August 2026 at around 5:45am, plain-clothes police officers raided Mr Fateel's flat in Bani Jamra while he and his family were asleep and arrested him. According to the information received, the officers did not present a warrant or explain the reason for the arrest before taking him away, allowing him only enough time to dress before placing him in a police vehicle. His children and mother were reportedly left deeply frightened by the raid. It was only after Mr Fateel had been taken outside that officers informed him his arrest was related to an outstanding financial payment linked to one of the earlier cases against him. The Observatory notes that Mr Fateel had in fact engaged with the authorities on this very payment: he is reported to have spoken with officials on 16 August 2026 to document the amount owed with a view to reaching a settlement, and to have been told at the time not to attend the police station but instead to approach the Public Prosecution and the Sentence Enforcement Judge. Notwithstanding this, he was transferred on 20 August 2026 from East Riffa Police Station to Jau Prison, where he remains held. He is reportedly held together with at least three other former political prisoners detained over the same underlying issue, amid reports that further individuals have been arrested on the same grounds. Among the cases against him was the 2015 Jau Prison case, in which he was one of the 57 defendants convicted in 2016 over protests inside the prison. The defendants were collectively ordered to pay approximately USD 1.35 million (approximately 1,16 million Euros) in compensation for alleged damages, with Mr Fateel's individual share calculated at approximately USD 23,700 (approximately 20,355 Euros), payable in monthly instalments of approximately USD 996 (approximately 855 Euros). Individuals unable to meet these payments reportedly risk imprisonment. On 16 June 2026, Mr Fateel and a group of others facing the same fines wrote directly to the Crown Prince and Prime Minister, His Highness Salman bin Hamad Al Khalifa, copying the Ministers of Justice and Interior and the Sentence Enforcement Judge, asking the authorities to recognise the effect of the 2024 pardon on these outstanding penalties, to halt enforcement measures that could return them to prison, to clarify their legal position, and to ensure that no one released under the pardon would be imprisoned solely for being unable to pay. The Observatory further recalls that, in its Opinion No. 65/2022 of 14 November 2022, the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention (WGAD) found Mr Fateel's earlier deprivation of liberty arbitrary on account of violations of international fair-trial standards, called on Bahrain to release him immediately and unconditionally, and to provide him with an enforceable right to compensation and other reparations, and called for a full and independent investigation into the circumstances of his arbitrary detention and his allegations of torture. The Observatory is seriously concerned that Mr Fateel's arbitrary re-arrest, less than two and a half years after a royal pardon and while he was actively engaging the authorities in good faith over the payment in question, amounts to judicial harassment against him for his previous human rights activities, and that the enforcement of financial penalties tied to convictions covered by the pardon may be used as a tool for returning pardoned defenders to prison by other means. Therefore, the Observatory calls on the Bahraini authorities to immediately and unconditionally release Mr Naji Fateel and put an end to the judicial harassment he is facing in connection with his legitimate human rights activities. Actions requested: Please write to the Bahraini authorities asking them to: Guarantee in all circumstances the physical and psychological integrity of Naji Fateel and of all human rights defenders in Bahrain; Release immediately and unconditionally Naji Fateel and any other former political prisoners held over the same financial liabilities; Clarify without delay the legal effect of the April 2024 royal pardon on financial penalties arising from the pardoned convictions, and ensure that no individual is imprisoned solely for an inability to pay such penalties; Comply with the WGAD's November 2022 opinion, including by providing Naji Fateel with an enforceable right to compensation and by conducting a full and independent investigation into his earlier arbitrary detention and his allegations of torture; More generally, ensure in all circumstances that human rights defenders in Bahrain are able to carry out their legitimate activities without harassment or fear of reprisal. Share KEN 001 / 0226 / OBS 012.1 Denial of entry / Obstacles to freedom of expression / Restrictions on freedom of movement /Right to fair trial K enya/Ethiopia 30 September 2026 The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership of the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), has received new information and requests your urgent intervention in the following situation in Kenya . New information: The Observatory has been informed about the denial of entry and the continued arbitrary restriction of the freedom of movement of Mr Brian Kagoro, Zimbabwean human rights defender, constitutional lawyer, and Africa Director of the Open Society Foundations (OSF). On 15 September 2026, Mr Brian Kagoro travelled from South Africa via Addis Ababa, Ethiopia, to return to Kenya and attend proceedings concerning his detention and deportation from Kenya in February 2026 . While on board of a Nairobi-bound flight in Addis Ababa, Mr Kagoro was removed from the aircraft by Ethiopian security personnel, questioned and prevented from reboarding. He subsequently returned to South Africa. The circumstances and legal basis for his removal from the aircraft have not been publicly clarified. Mr Kagoro's attempted return took place after the High Court of Kenya at Nairobi had issued a conservatory order on 8 June 2026 providing that he was free to enter Kenya for as long as he complied with the immigration laws and procedures applicable to other nationals of Zimbabwe. The Court further directed the Kenya National Commission on Human Rights (KNCHR) to supervise and ensure compliance with the order and to designate an officer to facilitate oversight of Mr Kagoro's admission, entry and movement in Kenya. The order was issued in the context of a constitutional petition challenging Mr Kagoro's detention and deportation from Kenya. Following his removal from the flight, his legal team returned to the High Court to seek clarification and enforcement of the order. The Court subsequently directed Attorney General Dorcas Oduor to explain why Mr Kagoro continued to be denied entry into Kenya despite the existing court order, giving her 14 days to respond. The Observatory recalls that, on 22 February 2026 , Kenyan security authorities denied Mr Brian Kagoro entry into Kenya upon his arrival at Jomo Kenyatta International Airport in Nairobi. Officers from the National Intelligence Service (NIS) arbitrarily held him at the airport for more than 10 hours and questioned him over allegations that he had been involved in financing and coordinating protest activities in Kenya, while denying him access to a lawyer and preventing him from contacting his family or colleagues. Immigration officials subsequently issued a removal order authorising his return to Johannesburg, South Africa, citing Section 54 of the Kenya Citizenship and Immigration Act of 2011, without providing any written explanation of the factual basis. Mr Kagoro rejected the allegations, and no formal charges were brought against him. This removal in Ethiopia by Ethiopian security personal takes place in a context of increased transnational repression in East Africa with cooperation between several governments to attack human rights defenders and civic space. The Observatory also recalls that this case takes place in a context of increased scrutiny by Kenyan authorities of civic actors and alleged foreign involvement in protest movements, particularly following the 2024 nationwide demonstrations against the Finance Bill. The Observatory had also previously raised concern about the deportation of Mr Martin Mavenjina , a senior legal advisor at the Kenya Human Rights Commission (KHRC), from Kenya in July 2025. These developments raise serious concerns regarding the protection of civic space in Kenya and the ability of human rights defenders and civil society actors to operate without interference. The Observatory further recalls that Kenya must comply with its obligations under international and regional human rights law, including the rights to liberty, freedom of movement, freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and association, as enshrined in Articles 9, 12, 19, 21 and 22 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights (ICCPR), as well as in Articles 9, 10 and 11 of the African Charter on Human and Peoples' Rights (ACHPR). Moreover, Article 47 of the Kenyan Constitution guarantees the right to fair administrative action, including the right to written reasons where rights are adversely affected. The Observatory is gravely concerned that Mr Kagoro was prevented from travelling to Kenya despite a High Court order expressly authorising his entry into the country, and that he was removed from a Nairobi-bound flight by Ethiopian security personnel. The Observatory is further concerned by the clear signs of cooperation between Kenyan and Ethiopian authorities to impede Mr Kagoro's freedom of movement and expression, and by the lack of transparency regarding the circumstances and legal basis of his removal from the flight. The Observatory calls on the Kenyan authorities to fully respect the High Court order of 8 June 2026 and to refrain from any further arbitrary measures, including through cooperation with Ethiopian authorities,restricting Mr Kagoro's freedom of movement or preventing him from participating in the judicial proceedings concerning his case. Actions requested: Please write to the authorities of Kenya asking them to: Immediately ensure full compliance with and implementation of the High Court order of 8 June 2026, including by guaranteeing Mr Brian Kagoro's right to enter and move within Kenya in accordance with the terms of the order; Provide an official, transparent and legally reasoned explanation of the circumstances and legal basis for removing Mr Kagoro from the Nairobi-bound flight in Addis Ababa and preventing him from continuing his journey to Kenya; Ensure that Mr Kagoro is able to participate freely and without obstruction in the judicial proceedings concerning his detention and deportation from Kenya; Ensure that all measures taken in relation to Mr Kagoro fully comply with Kenya's obligations under the Constitution, the ICCPR and the ACHPR, including the rights to liberty, freedom of movement, freedom of expression, peaceful assembly and association, and the right to fair administrative action; Guarantee in all circumstances that human rights defenders, including foreign nationals engaging in legitimate civic activities, can carry out their work without arbitrary interference, harassment, intimidation, restrictions or reprisals; Please write to the authorities of Ethiopia asking them to: Clarify the circumstances and legal basis for Mr Kagoro's removal from the Nairobi-bound flight in Addis Ababa; Refrain from any measures aimed at harassing, intimidating or otherwise interfering with Mr Kagoro on account of his legitimate human rights activities; Ensure that no cooperation with foreign authorities results in reprisals or restrictions against Mr Kagoro in relation to his human rights activities; Addresses of Kenya: H.E. Share THA 001 / 0422 / OBS 027.1 Conviction / Sentencing / Judicial harassment / Thailand 4 September 2026 The Observatory for the Protection of Human Rights Defenders, a partnership of the International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH) and the World Organisation Against Torture (OMCT), has received new information and requests your urgent intervention in the following situation in Thailand . New information: The Observatory has been informed of the conviction and sentencing of Ms. Tantawan "Tawan" Tuatulanon, a student activist associated with pro-democracy groups Draconis Revolution and Thalu Wang (Shattering the Palace), who has advocated for the abolition of Article 112 of the Thai Criminal Code ( lèse-majesté ) and the reform of the Thai monarchy. On 31 August 2026, the Bangkok Criminal Court convicted Ms. Tantawan on charges under Article 112 of Thailand’s Criminal Code and Article 14(2) and (3) of the 2007 Computer Crimes Act and sentenced her to three years in prison, reduced to two years, over a Facebook livestream she conducted on 5 March 2022 from a footpath on Ratchadamnoen Nok Road, opposite the UN ESCAP building in Bangkok, shortly before a royal motorcade was due to pass. The court held her remarks were intended to insult the monarchy rather than constituting an exercise of freedom of expression. Ms. Tantawan was also fined 600 baht (approximately 15.57 euros) for failing to comply with the police order to stop the livestream. The court reduced the three-year sentence to two years in consideration of her useful testimony in the case. She was granted temporary release on a 100,000 baht (approximately 2,606 euros) bail the same day pending appeal. FIDH President Alexis Deswaef attended the hearing as a show of solidarity with Ms. Tantawan and all human rights defenders unjustly prosecuted on lèse-majesté charges. In a separate case, on 6 July 2026, the Bangkok South Criminal Court acquitted Ms. Tantawan and six co-defendants of charges under Article 112 and Article 116 (sedition) of the Criminal Code, brought over a public opinion poll on royal motorcades that the group had conducted outside a Bangkok shopping mall on 8 February 2022. The court held that the campaign, which invited the public to give their opinion by placing stickers on a whiteboard, amounted to an exercise of the constitutionally protected right to freedom of expression, and found that it did not directly refer to the King, Queen, heir apparent or regent. Proceedings against co-defendant Ms. Netiporn "Bung" Sanesangkhom had been discontinued following her death in custody on 14 May 2024. Between November 2020 and August 2026, 293 individuals have been charged under article 112, including 20 children. Of these, 31 are currently detained (12 pending trial, and 19 serving their final sentences). The Observatory recalls that the UN Working Group on Arbitrary Detention (WGAD), in its Opinion No. 49/2023, adopted on 30 August 2023, found Ms. Tantawan’s deprivation of liberty stemming from her Facebook livestream case, arbitrary. The Observatory strongly condemns the conviction and prison sentence against Ms Tantawan Tuatulanon as it appears to be solely aimed at punishing her for her legitimate human rights activities and the exercise of her rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly. The Observatory calls on the Thai authorities to immediately and unconditionally quash the conviction and sentencing and end all forms of judicial harassment against her and all pro-democracy activists currently prosecuted. Actions requested: Please write to the Thai authorities asking them to: i. Guarantee in all circumstances the physical and psychological integrity of Tantawan Tuatulanon and of all human rights defenders in Thailand; ii. Quash the convictions against Ms Tantawan, cease all acts of harassment, including at the judicial level, against her and all other human rights defenders and pro-democracy activists in the country; iii. Guarantee in all circumstances the rights to freedom of expression and peaceful assembly, as enshrined in Articles 19 and 21 of the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights, to which Thailand is a state party; iv. Amend Article 112 of the Criminal Code to bring it into line with Thailand’s human rights obligations under the International Covenant on Civil and Political Rights. v. More generally, ensure in all circumstances that human rights defenders in Thailand are able to carry out their legitimate activities without hindrance or fear of reprisal. https://www.amnesty.org/fr/latest/news/2.body: La campagne de plus en plus hostile menée par le gouvernement Trump contre la Cour pénale internationale (CPI) va bien au-delà des juges, des procureur·e·s et des groupes de défense des droits humains qu’il a sanctionnés, dissuadant la société civile d’engager le dialogue avec la Cour et compromettant l’accès des victimes à la justice, ont déclaré Amnesty International, la Fédération internationale pour les droits humains et 36 autres organisations de la société civile, mercredi 23 septembre. Nous n’allons pas rester les bras croisés pendant que le président Trump détruit le Statut de Rome Agnès Callamard, secrétaire générale d’Amnesty International Le 22 septembre 2026, 38 groupes de la société civile ont présenté un mémoire destiné à éclairer la cour fédérale du district sud de New York, dans le but de soutenir une procédure engagée par l’American Friends Service Committee, le Center for Constitutional Rights, Human Rights Watch et l’Open Society Institute, qui remet en question la légalité des sanctions imposées au titre du décret (EO) 14203. Ces sanctions visent des procureur·e·s et des juges de la CPI, une experte des droits humains auprès des Nations unies, et trois groupes palestiniens de défense des droits humains. « Derrière toute organisation de la société civile réduite au silence ou dissuadée de travailler avec la CPI, se trouvent des victimes attendant d’obtenir justice. Ces sanctions perturbent les réseaux de personnes et d’organisations qui soutiennent les victimes apportant leur vécu et leurs éléments de preuve devant la cour, et elles répandent la peur bien au-delà des individus directement pris pour cible », a déclaré Alexis Deswaef, président de la Fédération internationale pour les droits humains. « Pour des victimes ayant déjà été abandonnées par la justice de leur pays, la fermeture de ces voies d’accès peut signifier la perte d’une de leurs dernières possibilités d’obtenir des comptes. » « Alors que le gouvernement Trump intensifie ses attaques contre la CPI et les organisations de la société civile essentielles au travail de celle-ci, il est crucial de montrer à cette cour fédérale étasunienne à quel point ces sanctions portent préjudice à la société civile mondiale, aux victimes de crimes de droit international, et à l’idée même de la justice internationale », a déclaré Agnès Callamard, secrétaire générale d’Amnesty International. « Nous n’allons pas rester les bras croisés pendant que le président Trump détruit le Statut de Rome. Le nombre élevé d’organisations de la société civile ayant contribué à ce mémoire fournit la preuve de la résilience et de la détermination de la société civile à s’opposer aux sanctions étasuniennes et à protéger la CPI. » Le dossier avance deux arguments fondamentaux. Tout d’abord, les sanctions fracturent les réseaux de la société civile qui sont essentiels au fonctionnement de la CPI. Organisations de la société civile et défenseur·e·s des droits humains, parmi lesquels des avocat·e·s, des représentant·e·s de victimes, et des victimes s’exprimant en leur propre nom, effectuent toutes sortes d’activités dont la CPI dépend : rapprocher victimes et témoins de la Cour ; recueillir des informations sur des crimes au regard du droit international ; soutenir la participation des victimes et l’obtention de réparations ; apporter une expertise juridique, contextuelle et culturelle essentielle ; et faire progresser la coopération de l’État, et les enquêtes et poursuites menées au niveau national, en particulier dans les pays auxquels la Cour a un accès restreint. Il est crucial de montrer à cette cour fédérale étasunienne à quel point ces sanctions portent préjudice à la société civile mondiale, aux victimes de crimes de droit international Agnès Callamard, Amnesty International Ensuite, en infligeant ou menaçant d’infliger des sanctions financières et judiciaires draconiennes à des organisations de la société civile et à des acteurs individuels, le décret 14203 porte atteinte aux droits à la liberté d’expression et d’association, et a grandement fragilisé le travail collaboratif et l’infrastructure dont dépend le système international de justice. Le décret EO 14203 a déjà : causé la perte, pour les entités concernées, de financements, de personnels, d’accès bancaire et de partenariats ; dissuadé des organisations de la société civile d’engager le dialogue avec la CPI ; et rompu des relations entre et au sein de nombreuses organisations de la société civile. En ont résulté des préjudices mesurables et irréparables, non seulement pour la société civile, mais également pour la CPI, l’administration de la justice pénale internationale et, au bout du compte, pour les victimes que ce système a été conçu pour servir. Complément d’information Les 38 organisations de la société civile présentant le mémoire sont : 1. Action for the Reform of Justice and Promotion of Human Rights (ARJPDH) 2. Amnesty International 3. Centre arabe pour l’indépendance de la profession judiciaire et juridique 4. Coalition arabe pour la Cour pénale internationale 5. Baltasar Garzón International Foundation (FIBGAR) 6. Center for Development of International Law (CDIL) 7. Center for Justice and Accountability (CJA) 8. Centre marocain pour la loi et la paix 9. Centro de Investigación y Promoción de los Derechos Humanos (CIPRODEH) 10. Chinese Initiative on International Law (CIIL) 11. Clinique de droit international pénal et humanitaire, Faculté de droit, Université Laval (CDIPH) 12. COMPPART Foundation for Justice and Peacebuilding-Nigeria 13. Croatian Helsinki Committee for Human Rights 14. Egyptian Initiative for Personal Rights (EIPR) 15. Centre européen pour les droits constitutionnels et les droits humains (ECCHR) 16. Global Justice Center 17. Human Rights Now 18. HuMENA for Human Rights and Civic Engagement 19. Indonesian Legal Aid Association for Women (APIK) 20. Fédération internationale pour les droits humains (FIDH) 21. Le Réseau international pour les droits économiques, sociaux et culturels (Réseau-DESC) 22. Just Access 23. Kurdish Organizations Network Coalition for the International Criminal Court (KONCICC) 24. Lawyers’ Rights Watch Canada 25. Libya Crimes Watch (LCW) 26. No Peace Without Justice 27. The Nuhanovic Foundation 28. Philippine Alliance of Human Rights Advocates (PAHRA) 29. Platform for Peace and Humanity 30. Refugees in Libya 31. Rights for Peace 32. Robert & Ethel Kennedy Human Rights Center 33. StoptheDrugWar.org 34. Students for Global Democracy Uganda 35. Syrian Center for Media and Freedom of Expression (SCM) 36. Women’s Initiatives for Gender Justice 37. Organisation mondiale contre la torture (OMCT) 38. World Without Genocide Le secrétariat de la Coalition pour la Cour pénale internationale, dont le rapport sur les sanctions imposées par les États-Unis, Criminalising Accountability: The US lawfare against the international justice system , a constitué une référence clé, a aimablement apporté son concours dans le cadre de la présentation du mémoire destiné à éclairer la cour, compilé par ces organisations de la société civile. Les organisations ont été représentées par le cabinet d’avocats Mascarenhas Law PLLC.

À la veille des matchs d’ouverture de la phase de poules de la Ligue des Nations masculine de l’UEFA 2026/27, au cours desquels l’Autriche, l’Irlande et le Kosovo affronteront Israël pendant la trêve internationale du 24 septembre au 6 octobre, Steve Cockburn, directeur régional pour l’Europe à Amnesty International, a déclaré : « Il est inadmissible que l’équipe de football masculine israélienne participe à la Ligue des Nations de l’UEFA cet automne, alors qu’il est démontré que la Fédération israélienne de football continue de soutenir les colonies illégales. « Au lieu d’envoyer un message clair indiquant qu’Israël doit assumer les conséquences de son occupation illégale du territoire palestinien et des crimes atroces commis à l’encontre des Palestinien·ne·s, l’UEFA lui offre une tribune internationale alors que l’occupation violente du territoire palestinien, le système d’apartheid imposé à tous les Palestinien·ne·s et le génocide touchant les Palestinien·ne·s de la bande de Gaza se poursuivent. « L’UEFA et la FIFA auraient dû suspendre depuis longtemps la Fédération israélienne de football (IFA), car elle a refusé d’exclure les clubs installés dans des colonies illégales du territoire palestinien occupé. Leur participation aux compétitions israéliennes bafoue les statuts de la FIFA et est contraire au droit international. En continuant de verser des fonds à l’IFA, la FIFA et l’UEFA risquent de contribuer à la pérennité des colonies illégales et à l’occupation illicite du territoire palestinien par Israël, et donc aux violations des droits des Palestinien·ne·s imputables à Israël. « Les décisions et avis rendus par les tribunaux internationaux, ainsi que les résolutions adoptées par l’Assemblée générale et le Conseil de sécurité des Nations unies au cours des dernières décennies, ont condamné à plusieurs reprises Israël pour ses violations multiples et flagrantes. « Le sport ne doit jamais servir de tribune de relations publiques à des États qui se livrent à des atrocités. Alors que l’équipe israélienne se rend en Europe, des familles palestiniennes sont déplacées et dépossédées : leurs terres sont volées, leurs oliviers déracinés et leur histoire effacée par des colons, avec le soutien de l’armée israélienne. » Le beau jeu » (le football) devrait rassembler les gens, et non valider l’apartheid Steve Cockburn, directeur régional pour l’Europe à Amnesty International « Alors que les leaders politiques et les instances sportives choisissent de rester sur le banc de touche, favorisant ainsi l’impunité d’Israël, les supporters envahissent le terrain pour exiger des comptes, la justice et le fair-play. Lorsque les règles sont bafouées, lorsque l’occupation, l’apartheid et le génocide se poursuivent, nous ne pouvons pas détourner le regard. » Complément d’information L’équipe masculine israélienne de football participera aux prochains matchs de poules de la 5 e édition de la Ligue des Nations de l’UEFA. Ces rencontres se dérouleront en deux temps : les quatre premiers matchs auront lieu du 24 septembre au 6 octobre, et les deux derniers du 12 au 17 novembre 2026. Israël évolue en Ligue B, aux côtés de l’Autriche, de l’Irlande et du Kosovo. En Irlande, la participation d’Israël à des compétitions de football suscite une forte opposition de la part de l’opinion publique, dans le cadre de la campagne Stop the Game . Des fédérations de football, joueurs·euses, militant·e·s, syndicats, artistes et responsables politiques ont appelé à des sanctions, au boycott ou à la suspension des prochains matchs entre l’Irlande et Israël, prévus les 27 septembre et 4 octobre. La Fédération d’Irlande de football ( FAI ) a officiellement demandé à l’UEFA d’envisager la suspension d’Israël des compétitions qu’elle organise. Toutefois, l’UEFA a validé le calendrier de la Ligue des Nations et l’utilisation de « terrains neutres » si besoin, dans des pays autres qu’Israël et l’Irlande. Les matchs entre l’Irlande et Israël doivent se dérouler en terrain neutre, en Hongrie et en Serbie, à huis clos, sans supporters dans les stades. En octobre 2025, Amnesty International avait adressé un courrier à la FIFA et l’UEFA pour demander la suspension de la Fédération israélienne de football (IFA), à moins que les clubs venant des colonies illégales du territoire palestinien occupé ne soient immédiatement exclus des championnats nationaux israéliens. En mars 2026, la FIFA a annoncé qu’aucune mesure ne serait prise à l’encontre de l’IFA quant à la participation aux compétitions israéliennes de clubs installés dans des colonies illégales. Par cette prise de position, la FIFA légitime indirectement l’occupation illégale imposée par Israël et les graves atteintes aux droits humains contre des Palestiniens, notamment le crime contre l’humanité d’apartheid, et risque de contribuer à ces agissements, tout en ignorant l’avis consultatif rendu en 2024 par la Cour internationale de justice. Suite à la décision de la FIFA de rejeter les plaintes concernant les clubs des colonies israéliennes, la Fédération palestinienne de football a soumis le cas au Tribunal arbitral du sport (TAS). Dans son récent rapport intitulé Éradiquer toute présence palestinienne : le nettoyage ethnique des communautés bédouines et pastorales de Cisjordanie par Israël , Amnesty International indique que le gouvernement israélien actuel a fait de l’annexion officielle, en vertu du droit israélien, des terres palestiniennes situées dans le territoire palestinien illégalement occupé un objectif explicite de sa politique, dont la mise en œuvre a été accélérée, notamment par le biais de violences imputables à des colons soutenus par l’État.

Le 13 septembre, à mon réveil, alors que je me trouvais dans le sud-ouest de la Turquie, j’ai appris qu’une opération de grande envergure visait les organisations LGBTI et les défenseur·e·s des droits humains dans tout le pays. Depuis, la police a arrêté au moins 116 personnes dans 15 provinces à la suite de descentes chez des particuliers, dans des lieux de rassemblement et dans les bureaux d’organisations de défense des droits des personnes LGBTI. Au moins 83 personnes ont été placées en détention provisoire, et plus de 160 font l’objet d’une enquête pénale. Des organisations de défense des droits des personnes LGBTI ont fait état d’allégations de fouilles au corps intrusives, d’insultes et d’humiliations, ainsi que de cas de défenseur·e·s des droits humains détenus à l’isolement en violation de leurs droits. Des centaines de comptes sur les réseaux sociaux appartenant à des organisations et militant·e·s LGBTI, à des journalistes et à des médias, entre autres, ont été bloqués ou soumis à des restrictions, de même que des sites Internet. Le compte d’Amnesty International Turquie sur X fait partie de ceux qui sont concernés. Alors que les manifestations prennent de l’ampleur en Turquie et que les condamnations internationales se multiplient, il apparaît clairement que les autorités turques ont bien l’intention d’intensifier la répression Milena Buyum, Amnesty International Les autorités ont baptisé cette opération « Ailem Güvende » (« Ma famille est en sécurité ») sous le prétexte fallacieux de « protéger la famille ». Or, comme le soulignent à juste titre des militant·e·s LGBTI et bien d’autres, les familles en Turquie souffrent de la pauvreté, de l’insécurité et d’une répression croissante de leurs droits civils et politiques, et la violence contre les femmes et les filles est endémique, y compris au sein de leur foyer. Cette répression de grande envergure, qui n’a rien à voir avec la protection des familles, ne fait que nuire davantage encore à des personnes qui luttent depuis des décennies contre la discrimination et l’intimidation. Alors que les manifestations prennent de l’ampleur en Turquie et que les condamnations internationales se multiplient, il apparaît clairement que les autorités turques ont bien l’intention d’intensifier la répression. Le ministère de la Justice a adressé une circulaire à 175 parquets généraux dans les 81 provinces de la Turquie concernant les contenus et activités qu’il juge contraires à la « morale publique » et préjudiciables aux familles, aux enfants et aux jeunes. Cette circulaire les charge d’examiner sans délai les plaintes et les signalements, de prendre immédiatement des mesures pour mener des investigations, de conserver les preuves numériques et, si nécessaire, de demander le retrait ou le blocage de contenus en ligne pour le motif vague d’« obscénité ». La police aurait utilisé du gaz poivre contre des manifestant·e·s pacifiques à İzmir, et plus d’une centaine de personnes auraient été arrêtées alors qu’elles se rassemblaient pacifiquement devant le palais de justice d’Istanbul, dans le quartier de Çağlayan. Alors que des manifestations sont attendues dans tout le pays dans les jours et les semaines à venir, de nouvelles arrestations sont à craindre. Cette répression s’inscrit dans le cadre d’une vaste offensive contre les droits des personnes LGBTI et contre celles et ceux qui défendent ces droits. Les marches des fiertés, notamment celle d’Istanbul, sont interdites depuis 2015. Au cours des deux dernières années, des propositions visant à réprimer pénalement, avec des sanctions, l’expression des identités LGBTI et les relations sexuelles consenties entre personnes du même sexe ont à plusieurs reprises été divulguées et portées à la connaissance du public. Elles ont été retirées à la suite d’un tollé général et de la résistance de la société civile. Si ces manœuvres législatives du gouvernement ont échoué, l’opération « Ma famille est en sécurité » constitue une nouvelle tentative d’exclure les personnes LGBTI. Le mois de juillet a marqué le 10 e anniversaire de la tentative de coup d’État manquée qui a entraîné l’adoption de dispositions sur l’état d’urgence restées en vigueur pendant deux ans. Ces dispositions se sont transformées en une série de lois répressives visant la société civile, avec un affaiblissement de l’indépendance du pouvoir judiciaire, une instrumentalisation des tribunaux nationaux, un dédain pour les tribunaux internationaux et le non-respect des traités et des normes. La Turquie a connu au cours de la dernière décennie un embrasement autoritaire persistant qui atteint tous les aspects de la société turque, réduisant au silence la dissidence, attisant les divisions et semant la peur. Des milliers de personnes en Turquie ont fait l’objet de poursuites judiciaires et de condamnations sans fondement, avec plusieurs affaires emblématiques. Le prisonnier d’opinion Osman Kavala, qui est toujours emprisonné malgré deux arrêts contraignants de la Cour européenne des droits de l’homme (CEDH) rendus en 2019 et 2026 ordonnant sa libération, et malgré une procédure d’infraction engagée contre la Turquie par le Conseil de l’Europe en 2022. Selahattin Demirtaş et Figen Yüksekdağ, anciens dirigeant·e·s du Parti démocratique des peuples, sont eux aussi toujours en prison malgré des arrêts de la CEDH ordonnant leur libération immédiate. Taner Kılıç , président honoraire d’Amnesty International Turquie, a été jugé aux côtés d’ İdil Eser , ancienne directrice d’Amnesty International Turquie, et de neuf autres défenseur·e·s des droits humains, appelés « les 10 d’Istanbul », sur la base d’allégations sans fondement d’« appartenance à une organisation terroriste ». Ces personnes ont finalement toutes été acquittées, l’acquittement de Taner Kılıç intervenant près de huit ans après son arrestation, en 2017, qui a été suivie de 14 mois de détention. Les droits à la liberté de réunion pacifique, d’association et d’expression font l’objet d’offensives persistantes, avec des restrictions arbitraires et des interdictions généralisées. Les manifestant·e·s pacifiques se heurtent aux violences policières et seraient torturés en détention aux mains de la police. Les marches organisées pour la Journée de la femme ont également fait l’objet d’interdictions, alors que les droits des femmes et des filles subissent une grave érosion. En 2021, la Turquie s’est retirée de la Convention d’Istanbul, un traité historique visant à prévenir et à combattre la violence à l’égard des femmes et la violence domestique. Ce faisant, la Turquie est non seulement devenue le premier membre du Conseil de l’Europe à se retirer d’une convention internationale relative aux droits humains, mais elle a également supprimé des protections essentielles dans un pays où la violence liée au genre reste pourtant endémique. Il est temps de nous unir contre la répression des personnes LGBTI en Turquie Milena Buyum, Amnesty International Dix ans après la tentative de coup d’État manquée, le chemin parcouru par la Turquie sur la voie de l’autoritarisme est flagrant, mais cette trajectoire peut encore être inversée. Les mesures visant les communautés LGBTI doivent cesser immédiatement et les autorités turques doivent garantir la libération immédiate de toutes les personnes détenues uniquement en raison de leur action en faveur des droits humains. Les défenseur·e·s et associations LGBTI doivent être autorisés à exercer leurs activités et à mener à bien leur travail essentiel sans faire l’objet d’une discrimination ni d’une répression pénale, de manœuvres d’intimidation ou de représailles. Vendredi, des personnes sont descendues dans les rues dans plus de 50 villes à travers le monde pour réclamer la fin de la répression. Il est temps de nous unir contre la répression des personnes LGBTI en Turquie, de faire entendre nos voix et de rendre notre solidarité encore plus visible. Les dirigeant·e·s du monde entier doivent condamner publiquement cette répression,

Après l’ annonce de la dissolution du Gouvernement d’union nationale de transition du Soudan du Sud , une étape décisive vers les premières élections du pays, prévues pour le 22 décembre, Tigere Chagutah, directeur régional pour l’Afrique de l’Est et l’Afrique australe à Amnesty International, a déclaré : « En prévision de ces élections historiques et attendues de longue date, les autorités du Soudan du Sud doivent garantir qu’un environnement propice soit établi afin que les personnes puissent voter et se présenter aux élections, notamment en veillant à ce que les droits humains soient respectés et puissent être exercés, et à ce que personne ne soit victime de discriminations ou de restrictions injustifiées et disproportionnées. « La légitimité de toute élection dépend non seulement de sa tenue, mais également de la possibilité pour les personnes d’exercer leurs droits librement, en sécurité et en toute égalité. Cela fait des années qu’Amnesty international et d’autres organisations recensent les tactiques répressives déployées par les autorités du Soudan du Sud pour réduire l’opposition au silence, arrêter les personnes qui les critiquent et restreindre la liberté d’expression et le droit de manifester. En prévision de ces élections historiques et attendues de longue date, les autorités du Soudan du Sud doivent garantir qu’un environnement propice soit établi afin que les personnes puissent voter et se présenter aux élections, notamment en veillant à ce que les droits humains soient respectés et puissent être exercés, et à ce que personne ne soit victime de discriminations ou de restrictions injustifiées et disproportionnées Tigere Chagutah, directeur régional pour l’Afrique de l’Est et l’Afrique australe à Amnesty International « En ce moment crucial, nous demandons aux autorités du Soudan du Sud de : garantir immédiatement les droits à la liberté d’expression, d’association et de réunion pacifique ; faire cesser les menaces visant les journalistes, les acteurs de la société civile et les opposant·e·s politiques, ; et créer des conditions permettant à tous les habitant·e·s du Soudan du Sud de participer aux affaires publiques librement et sans crainte. » Complément d’information Le 21 septembre, le président Salva Kiir Mayardit a promulgué un projet de loi de modification de la Loi de 2012 relative aux élections nationales, qui l’habilite à rester en exercice tout en conservant ses pleins pouvoirs constitutionnels, tout au long de la période électorale, et l’autorise à dissoudre le gouvernement de transition. En août, la Commission des Nations Unies sur les droits de l’homme au Soudan du Sud a indiqué que des élections menées en l’absence de garanties adéquates pourraient alimenter un renouvellement du conflit et aggraver le risque de graves violations des droits humains et d’atrocités. En juillet, sur fond d’ inquiétudes relatives aux procédures , à la légalité et à la légitimité, le président Salva Kiir Mayardit a promulgué des modifications apportées à l’accord de paix de 2018, supprimant des conditions préalables cruciales à la tenue d’élections, notamment un recensement national de la population et des logements, et l’adoption d’une Constitution permanente, reportant ces deux processus à la période post-électorale.

En réaction à la déclaration de la Banque centrale d’Irlande qui a confirmé que la commercialisation en Europe des « Israel Bonds » (obligations émises par l’État israélien) prend fin à l’expiration du prospectus les concernant, Stephen Cockburn, directeur pour l’Europe à Amnesty International, a déclaré : « Ce résultat témoigne de la persévérance des militant·e·s qui manifestent devant la Banque centrale depuis plus d’un an, avec le soutien des parlementaires qui n’ont cessé de faire pression au sein des sphères du pouvoir pour que l’Irlande respecte le droit international, et de tous ceux qui se sont élevés contre la vente de ces obligations en Europe. La confirmation le 23 septembre 2026 de la fin de la commercialisation des “Israel Bonds” en Europe illustre ce que la solidarité peut accomplir Stephen Cockburn, directeur pour l’Europe à Amnesty International « Les États sont clairement tenus d’agir pour mettre un terme aux violations commises par Israël à l’encontre des Palestinien·ne·s. Refuser toute implication dans le génocide, l’apartheid et les crimes internationaux perpétrés par Israël exige du courage et de la détermination, tandis que des États en Europe continuent de réprimer ce militantisme essentiel. « La confirmation le 23 septembre 2026 de la fin de la commercialisation des » Israel Bonds » en Europe illustre ce que la solidarité peut accomplir. Nous devons continuer de parler de la vie des Palestinien·ne·s et de rejeter la complaisance et la complicité. » Complément d’information Pour commercialiser ces obligations dans l’Espace économique européen (EEE), le prospectus concernant les « Israel Bonds » doit être approuvé par l’autorité compétente d’un État membre de l’Union européenne (UE). Depuis 2021, l’Irlande est l’« État membre pays d’accueil » des « Israel Bonds ». En raison de la pression de l’opinion publique suscitée par le génocide perpétré par Israël à l’encontre de la population palestinienne dans la bande de Gaza occupée, la Banque centrale d’Irlande a transféré en 2025 le prospectus au Luxembourg et son autorité financière compétente l’a approuvé. Ce prospectus a expiré le 31 août 2026. En juillet, l’organisme de régulation des marchés financiers du Luxembourg a refusé d’approuver le prospectus pour une nouvelle année. Cette décision a été prise en raison de la pression croissante exercée par la société civile et des experts juridiques. Ils se sont mobilisés et ont publié des recherches afin d’étayer leur demande soumise aux autorités pour stopper la vente des obligations. Amnesty International demande à l’Irlande, au Luxembourg et à tous les États membres de l’UE de ne plus autoriser la vente des « Israel Bonds » en Europe.

https://odihr.osce.org/odihr/668379.body: Press release ODIHR and Kazakhstan’s Human Rights Commissioner renew co-operation on human rights Date: 8 October 2026 Place: WARSAW Source: OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights WARSAW, 8 October 2026 – The OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights (ODIHR) and the Commissioner for Human Rights in the Republic of Kazakhstan today signed a new agreement to continue their co-operation in protecting and promoting human rights. The Memorandum of Understanding was signed in Warsaw by ODIHR Director Maria Telalian and Kazakhstan’s Commissioner for Human Rights, Artur Lastayev. It sets out a framework for co-operation until the end of 2030. “Independent national human rights institutions have an important role in protecting human rights and ensuring that OSCE commitments and international standards are reflected in law and practice,” said ODIHR Director Maria Telalian. “This Memorandum provides a practical framework for continuing our co-operation with the Commissioner’s Office, strengthening its effectiveness in promoting and protecting human rights, in line with ODIHR’s mandate.” Areas for co-operation include capacity-building for the Commissioner’s Office, legal opinions on draft or existing legislation upon official request, human rights education and engagement with civil society. The memorandum also covers the strengthening of the protection of human rights defenders, torture prevention and the National Preventive Mechanism, as well as human rights challenges arising from digital technologies. “Our institution has been granted guarantees of independence, an expanded mandate, and a stronger institutional framework, supported by a nationwide network of regional offices. We continue to strengthen the National Preventive Mechanism, work to prevent torture and domestic violence, and protect the rights of vulnerable groups,” said Artur Lastayev, the Commissioner for Human Rights. “The Memorandum we are signing today lays a solid foundation for further deepening our co-operation in improving legislation and advancing human rights education.” The agreement also provides for consultations and dialogue involving the Commissioner’s Office, relevant public institutions, civil society organizations and experts. https://odihr.osce.org/odihr/668244.body: Press release Genuine competition in Bosnia and Herzegovina’s elections in fragmented political environment and with difficulties in electoral administration, international observers say Date: 5 October 2026 Place: SARAJEVO Source: OSCE Office for Democratic Institutions and Human Rights SARAJEVO, 5 October 2026 – There was genuine competition in Bosnia and Herzegovina’s 4 October general elections and contestants were largely able to reach voters. The political landscape is deeply fragmented, characterised by conflicting narratives still rooted in wartime divisions, the international election observers said in a statement of preliminary findings and conclusions today. The first-time countrywide use of information and communication technologies (ICT) was introduced to address longstanding electoral integrity concerns, although delays and shortfalls limited transparency in the implementation stage, the statement says. The election administration made considerable efforts, but persistent institutional and operational constraints, combined with its increased responsibilities, affected the efficiency and timeliness of its work, the observers said. Suffrage rights continue to be subject to discriminatory restrictions based on ethnicity and residence. Some broad legal provisions unduly restricted political discourse in the pre-election period. “Yesterday marked an important milestone for elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina, with new voting technologies used country-wide for the first time. This achievement was made possible in part thanks to the sustained efforts of the Central Election Commission, and to all those who participated in and contributed to this process,” said Luis Graça, Special Co-ordinator and Leader of the OSCE short-term observer mission. “We encourage the newly elected leadership and legislators to build on this progress, advance further electoral reforms, and continue strengthening democratic institutions and processes in Bosnia and Herzegovina.” “More than three decades after the Dayton Peace Agreement, the stability of Bosnia and Herzegovina remains important for the security of the entire Western Balkans and the wider Euro-Atlantic area," said Sverre Myrli, Head of the NATO PA observer delegation. “The NATO Parliamentary Assembly is pleased to contribute to international efforts to support election monitoring and strengthen democratic governance. Strong democratic institutions, respect for the rule of law, and political dialogue are fundamental elements of that stability, which we will continue to support jointly with the rest of the international community.” The election-related laws and regulations overall provide an adequate basis for holding democratic elections and recent amendments strengthened safeguards. Still, important ODIHR and Venice Commission recommendations remain unaddressed, including on ethnicity- and residency-based restrictions on suffrage rights, misuse of public resources, election dispute resolution, campaign finance oversight and dissuasive sanctions. The technical preparations were marked by significant challenges, including notable delays in the receipt of the ICT devices, difficulties in forming polling station committees and recruiting technical operators, as well as late and insufficient training of election commissioners and voter education on the new voting methods and the new ballot. The 2024 legal amendments provide for countrywide use of electoral ICT. The introduction of ICT was made in response to previous concerns of voter impersonation and fraudulent counting. The law lacks sufficient provisions for effective implementation, and the deployment of ICT devices was carried out hastily, with limited time for testing, voter education, and training of election officials. “Election day unfolded in a generally calm and peaceful atmosphere, both inside polling stations and in their surroundings. Our observers were able to follow the process without impediment and were welcomed by election officials across the country,” said Allessia Claes, Head of the OSCE PA observer delegation. “This is encouraging, but our observation also identified shortcomings that should be addressed. We encourage the authorities and all relevant stakeholders to draw on these findings and continue working to strengthen the electoral process ahead of future elections.” Election day proceeded in an orderly manner, but a number of technical difficulties and issues with the complex voting process were observed. Polling officials generally managed the use of the devices adequately, but the process was assessed negatively in a significant number of polling stations observed. Negative observations were mainly attributed to serious shortcomings in ensuring secrecy of the vote and technical issues with the new devices. In one-fifth of the polling stations observed for the count, there were significant procedural omissions, indicating polling officials had a limited understanding of the complex procedures and made attempts to find practical shortcuts. There were only minor discrepancies between the manual and electronic counts in polling stations observed. Fundamental freedoms were respected, although the broad application of the ban on early campaigning resulted in numerous political actors being sanctioned, affecting political discourse. In the absence of sufficient regulation against the misuse of public resources, entity, cantonal and municipal authorities increased salaries and pensions, and provided social benefits and one-time payments to entice voters, undermining the equality of opportunity for contestants. “The introduction of new technologies strengthened the integrity of the vote,” said Davor Ivo Stier, Head of the EP observer delegation. “On the country’s EU path, further reform of electoral legislation is needed to address the rulings of the European Court of Human Rights and the Constitutional Court of Bosnia and Herzegovina.” “Democracy begins with a simple principle: Every citizen matters and every vote counts,” said Jone Blikra, Head of the PACE observer delegation. “Free and fair elections must guarantee that people can make their choice freely, that all votes are treated equally, and that the will of the voters is respected. These are fundamental values of the Council of Europe.” In an overall inclusive process, the CEC registered 7,028 candidates, including 2,977 women. Despite uniform compliance with the 40 per cent gender quota for candidate lists, women headed only about 14 per cent of lists for state and entity legislatures and concerns about their nomination as mere placeholders persisted. Recent amendments requiring parties to promote gender equality during campaigning did not result in a tangible increase in the visibility of women candidates in these elections. Campaign regulations are also applicable online, but institutional frameworks for addressing issues in the online environment are insufficient. ODIHR’s social media monitoring identified a polarized online environment, shaped by anonymous media websites and social network accounts, clickbait networks and AI-generated content, which often included misleading information, divisive and inflammatory rhetoric. The absence of safeguards to protect the online information environment, coupled with the lack of obligations on big tech companies to mitigate risks, leaves voters more vulnerable to manipulative information. “ODIHR has been present in Bosnia and Herzegovina for six weeks, and in this time, we have seen how the divisions in the country are reflected in campaign rhetoric, in the information available to voters both online and in traditional media, and in the election administration. This has continued to impact the level of trust in the election process,” said Tana de Zulueta, Head of the ODIHR election observation mission. “The introduction of new technologies could contribute to building this trust, but the process needs to be more transparent, and vo

https://rfom.osce.org/representative-fre.body: Media advisory OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media to pay an official visit to Kyrgyzstan and convene the Central Asia Media Conference in Bishkek Date: 5 October 2026 Place: VIENNA Source: OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media VIENNA, 5 October 2026- On 9 and10 October, the Office of the OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media, in collaboration with OSCE field operations from the region, will hold the Central Asia Media Conference, "Building Shared Reality: Information Integrity, Media Ethics and Trust in the Digital Age", at Novotel Bishkek City Center, starting at 9:30. Key themes of the conference include: Fostering trusted information landscapes Implementing the RFoM Policy Manual on Media Freedom in the Age of Big Tech Platforms and AI in Central Asia Information integrity in Central Asia Digital security for journalists Strengthening journalist protections through a gender-sensitive approach Journalism education and professional standards Newsroom policies on the use of artificial intelligence Journalists are invited to cover the conference. More information is available at: https://rfom.osce.org/event/667392 In addition, on 9 and10 October, the OSCE Representative on Freedom of the Media, Ambassador Jan Braathu, will pay his first official visit to Kyrgyzstan. During his visit, he will meet with high-level officials, as well as representatives of civil society and various media stakeholders in the country. For interview requests during the Representative’s visit to Kyrgyzstan, please contact Adis Mustedanagic at adis.mustedanagic@osce.org or call +4366488474962. https://dushanbe.osce.org/news/programme.body: News News Item OSCE Youth School equips young people with tools for good governance in Tajikistan From 28 September to 2 October 2026, the OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe organized a five-day Youth School on Good Economic and Environmental Governance in Hisor, on the outskirts of Dushanbe, bringing together 20 young people aged 18 to 25 from across Tajikistan. Issued on: 8 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe Fields of work: Good governance From 28 September to 2 October 2026, the OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe organized a five-day Youth School on Good Economic and Environmental Governance in Hisor, on the outskirts of Dushanbe, bringing together 20 young people aged 18 to 25 from across Tajikistan. The Youth School was the first joint initiative of five units of the Programme Office’s Economic and Environmental Department, covering good governance and anti-corruption, economic challenges to security, environmental threats to security, water management and energy security, and disaster risk reduction. It explored how good governance principles can be applied to economic, environmental, water, energy, climate and disaster-related challenges. Through interactive sessions, case studies, role-plays and group exercises, participants strengthened their understanding of six principles of good governance: transparency, accountability, participation, the rule of law, integrity and co-ordination. They also discussed civic participation and access to environmental information under the Aarhus Convention, as well as disaster risk reduction. “For me, the Youth School was not only about learning. We exchanged ideas, worked together and made friends with other young people. The opportunity to build a network was one of the most valuable parts of the School,” said Surush Alisherzoda, a participant. Robiya Muhamadieva, another participant, said the format made the learning more engaging: “What I liked most was the way the sessions were conducted. We had different trainers and topics, but instead of just listening to lectures, we spent much of our time debating, working through real-life cases and developing our own projects. This made the information much clearer and easier to remember.” International OSCE expert Raimundas Kalesnykas from Vilnius, Lithuania, highlighted the participants’ enthusiasm: “The School showed how interested young people are in good governance and economic and environmental issues. They were actively involved in the interactive sessions and contributed their ideas. I believe they will be able to put the knowledge and skills they gained here into practice in the future.” On the final day, participants developed youth-led initiatives addressing regional challenges related to the green economy, water and energy, climate change and disaster risk reduction. The School also helped participants build connections and skills for more transparent and sustainable decision-making. Participants celebrate the completion of the Youth School on Good Economic and Environmental Governance with their certificates, Hisor, 2 October 2026. The OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe continues to promote youth engagement and practical learning opportunities that contribute to good governance, sustainable development and environmental security in Tajikistan. News News Item OSCE fosters collaboration among Central Asian specialists through a Regional Explosive Ordnance Disposal course in Tajikistan On 2 October 2026, the OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe, in partnership with the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Tajikistan, organized a three-week Regional Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) Level 1 course at the Regional Explosive Hazard Training Centre (REHTC) of Tajikistan’s Ministry of Defence in Chorgulteppa, Rudaki District. Issued on: 8 October 2026 Issued by: OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe Fields of work: Arms control On 2 October 2026, the OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe, in partnership with the Ministry of Defence of the Republic of Tajikistan, organized a three-week Regional Explosive Ordnance Disposal (EOD) Level 1 course at the Regional Explosive Hazard Training Centre (REHTC) of Tajikistan’s Ministry of Defence in Chorgulteppa, Rudaki District. The course, conducted in compliance with the International Mine Action Standards, enhanced the professional skills and knowledge of specialists from the armed forces, law enforcement agencies, security services and humanitarian mine action organizations across Central Asia involved in EOD and humanitarian mine action, A total of 18 specialists from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan improved knowledge on explosive ordnance, safety measures, EOD equipment and protective gear. Participants also learned about reconnaissance, initiation methods and the safe transportation, storage and disposal of explosive ordnance. A participant demonstrates techniques for the controlled destruction of explosive ordnance, Chorgulteppa, Rudaki District, 1 October 2026. In addition to technical EOD training, participants exchanged experience and good practices, discussed practical approaches to EOD operations and established new professional contacts. Colonel Tohir Holmakhmadzoda, Head of the REHTC of Tajikistan’s Ministry of Defence, emphasized: “By clearing explosive ordnance, you are not simply making the land safer; you are paving the way for life, security and a peaceful future.” Speaking at the graduation ceremony, Major General Asozoda Abdulmumin, Director of the State Institution “National Mine Action Centre of Tajikistan”, noted: “The knowledge and skills you have acquired today will strengthen your professional capabilities. They will also contribute to humanitarian mine action and, most importantly, to saving human lives.” Abdugani Vahobov, National Training Officer at the OSCE Programme Office in Dushanbe, said in his concluding remarks: “Today, we are completing this course, but we are not completing our shared mission. The knowledge you have gained will strengthen your professionalism, our co-operation will build trust, and our joint efforts will contribute to enhancing security in Central Asia.” Participants from Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan, Tajikistan, Turkmenistan and Uzbekistan receive certificates upon completion of the Regional EOD Level 1 course in Chorgulteppa, Rudaki District, 2 October 2026. The OSCE remains committed to strengthening regional co-operation and supporting national capacities to address the risks posed by explosive ordnance across Central Asia.
