https://www.trend.az/azerbaijan/4232633..body: Home Azerbaijan Azerbaijan's parliament calls European Parliament resolution biased Azerbaijan News 8 October 2026 17:52 (UTC +04:00) Photo: Trend News Agency Alish Abdulla Read more BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 8. Azerbaijan’s parliament has rejected the allegations contained in the European Parliament’s October 8 resolution on human rights and freedoms in Azerbaijan, describing the document as a biased political action. The Azerbaijani parliament made the remarks in its response to the European Parliament’s resolution. The parliament said the European Parliament’s targeted political approach toward Azerbaijan had become more confrontational following the Second Karabakh War. It said resolutions adopted in recent years, along with calls for political pressure and sanctions against Azerbaijan, demonstrated that the organization had failed to accept what it described as the new geopolitical realities in the South Caucasus. The response also criticized the European Parliament for seeking to determine the scope of authority of Azerbaijan’s state bodies, issue instructions to law enforcement and judicial institutions, and set political conditions for bilateral relations. According to the parliament, this raises questions about whether the European Parliament seeks to build relations with Azerbaijan based on equality, mutual respect and non-interference in internal affairs. The parliament also referred to issues of corruption and illicit lobbying influence within the European Parliament, stressing the importance of the organization consistently applying its own standards. The response further said that the European Parliament applies double standards in its approach to human rights. It noted that while resolutions are adopted concerning Azerbaijan, European countries themselves continue to face problems related to police violence, restrictions on freedom of peaceful assembly and accountability for human rights violations. The parliament said the adoption of the resolution at a time when the Azerbaijan-Armenia peace agenda is advancing was also a matter of concern. It said unilateral initiatives and what it described as misguided assessments make it more difficult to build an environment of mutual trust and create additional obstacles to normalizing relations. The response also highlighted what the parliament described as a contradiction between the European Parliament’s call to restore cooperation with the Azerbaijani parliament and its adoption of documents that create interparliamentary tensions. The parliament said restoring trust requires abandoning confrontational rhetoric and recognizing the equal nature of interparliamentary relations. The Azerbaijani parliament said the country remains committed to protecting human rights and fundamental freedoms, ensuring the rule of law and implementing the principles of a state governed by law. The response also said that, while making allegations against Azerbaijan, the European Parliament remained silent about the rights of Azerbaijani refugees and internally displaced persons who, according to the parliament, were subjected to ethnic cleansing and other serious human rights violations during Armenia’s occupation of Azerbaijani territory. The Azerbaijani parliament called on the European Parliament to abandon what it described as confrontational rhetoric toward Azerbaijan and refrain from interfering in the country’s internal affairs. The parliament stated that no force can divert Azerbaijan from its path of democratic development. Uzbekistan and Georgia agreed to develop a joint roadmap for parliamentary cooperation for 2027–2028 during a meeting in Tashkent. The establishment of bilateral strategic partnership relations during the Uzbek president’s state visit to Georgia in July opened new opportunities for cooperation between the two countries, according to the Uzbek side. The officials emphasized the need to intensify contacts between relevant parliamentary committees and interparliamentary cooperation groups and involve them more actively in discussions on specific areas of bilateral cooperation. "The joint roadmap for 2027–2028 is intended to support the consistent development of interparliamentary dialogue, identify concrete measures in priority areas of cooperation and support the Uzbekistan-Georgia strategic partnership at the parliamentary level," the Uzbek Senate said. In addition, the sides exchanged views on prospects for expanding trade and economic ties, transport connectivity, investment and digitalization. They highlighted the importance of strengthening cooperation in education, tourism, culture and humanitarian affairs. https://www.trend.az/azerbaijan/4232414..body: Home Azerbaijan Azerbaijan's trade turnover with Central Asian countries grew by more than 50 percent last year - President Ilham Aliyev (FULL SPEECH) Azerbaijan News 8 October 2026 11:24 (UTC +04:00) Photo: Press service of the President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Laman Zeynalova Read more TURKMENBASHI, Turkmenistan, October 8. Last year, Azerbaijan's trade turnover with the countries of Central Asia grew by more than 50 percent, President Ilham Aliyev said as he addressed the 8th Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of the Republic of Azerbaijan and Central Asia in Turkmenbashi, Trend 's special correspondent reports. Speech by President Ilham Aliyev - Esteemed Serdar Gurbangulyevich, Distinguished heads of state, Dear friends, First of all, I express my gratitude to the President of Turkmenistan for the invitation and traditional hospitality. I am glad to be back in brotherly Turkmenistan, in beautiful Awaza. In November last year, Azerbaijan became a full-fledged participant in the Consultative Meeting of the Heads of State of Central Asia. Once again, I express my gratitude to all my respected colleagues for their unanimous support for this historic decision. In this regard, I would like to note the role played by Turkmenistan and, personally, by the respected Gurbanguly Myalikgulyevich Berdimuhamedov. It was right here, in Awaza, in August last year, that he initiated Azerbaijan's full participation in this format. Azerbaijan-Turkmenistan relations have been developing dynamically in recent years. Since last year, five high-level visits have already taken place. This reflects the intensity of our political dialogue and the mutual desire to further strengthen bilateral ties. I would particularly like to highlight the construction of a mosque in the city of Fuzuli, initiated by the respected Gurbanguly Myalikgulyevich Berdimuhamedov. Last year, we jointly participated in laying its foundation. This gift from brotherly Turkmenistan to our country is yet another testament to the friendship and spiritual closeness of our peoples. Brotherly support in the restoration of the liberated territories of Azerbaijan holds special significance for us. In Fuzuli, a school named after Mirzo Ulugbek has already been built by Uzbekistan, and the Kurmangazy Children's Creativity Center has been built by Kazakhstan; in Aghdam, a school named after Manas has been built by Kyrgyzstan. We highly value this assistance. Azerbaijan's interaction with the countries of Central Asia has expanded significantly in recent years. Political ties are at a high level, and mutual high-level visits have become regular. Trade and economic cooperation are growing stronger, mutual investments are increasing, and joint projects are being implemented. Last year, Azerbaijan's trade turnover with Central Asian countries grew by more than 50 percent. Today, over 400 companies with capital originating from Central Asian countries actively operate in our country. In recent years, Azerbaijan has established joint investment funds with Kazakhstan, Uzbekistan, and Kyrgyzstan. The capital of each of these funds amounts to hundreds of millions of dollars. I believe their potential should be utilized more actively, primarily for the implementation of joint projects, the creation of new manufacturing facilities, and the expansion of industrial cooperation. We must not only increase mutual trade; it is important to jointly invest, produce, and enter external markets. Transport is one of the primary areas of our cooperation. The Caspian Sea plays an increasingly vital role today in the transport connectivity of our countries. The transport infrastructure on both shores of the Caspian is of key importance for connecting Central Asia with Azerbaijan and further onward to international markets. In recent years, we have consistently increased our transport capabilities. We have made major investments in transport infrastructure, developing seaports, airports, railways, and highways. Today, we are observing significant growth in cargo transit volumes across the Caspian. Our common task is to make these routes more efficient and competitive. In parallel, the Digital Silk Way project is being implemented, and work is underway to lay fiber-optic lines along the bed of the Caspian Sea. The Middle Corridor is acquiring ever greater significance; last year, the volume of transit cargo along this route grew by more than 10 percent, and in the first eight months of the current year, by almost another 20 percent. The energy sector holds a special place in our cooperation. Azerbaijan plays an important role in the transit of energy resources from Central Asia to international markets. Oil from Turkmenistan and Kazakhstan is transported through the territory of our country, and the volume of these shipments is growing. Our cooperation in renewable energy is consistently expanding. We are working jointly with Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan to create a green energy corridor. Dear colleagues, The geopolitical importance of our cooperation format lies not only in joint projects in the energy and transport sectors. Peace, security, and political and economic stability in our countries form the foundation of all our successes and serve as a guarantee for the future successful development of the Central Asian states and Azerbaijan, as well as the strengthening of our interaction. Thank you for your attention. What is your objective now in the conflict? -Ceasefire cannot be achieved unilaterally. It must be a bilateral decision and also it must be implemented on the ground. As you know Armenia attacked us on the 27th of September, attacking our military positions and damaging our infrastructure, attacking civilians. So far we have almost 30 civilians killed as a result of Armenian attack, including the ballistic missiles, and the cluster bombs. So, our counter-attack was successful. We managed to liberate part of the occupied territories and our main objective is restoration of territorial integrity of Azerbaijan. And after that I think the effort must be imposed on achieving the ceasefire. -The countries that you’re referencing have repeatedly asked for a ceasefire. Why isn’t that happening now? Our army defeated them. Then, on August 23, they send a sabotage group to commit terror acts against our civilians and military personnel. That also was a failure for them, because the head of the sabotage group was detained and he gives evidences exactly about what I am saying. And in the end of September they launched a massive attack on our villages and cities. I can tell you that up to today we have almost 900 houses totally demolished, or damaged and many casualties and wounded people among civilians. And now after Armenia is suffering a very bitter defeat, they are pleading for a ceasefire. They made violation of ceasefire themselves. They ignore United Nations Security Council resolutions which demand full, complete, immediate and unconditional withdrawal of Armenian troops. They want to keep status quo unchanged, and the Minsk Group co-chairs United States, Russia and France, their presidents many times made the statements that the status quo is unacceptable. Armenia ignored it, but now Azerbaijan itself is changing the status quo, and I think that will be an important step towards the soonest resolution of the conflict. -Mr. President, civilians have been killed on both sides of this conflict. How do you reconcile that with your aims? -Of course, we regret that civilians are being killed and of course, we were not the purpose, we were not the source of this attack. Because it was a first thing in the morning on the 27th of September, what they did, they attacked our cities and villages. And we had to respond. But our response mainly is and primarily is on their military positions, on their tanks and guns and what we are doing on the battlefield is available in internet. What we are seeing right now is the opposite of that. How are you trying to limit the suffering of civilians? -You know we are not responsible for this outbreak. As I said, we were a subject of a physical attack from Armenian army which is situated on the occupied territories of Azerbaijan Above from that, the current Armenian regime did everything in order to destroy the negotiation process. Exactly one year ago, Armenian prime Minister at the rally in the occupied area of Azerbaijan made a statement that ‘Karabakh is Armenia’ and that statement actually destroyed negotiation process. Because the principles which are on the table and which are the basis for settlement demand the return of the occupied territories to Azerbaijan. And when Armenian prime minister says that not a centimeter of land will return to Azerbaijan, when he says that ‘Karabakh is Armenia’, when they organize illegal settlement of foreign people on the occupied territories which is a brutal violation of Geneva Convention, they destroy negotiation process. After that, in order to make us responsible for that, they attack us three times-on July, August, and September. When we beat them on the battlefield, they call everywhere, they make a plea to everyone, ‘stop Azerbaijan’. We want to stop, but we want the occupation to stop. Therefore, the main message should be to Armenia, we are not on Armenian land, we are on our land. But Turkey in no other way is involved in this conflict. Armenia bringing such fake news to the media wants to diminish the capacity of Azerbaijani army. We are fighting ourselves. So, the fact that we buy modern Turkish equipment including the fighter drones should not be a problem for anyone. Because Armenia gets weapons free of charge. We pay for them and Armenia gets free of charge. Turkey in no other way is involved in the conflict. -We keep talking about weapons and we keep talking about fighting here. Is diplomacy still an option? Will you sit down, have talks with the prime minister of Armenia to find a different way out of this conflict? I can tell you, that during my term as the president, I had maybe tens of talks with two former Armenian presidents and the current prime minister. Negotiations are taking place since 1992. Can you imagine? For almost 30 years. And we were living with hopes, mediators were telling us that you should wait a little bit, there will be more constructive approach from Armenian side. But when this prime minister came to power, as a result of the coup d’état two years ago, he destroyed completely negotiation process. And I had meetings with him many times. https://www.trend.az/azerbaijan/4231747..body: Home Azerbaijan Chronicles of Victory (October 7, 2020): President Ilham Aliyev interviewed by CNN-Turk TV (PHOTO/VIDEO) Azerbaijan News 7 October 2026 07:05 (UTC +04:00) BAKU, Azerbaijan, October 7. President of the Republic of Azerbaijan Ilham Aliyev has been interviewed by CNN-Türk television. Trend presents the interview. Mr. President Ilham Aliyev, welcome to CNN-Türk. Thank you for giving this interview on such historic days for Azerbaijan. Without further ado, let me immediately move on to the questions. First of all, what is the latest situation in the operations? Are they going as planned? What territory has been liberated from occupation? -Everything is going according to plan. The Azerbaijani army is restoring the territorial integrity of the country these days. The operation continues successfully. One city and many villages have already been liberated from the occupation. This once again proves that the Azerbaijani people will never put up with the occupation. We have repeatedly said this: Karabakh is our historical and ancestral land! Unfortunately, the negotiations held for a long time did not lead to any results. Therefore, of course, Azerbaijan had to restore its territorial integrity on its own and is doing exactly that. As you know, on 27 September the Armenian armed forces launched a new offensive against us. Many of our cities and villages are being shelled. Today the death toll among our civilians is about 30 people. The Armenian armed forces are shelling our cities and villages, about a thousand houses have been destroyed or seriously damaged. But everything is going according to plan, and I hope that the tasks before us will be fulfilled. -Mr. President, I would like to return to the processes in the zone of operations again. As we know, the Armenian army began shelling Azerbaijani cities outside the conflict zone with ballistic missiles. In particular, it is targeting settlements in the second largest city of Azerbaijan, Ganja, a power plant in Mingachevir with ballistic missiles. What do you think was the goal? -In my opinion, this is a sign of helplessness of the Armenian army and the crimes of the military-political leadership of Armenia because violence against civilians, the shelling of settlements and the destruction of peaceful cities with ballistic missiles is considered a war crime. This indicates that Armenia cannot resist us on the battlefield. Losing the battle and in an effort to stop us, and in order to harm the civilian population as much as possible, it resorts to such heinous acts. As you noted, Ganja and Mingachevir are cities that are far from the war zone. At the same time, our cities located near the front zone are bombarded every day. The nearest district is Tartar. From one to two thousand shells are dropped on the city of Tartar every day. The main purpose of this is violence against civilians. This once again demonstrates the fascist essence of Armenia, the fascist essence of its regime. But this does not frighten the Azerbaijani people and has no impact whatsoever. Our citizens living in these regions, in these cities and villages stand firmly. They say: long live the Motherland, may our lands be liberated from occupation as soon as possible. They will remain in these places to the end and will provide our army with moral support. -If Armenia continues shelling civilian settlements, will there be any change in your current position? -No, there should be no change in our position. We are not fighting against the Armenian people. I have already spoken about this many times. We are waging a fair fight. We want to restore our territorial integrity, we are doing this and we have achieved success in this matter and in this direction. Azerbaijan has never fought against the civilian population and against civilians. The other day I said that we have no problems with the Armenian people. Thousands of Armenians live in Azerbaijan, and they are our citizens. The Armenians living in Nagorno-Karabakh today are also our citizens. All our goals are military. We have every right to destroy military targets because they have caused great damage to our army and cities. Therefore, our duty is to destroy them and ensure the safety of our population. -Armenia's bombardment of civilian settlements with ballistic missiles is essentially a war crime, an act contrary to the Geneva Convention. In this context, do you plan to put forward any initiatives regarding war crimes before the UN? Do you collect evidence of these crimes on the ground? -We certainly do. All of their war crimes are already being recorded. Unfortunately, the international community did not react to the war crimes that were committed against Azerbaijan and our people earlier. The Khojaly massacre is an act of genocide that took place in front of the whole world. However, the then military-political leadership of Armenia was not held accountable for this. The destruction of our cities and villages, the appearance of more than a million internally displaced persons – the international community did not take any action in this regard. Therefore, this issue has not been resolved for many years because no distinction is made between the occupier and the victim of the occupation. And the shelling of our cities and villages by the Armenian armed forces with ballistic missiles today is a war crime. The leadership of Armenia, of course, must and will bear responsibility for this. -So far you have received several calls for a ceasefire. You have personally answered them. But looking at the 30-year history of the conflict, do you think that these calls will produce results? -I believe that these calls should not be just calls for a ceasefire. We have repeatedly said that sanctions should have been applied to the occupying state of Armenia. If sanctions had been applied in due time, then, perhaps, this issue would have been resolved long ago. Very serious pressure should have been put on Armenia – not in word but in deed. Unfortunately, this did not happen. Therefore, this process dragged on for 30 years. Negotiations that have been fruitless for 30 years are already losing their point. In addition, recently, the military-political leadership of Armenia, both with aggressive actions and aggressive statements, disrupted the process of negotiations. In other words, it dealt a crushing blow to the talks. To say that "Karabakh is Armenia" essentially means an end to the negotiations because the essence of the negotiations is that the occupied lands should be gradually and on a step-by-step basis returned to Azerbaijan. This is enshrined in the fundamental principles. To say that "Karabakh is Armenia" actually means an end to this process. There were other similar statements. After that, in July, Armenia attacked Azerbaijan in the direction of the state border, killing many soldiers and one civilian. Therefore, the restoration of the ceasefire must be ensured on certain conditions. First of all, we should be given a schedule for the withdrawal of the Armenian armed forces from the occupied lands. We have already communicated our position on this issue to the Minsk Group. I hope that our calls and proposals will not remain unanswered. -I think that speaking about the Minsk Group of the Organization for Security and Cooperation in Europe, France should be mentioned separately. What can you say in connection with France's position on this issue? -I have already spoken about this several times. We have always perceived the Minsk Group as a group, and this is still the case today. We believed that the co-chair countries of this group should remain neutral, not support any of the parties, because otherwise their mediation mission would be called into question. The bread-loaf-sized satellite will use an array of cameras and sensors to monitor crops, the impact of natural disasters, and “identify early signs of drought,” according to a September 24 statement about the spacecraft from the Kyrgyz Agriculture Ministry. A Kyrgyz specialist explains the functions of the domestically produced satellite. According to Ilya Cherny, the director of Kyrgyz Electronics, the technology company that oversaw the project, a team of about 10 Kyrgyz engineers worked on the 5 kilogram spacecraft over two and a half years. It has an estimated lifespan of 15 years and local reports estimated its build cost at around $130,000. Kyrgyz officials describe the spacecraft as domestically developed and assembled, although Cherny noted that “most of the technologies” inside the nanosatellite are Russian, "because development from scratch takes 5-10 years." The launch of the Kyrgyz satellite into orbit from California, scheduled to take place on October 1, marks the latest landmark in a space race that is heating up in Central Asia. A February presentation that shows a model of an Uzbek satellite. In August, Uzbekistan sent a Chinese-made satellite into orbit that included an “artificial intelligence module developed by specialists from the Uzbekcosmos Agency.” Additionally, Tashkent recently announced plans to produce its own satellite by 2028. Kazakhstan has several domestically made satellites currently in orbit and in September the country announced plans to establish “an international constellation of nine satellites intended for Earth observation.” The constellation is set to include satellites provided by Mongolia, the Republic of the Congo, and Nigeria. Nelly Bekus , an expert on Central Asia at the University of Exeter, told RFE/RL that for those states able to produce their own space infrastructure, the effort and expense is viewed as worthwhile from a national security standpoint. "In recent years, as geopolitical tensions have increased worldwide, independent access to satellite data operated by national teams has also become increasingly important for state security," she said. Bekus added that "spacefaring capabilities have long been associated with ideas of progressive nationhood, providing highly visible evidence of a nation’s technological prowess and its standing on the world stage." Other Western analysts have pointed to the impulse among authoritarian governments to maintain a “kill switch” for communications during civil unrest. Astana switched off Kazakhstan’s Internet for several days amid mass protests in the country in early 2022 and Uzbekistan has stated that its domestically made satellite planned for 2028 will ensure what it calls “a sovereign and objective source of information” in the country. When Kazakhstan was involved in discussions to introduce Starlink for its rural populations, negotiations with Elon Musk’s SpaceX reached an impasse over a Kazakh requirement that ground stations -- communications dishes that feed signals to passing satellites -- be built inside the country, allowing Astana to maintain control. https://www.atlanticcouncil.org/dispatch.body: A view of the Medical Assistance and Rescue Centre, an infectious diseases hospital, in the town of Shelekhov in the Irkutsk region, Russia, October 5, 2026. (REUTERS) WASHINGTON—The unexplained death of a twenty-eight-year-old employee at Russia’s Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute has triggered conflicting official accounts as authorities place hundreds of contacts under observation or quarantine. While there are far more questions than answers at this stage, the Russian explanations should be assessed with skepticism given the country’s track record, and global policymakers should push for an outside investigation into this incident. Darya Shipilova died in the hospital overnight between October 1 and 2 after developing severe pneumonia. Russian outlets initially reported that she died of plague after a test tube allegedly broke on September 25. But on October 4, Rospotrebnadzor, Russia’s public health agency which also oversees the Institute, said that she had pneumonia of unknown origin and that no organism linked to her work had been identified. Irkutsk Governor Igor Kobzev described the cause only as a particularly dangerous infection. Rospotrebnadzor chief Anna Popova flew in from Moscow, and reports put about two hundred contacts under isolation or quarantine, with most of them reportedly hospitalized for observation. On October 4, a US administration official told Axios that the White House is aware of the situation, monitoring the outbreak , and assessing options. Although the cause of Shipilova’s death is still unknown, the conflicting accounts, scale of the response, and Russia’s record on biological weapons and lab safety raise five issues worth considering. 1. Russia has a long history of experimenting with plague as a weapon and of deadly lab accidents. The Soviet biological weapons program began in the late 1920s and expanded through the 1930s. It continued to grow even after the USSR signed the Biological Weapons Convention in 1972. The program was particularly advanced, with scientists experimenting with modifying and combining different types of biological agents to create more potent weapons. Plague was a priority agent, and defectors have described work on developing antibiotic-resistant strains. The Irkutsk Institute itself opened in 1934 as a plague-control institute and still publishes open research on plague, including a 2025 study of different strains in the Tuva region and a 2026 paper on immunity after plague vaccination. Historically, the institute devoted only a small portion of its activities to weapons work, according to the microbiologist Raymond Zilinskas , who concluded that the Soviet anti-plague system as a whole almost certainly supplied virulent strains to Biopreparat, the program’s nominally civilian arm, and to military facilities related to the biological weapons program. 2. Russia’s offensive biological weapons program never ended, and military-linked laboratories are expanding. The State Department’s 2025 compliance report found that Russia maintains an offensive biological weapons program in violation of its treaty obligations. The Office of the Director of National Intelligence’s 2026 annual threat assessment adds that Russian scientists continue to develop new chemical and biological capabilities and warns that dual-use biotechnology could raise the risk of accidental pathogen releases. Satellite images reported by the Washington Post in October 2024 showed about ten new buildings covering more than 250,000 square feet at Sergiev Posad-6, a military site northeast of Moscow. Experts said the buildings’ design was consistent with high-containment laboratories, although Russia says the work there is defensive. Radio Free Europe/Radio Liberty reported in September that the Center of Experimental Physiology, a new laboratory complex on Lisy Island in a reservoir in the Tver region, is directed by Vladimir Maksimov, who led the military virology unit that became the 48th Central Research Institute, Russia’s military biological-defense research organization. Ukrainian military intelligence alleged in August that the center is experimenting with dangerous viruses for the armed forces. Although Shipilova’s death occurred at a different research facility and has not been linked to these programs, these expansions demonstrate Russia’s ongoing interest in biological research within a military context, including work with potential dual-use applications. Ukraine is a war of trenches, drones, and chemical weapons. The 2026 US threat assessment documents thousands of Russian chemical attacks on Ukrainian forces since 2022, though it also says Moscow probably will keep abiding by the norm against large-scale use of chemical, biological, and nuclear weapons absent a “ significant shift ” in the war. That makes it important for the United States and its allies to maintain attribution capabilities strong enough to detect even low-level deployment should Russia decide to employ biological weapons. 3. Denial and deflection are part of a Kremlin playbook around toxins and biological agents. In February 2026, the United Kingdom, Sweden, France, Germany, and the Netherlands said that Russian opposition leader Alexei Navalny, who died in a Russian prison in 2024, was poisoned with epibatidine, a toxin found in South American dart frogs and not known to occur naturally in Russia. The Kremlin called the accusation “ biased and baseless .” Toxins fall under the Biological Weapons Convention, making the finding relevant to the broader question of the Kremlin’s compliance with the treaty and transparency around substances it covers. The official response also fits a pattern. Soviet authorities blamed the Sverdlovsk anthrax outbreak on bad meat, and Moscow today regularly accuses the United States, without evidence, of running biological weapons labs in Ukraine. That history gives observers reason to scrutinize official explanations in Irkutsk as well. 4. Russia’s safety and transparency record gives reason to doubt that the world will get the full story. Russia’s history of concealing previous biological incidents makes the early conflicting reports especially unconvincing. Rospotrebnadzor says the cause of Shipilova’s death is unknown and that no laboratory accident occurred, yet most of the roughly two hundred contacts were reportedly hospitalized for observation. The head of Buryatia initially wrote that Shipilova had died of plague, then edited the post to say she may have. Independent local news outlet Lyudi Baikala , citing a law-enforcement source, reported that officers of the Federal Security Service (FSB) escorted ambulances carrying her contacts. Russia has a history of lab accidents and subsequent coverups. At Sverdlovsk in 1979, anthrax escaped from a military compound and killed at least sixty-eight people. For nearly thirteen years, Soviet officials blamed contaminated meat, until then-Russian President Boris Yeltsin acknowledged military responsibility in 1992. The concealment delayed an accurate account of a lethal lab accident for more than a decade. Then, in 1988, researcher Nikolai Ustinov died at the Vektor laboratory after an accidental needle stick exposed him to Marburg virus. Russia also fares poorly in international assessments of biological safety and oversight. The Global Health Security Index ranked Russia sixty-third of 195 countries in 2019, with a score of 44.3 out of 100, and forty-seventh in 2021, with a score of 49.1. Its oversight of dual-use research scored at zero both years. Global BioLabs gave Russia a governance score tied with Gabon for the lowest among countries with biosafety level 4 (BSL-4) laboratories. Accidental releases are already a serious vulnerability everywhere: 309 laboratory-acquired infections and sixteen accidental pathogen escapes were documented worldwide between 2000 and 2021. The difference is whether outsiders will get to look at the evidence. And it is unlikely t

https://thediplomat.com/2026/10/a-tajik-.body: Credit: Shutterstock Subscribe for ads-free reading Tajikistan’s Humo Bank has warned its Russian clients that their cards will be blocked on October 1 unless they visit one of its offices in Tajikistan by September 30 to undergo biometric identification. “If you can’t come to Tajikistan in person and complete the identification, unfortunately, your card will be closed,” the bank told Russian news site Lenta.ru, advising clients to move their remaining balances to ruble cards before the deadline. The bank cited the need to protect clients from fraud. A Russian client, however, told the Telegram channel Ostorozhno Novosti that the bank’s support staff explained it had decided to restrict services for “certain categories of non-resident individuals” whose cards were opened online. She said a transfer of about 300 euros had been stuck for a week and that the bank had stopped responding to her complaints. Humo offered her a new card if she traveled to Tajikistan, valid only for the duration of her legal stay and for no longer than a year. With Visa and Mastercard gone from Russia since 2022, Russians have relied on cards issued in “friendly” countries to make payments abroad. When Kazakhstan limited non-resident cards to 12 months and required in-person issuance in January 2025, intermediaries moved their business to Tajikistan, Kyrgyzstan, and Uzbekistan. Humo and the International Bank of Tajikistan began offering remotely issued five-year cards in U.S. dollars and euros, sold through intermediaries for roughly 15,000 to 70,000 rubles. Humo is a newcomer to banking. Owned by the Japanese investment holding Gojo & Company , the former microcredit deposit organization received a full banking license from the National Bank of Tajikistan in July 2025. It was also among the few Tajik financial institutions with access to Visa Direct, a real-time payment service that became a conduit for Russian money headed to Europe. An investigation by The Bell found last year that Sberbank clients could send money to Revolut and N26 accounts through Central Asian intermediaries, with the funds appearing to originate from Dushanbe or Tashkent. The Humo ultimatum follows a year of Western pressure on Tajik banks. In October 2025, the European Union included Dushanbe City Bank, Spitamen, and Commercebank of Tajikistan in its 19th sanctions package, targeting banks closely linked to Russia’s financial system or processing cross-border payments that support the Russian economy. The three banks held roughly a fifth of all deposits in Tajikistan, and other Tajik banks responded by restricting transfers to Russia. In December, Revolut stopped accepting top-ups from cards issued in Tajikistan, Kazakhstan, and Uzbekistan for EU residents, citing payment systems’ classification of those countries as high-risk. The EU removed the three Tajik banks from its sanctions list in April 2026, with the National Bank crediting improved compliance and anti-money laundering standards. For Dushanbe, the stakes go well beyond fees collected from Russian cardholders. Remittances, mostly from Tajik migrants in Russia, reached $5.8 billion in 2024, or the equivalent of 45.3 percent of Tajikistan’s GDP, the highest share in the world. By the end of 2024, over 90 percent of payments in Tajik-Russian trade were settled in rubles, and the head of the National Bank said Tajik banks work only with Russian banks not under sanctions. Tajikistan needs its financial channels to Russia open and its banks connected to SWIFT and Visa at the same time. Neither Humo nor the National Bank has said whether the decision came from regulators, payment systems, or the bank’s own risk assessment. But a young bank that watched three of its peers cut off from European counterparties has every reason to shed remotely onboarded Russian clients before Brussels or Visa forces its hand. Russians will likely take their business to Kyrgyz and Uzbek banks, as they did when Kazakhstan closed its doors, until those banks face the same pressure. Already have an account? Log in . https://www.ng.ru/cis/2026-10-07/5_9598_.body: В офис канцлера Германии, в МИД страны, а также по линии спецслужб направлен протест властей Азербайджана, утверждает агентство dpa. Протест связан с публикацией журнала Der Spiegel по поводу расследования в отношении бывшего главы германской Федеральной разведывательной службы (BND) Августа Ханнинга. По данным Der Spiegel, Ханнингу инкриминируется шпионаж в пользу Азербайджана. Якобы он подготовил аналитический материал для азербайджанской разведки, использовав для этого секретные документы. Между тем с осуждением публикации открыто выступил Совет по медиа и вещанию Азербайджана. В его заявлении выражается обеспокоенность тем, что «необоснованные утверждения, связывающие Азербайджан с упомянутым расследованием, первоначально распространенные немецким изданием Der Spiegel», преподносятся «широкой аудитории как факты». 80-летний Ханнинг был задержан 6 октября в Баварии. Также задержали его бывшего помощника, Манфреда Д., возглавлявшего аппарат нескольких руководителей БНД в период с марта 2012-го по март 2026 года. Их обоих подозревают в работе на иностранную разведку. Ханнинг возглавлял БНД в 1998–2005 годах. Пресс-служба Федеральной прокуратуры Германии, сообщившая 7 октября об аресте Ханнинга, не уточнила, шпионаж в пользу какой страны ему инкриминируется. Известно только, что, по версии следствия, Манфред Д. по меньшей мере с 2010 года передавал за деньги секретную информацию своему бывшему шефу. Предположительно, Ханнинг получил, таким образом, в общей сложности 2 тыс. документов. Многие из них были секретными. По информации Интерфакса

https://thediplomat.com/2026/09/why-paki.body: Subscribe for ads-free reading On the night of February 21, 2026 Pakistan launched air and missile strikes on three border provinces in Afghanistan . What was Pakistan bombing? Suspected camps of the Tehreek-e-Taliban Pakistan – the TTP for short – and the Islamic State of Khorasan Province. The Taliban regime in Afghanistan retaliated by hitting Pakistani border posts. Pakistan then upped the ante. Its military launched Operation Ghazab Lil-Haq — which means Righteous Fury — against Afghanistan. “Our patience has now run out. Now it is open war between us,” Pakistan’s defense minister said on February 27. Pakistan and Afghanistan have engaged in numerous strikes and counter-strikes in the months since. While these have declined in frequency and magnitude, thanks to mediation efforts by China, the military strikes were still happening into September 2026. TTP attacks in Pakistan have also continued. Few would have expected Pakistan and the Afghan Taliban to turn on each other. They had been close allies for over 30 years – through the Taliban’s entire existence. When the Taliban captured power in Kabul in August 2021, Pakistan celebrated. So why did Pakistan declare “an open war” against its one-time protégé? Is there more to Pakistan’s military strikes on Afghanistan than taking out TTP camps? And can the Afghanistan-Pakistan relationship be salvaged? Already have an account? Log in . https://thediplomat.com/2026/10/investig.body: Credit: olympic.uz Subscribe for ads-free reading In April 2023, when he was serving as deputy head of the Presidential Security Service, Otabek Umarov – Uzbek President Shavkat Mirziyoyev’s son-in-law – reportedly acquired citizenship in the United Arab Emirates. He’s also alleged to be the owner of around $7 million worth of Dubai real estate. Those are the central allegations of a new investigation published by the Organized Crime and Corruption Reporting Project (OCCRP) and RFE/RL’s Uzbek Service, Ozodlik . Under Uzbek military law, which governs the position Umarov held at the time, holding a second citizenship is prohibited. Since acquiring citizenship typically includes swearing an oath of allegiance, many countries bar security (and other) officials from doing so – a second passport represents possible divided loyalties and a counterintelligence risk. As OCCRP and Ozodlik reported, “Under UAE law, foreigners can only obtain citizenship through a nomination by a royal court or senior official, and [the process] requires swearing an oath of allegiance to the Emirates.” Umarov was shifted out of his security service role in November 2024, in the extended wake of the assassination attempt on Komil Allamjanov. Allamjanov, at the time of the October 2024 attempt, had recently stepped down from his role as deputy head of the presidential administration. He has since returned to government service, as an adviser to the powerful head of the presidential administration, Saida Mirziyoyeva (the president’s eldest daughter). As of January 2026 he was also appointed to a seemingly bespoke role: advisor-ambassador and representative of the presidential administration in the United States. Umarov, meanwhile, was named first deputy chairman of Uzbekistan’s National Olympic Committee – his father-in-law, the president, is the chairman. According to OCCRP and Ozodlik, at some point in 2025, Umarov became the owner of 13 properties in Dubai, worth around $7 million. The properties previously belonged to his younger brother, Oybek Umarov, who purchased them in 2021 and 2022, according to leaked Dubai real estate data obtained by OCCRP. It is not clear precisely how or when they came to be listed with Umarov’s name on the deeds, whether the properties were gifted or purchased. While Umarov has notably expensive tastes – for example, he’s been pictured wearing a limited edition Richard Mille watch valued at up to $1.9 million – his government position doesn’t quite explain his apparent wealth. Uzbek officials do not have to disclose their income declarations publicly. OCCRP and Ozodlik reported, “Public commercial registries show no record of [Otabek Umarov] owning private companies during his time as deputy presidential security chief.” His brother, however, does have extensive business holdings, including in banking, cement, and metalwork. A high-ranking government source told The Diplomat in late 2024 that Umarov’s assets and businesses were held in the names of others, including Ulugbek Shadmanov who was implicated in an apparent attempt to manipulate the U.S. sanctions system to target Allamjonov and another Uzbek official in the months before the assassination attempt. Shadmanov was earlier named in the Pandora Papers as connected to an offshore company, though there are few details available. In December 2024 he was detained in Dubai and extradited rapidly – apparently without the proper legal process – to Uzbekistan, regardless of the fact that he held what’s known as a “ Golden Visa ” in the UAE. Despite high-powered legal representation and a campaign on his behalf, very little has been reported since about his case. Ultimately, the OCCRP and Ozodlik investigation raises far more questions than it answers; that’s the nature of investigations into the opaque underbelly of Uzbek politics (and those of the UAE, to boot). As I told Ozodlik , we don’t know exactly how Umarov acquired UAE citizenship, who was involved, and who knew about it. As noted above, the process to acquired UAE citizenship necessitates a nomination by a royal court or senior official. It’s nearly impossible to believe that Umarov’s role and connections were unknown at the time to the UAE’s authorities. Then there are questions of what comes next. Uzbekistan does not officially recognize dual citizenship. Holding a second citizenship isn’t illegal per se – though it does violate laws related to Umarov’s specific position at the time. Nevertheless, “voluntarily acquiring a passport of a foreign state” is listed as possible grounds for revocation of Uzbek citizenship. Already have an account? Log in . https://thediplomat.com/2026/09/uzbekist.body: Legislative Chamber of the Oliy Majlis Credit: Uzbekistan Presidency Subscribe for ads-free reading For the second time in the span of a year a brutal child abuse case has sparked heated public discussion in Uzbekistan. Reportedly, a five-year-old girl was repeatedly raped in a public kindergarten by a facilities manager who worked at the school in the Uchkurgan district of Namangan. According to the mother of the survivor, the alleged perpetrator is their neighbor and she became suspicious after she saw him smiling at her five-year-old daughter. She gently asked the girl questions only to find out that the facilities manager would buy sweets for the girl, tell her he loved her, and promised to buy more presents and sweets if she didn’t expose him. The mother suspects the man had threatened her daughter. Last year a similar case, which also occurred in Namangan, where a previously imprisoned convict raped a seven-year-old girl, caused a wave of demands by the public to restore the death penalty for serious crimes such as the sexual assault of minors. Public discussions over the death penalty typically emerge in Uzbekistan after news of an especially brutal crime against children breaks. An earlier wave of loud discussions took place in 2024 after a three-year-old was stabbed 12 times. What’s new this time is that high-ranking political figures are getting involved. Saida Mirziyoyeva, the head of the presidential administration and a deputy chair of the Security Council (and also the president’s daughter) chimed in. “In my opinion, the death penalty should be used for such heinous crimes. Unfortunately, the current legislation does not provide for the death penalty,” she wrote on her Telegram channel on September 27. “We are preparing a proposal to amend the legislation to maximize liability for this type of crime,” she added. Echoing Mirziyoyeva’s words, Alisher Qodirov, leader of the Milliy Tiklanish (National Revival) Democratic Party and deputy speaker of the Uzbek parliament, called death penalty a “necessity.” Qodirov is famous for making nationalist, sometimes controversial statements. “The continued existence of those who intentionally kill innocent people, especially child murderers and pedophiles, is a motivation for further crimes of this kind!” Qodirov wrote on his Telegram, reposting Mirziyoyeva’s earlier statement. This is not the first time Qodirov has voiced his position on the death penalty. Previously, in 2024, after news reports about a three-year-old girl being murdered, Qodirov suggested “cleansing” society. “It’s illogical to use our taxes to support a criminal who’s become an animal, keep him healthy, feed him, and then wait for someone else to die! Society needs to be cleansed of such people!” he wrote . Both Mirziyoyeva and Qodirov know that Uzbekistan abolished capital punishment in 2008 and acceded to the Second Optional Protocol to the ICCPR aimed at abolition. Uzbekistan has no mechanism to reinstate the death penalty without a much larger legal overhaul, and no such overhaul is presently underway. In a rather unusual course of developments for Uzbekistan, the discussion over the death penalty divided the country’s political parties. As a new bill to increase liability for violence against children was introduced to the Legislative Chamber on September 29, Qodirov announced a neutral position on the proposed bill and doubled down on his stance regarding the need to resurrect the death penalty. Qodirov referred to Norwegian neo-Nazi and mass murderer Anders Behring Breivik , stating that he had complained “about the lack of facilities for writing a book, and those conditions were subsequently provided for him.” Qodirov’s interpretation isn’t quite accurate. While Breivik did complain about the “stab-resistant” pen he was made to write with and was reportedly provided with an electronic typewriter, Breivik’s communications continue to be censored by prison authorities and he has not published a book. Nevertheless, using Breivik as a point of reference, Qodirov questioned the compatibility of Uzbek values and international law. “Whose footsteps are we following!?” he asked. “We will also be forced to create conditions for our pedophile if he asks, because the international law we follow sees him as a human being, not as a dead person.” Bobur Bekmurodov, a member of the Legislative Chamber of the Oliy Majlis and leader of the Yuksalish movement, opposed Qodirov’s statements openly. His arguments are clear: the constitution prohibits the death penalty, bringing the death penalty back could put child victims in greater danger, break Uzbekistan’s international obligations and raise the possibility of errors in judicial practices. “If child rape is punishable by death, there is nothing to stop the perpetrator from destroying the only witness, the child himself,” wrote Bekmurodov. While the grief over the case is genuine, the debate over the death penalty is a populist, opportunistic response. In a country where no other important questions are debated by high (or low) profile politicians, children and women’s abuse is a risk-free topic. Not only does it attract empathy from millions of citizens, but it also gains praise from international organizations. Siding with an innocent child is always a winning move. As outrage grows, officials do their best to appease the public. The investigation over the case is now under the prosecutor general’s control . Shakhnoza Mirziyoyeva, another daughter of President Shavkat Mirziyoyev and the first deputy director of the National Agency for Social Protection, reported that her agency is also involved in the case and the survivor’s family will be moved to another city and provided with housing. The agency also suggested changing the girl’s surname to ensure her privacy as she rehabilitates. The Ministry of Preschool and School Education formed a working group to address the situation. Right now, all attention is being given to maximizing punishment for one perpetrator and not letting another incident happen. What is left out of these debates is the failure of the systems that should have protected this girl. The mother of the survivor told local media that the cameras in the kindergarten did not record anything that day. And more absurdly, she had been told that the perpetrator was responsible for the cameras. The perpetrator’s wife allegedly offered her a bribe to close the case, too. The staff of the kindergarten who are supposed to protect the children in their care, are hiding behind paperwork instead of showing compassion. The director of the kindergarten said she was on a holiday when the alleged incident occurred and she had already provided explanatory letters to the police. She also added that children are never left unsupervised. The girl’s teacher also swore the girl was never left alone – “Not an hour, not a minute, would [she] be left unattended.” Local media outlets and the authorities have not disclosed the perpetrator’s name or released a mugshot. Netizens, however, have found his photos and full name and doxed his identity on social media pages. Yesterday, Shakhnoza Mirziyoyeva noted that her agency, together with other relevant bodies, had been working on a draft law that would introduce life imprisonment for crimes involving child sexual abuse. “We also propose to strengthen the responsibility of parents for neglecting children and of educators for allowing violence and discrimination, and to provide legal assistance and protection to child victims at every stage of the investigation and trial,” the agency’s Telegram post stated . From 2022 to 2026 445 cases of rape involving minors under 14 years old were formally registered in Uzbekistan. Not all cases make headlines. Journalist and economist Bakhodir Abdullayev noted that the legislation on lifetime imprisonment for sexual abuse of minors was supposed to be passed by April 2026. https://thediplomat.com/2026/09/can-a-ne.body: Condos in Bishkek, the capital of Kyrgyzstan, often use scarce potable water to support non-native plants such as roses. Credit: Walt Ohnesorge Subscribe for ads-free reading Can gardens act as a network of miniature sponge cities to have a positive impact on climate change in Central Asia? A preponderance of aesthetic decisions and other barriers hold back the adaptation of Central Asia’s cities, but individuals and local authorities can make a difference. Kyrgyzstan, and Central Asia more broadly, are experiencing stress on available groundwater reserves. As Dr. Eric Rudenshiold noted in an article for the Caspian Policy Center last year, “Driven by regional temperature increases, the region’s glaciers are melting at a rate four times faster than the global average and far faster than anticipated.” Central Asia’s glaciers feed rivers and streams throughout the year. One can easily imagine a future in which rivers run dry and entire cities are required to use only water gathered from rain that falls in just a few short months of the year. In a future like this, having the ability to retain water in place could mean the difference between thriving and ceasing to exist. Stronger storms, floods, droughts, deadly heatwaves, and mass migration are putting pressure on policymakers to follow through with plans to update infrastructure. An empty canal in Bishkek. Water from rain and glacial melt is directed through and away from the city to evaporate downstream. (Photograph by Walt Ohnesorge) What Can Central Asia Learn from Sponge Cities? During a public lecture in 2003, architect Kongjian Yu coined the term “sponge cities” while outlining a set of urban planning principles developed to manage water in flood-prone regions of China. Sponge cities have since been enshrined in Chinese public policy by the Chinese Communist Party as a regulatory framework for development in the country. Kyrgyzstan has been interested in China’s governance model as a way to alleviate poverty, but its development and domestic urban planning initiatives offer other lessons. Time is running out for risk-prone areas of the world to make lasting, meaningful changes in the face of climate change, and some adaptation ideas may have been overlooked in parts of Central Asia. This oversight is evidenced by the colossal loss of green space in Bishkek since the Soviet era. While Kyrgyzstan’s cities have lost greenery, China has mandated the construction of climate-resilient urban spaces. Adopting a strong approach to state funding and regulation of green spaces is likely to create jobs in the industry and holds potential, where green spaces are fruit-bearing, to reduce food insecurity. Both of these outcomes could reduce poverty in Kyrgyzstan, and Bishkek’s own Green Cities Action Plan acknowledges the need for climate resilience and adequate green spaces. However, in lieu of decisive regulatory action and funding, much of the work of adapting to new climate realities falls on individual gardeners and cooperatives. Climate change has a disproportionate impact, both geographically on specific regions of Kyrgyzstan, and particularly on marginalized communities. As members of the El-Too foundation point out, “at the municipality and political level, women are not included in the decision-making processes; all issues related to land are discussed with the participation of men mainly... The situation is especially difficult for women that are employed as invisible forces in agriculture and have no other source of income.” Miniaturizing Sponge Cities While researching this topic, we were struck by a lack of sources for community-lead gardening initiatives in Kyrgyzstan. We discovered that Bishkek has no immediately identifiable grass roots collectives piloting alternative or sustainable agriculture inside the city. Even a cursory glance at New York City yields several sources and projects, and the same is true for other global cities. It is far easier to identify the challenges, like existing attention to inefficient practices, than attempts at solutions. The scale of new development in Bishkek is profound, dwarfing initiatives to create a greener city, preserve green spaces, and retrofit existing spaces for greater efficiency. With that in mind, we considered what it might look like if individuals in Bishkek took it upon themselves to implement better water preservation systems. Homemade drip irrigation feeds an area near a condo in Bishkek, where residents improvise to utilize water efficiently during summer months. (Photograph by Walt Ohnesorge) One dacha owner, Asel, shared that she has never thought of climate change when managing her garden. She planted species that her landscape designer recommended, who was guided by beauty rather than water management or other climate change concerns. The same could be said about the managed gardens of some condominium buildings. Bakyt, a groundskeeper at one such building, said, “We plant roses here and use drinking water to water them.” Another dacha owner, Zarina, said she’d never seen a list of plants recommended for the local climate, but expressed interest in such a list. This interest leads us to believe that, given a coordinated campaign to make information and tools available, individuals might be easily motivated to shift their habits toward more sustainable gardening practices. A small container garden near a condo in Bishkek reflects a local desire for more green spaces. (Photograph by Walt Ohnesorge) As Walt Ohnesorge, an artist and designer (and one of the authors of this piece) observed of many condos in Bishkek, “they could attach a catchment system to the gutter and plant perennial, food bearing plants to save drinking water, supplement tenants’ groceries, and utilize rain water for a more efficient system.” Nuraiym Syrgak, Kyrgyzstani social researcher and ecologist, and former executive director of the El-Too Public Foundation and a board member of the Association of Legal Entities “Green Alliance of Kyrgyzstan,” shared her ideas and experience implementing ecological projects. There are things people can do, at all levels, to help the land adapt to a changing climate. She noted that specific patterns of water allocation in villages have consequences. “Water for irrigation is mainly given to large plots. Gardens and zones within the village receive little water,” Syrgak said. “Therefore, we wanted precisely these small areas to become the center of attention.” Syrgak added that women, in particular, are good agents of change. “Men tend to be skeptical of anything new, especially at first, whereas women try to apply every new thing. In this sense, women are fantastic change agents. That is why we started working with them and later brought the men on board. As a result, we ended up with a family-based approach to agriculture.” Beyond villages and gardens, parks can also be transformed into miniature sponges within urban landscapes. “We often see these trees in our parks, which are not adapted to our climate,” Syrgak noted “Of course, they are beautiful. But at the same time they do not give more function. They do not give shade. They require a lot of work. And permaculture is such a philosophy, so that a person works less. And cooperates with nature to minimize work.” Syrgak stressed that there was no clear list of priority species for cultivation to fight climate change, but the centering of local species is a good place to start. “If you look at our deserts or abandoned zones, there are always these elms, which is a local type of tree and does not require watering,” Syrgak pointed out. “Then there are a lot of species like local shrubs, which could be useful for changes. https://thediplomat.com/2026/09/chinas-y.body: Credit: Shutterstock Subscribe for ads-free reading In the U.S. state of Hawai‘i, Iris lives far from the pressures of urban China. Growing up in Zhejiang, she spent much of her childhood on what her mother called “self-improvement”: Olympiad math, piano lessons, and daily swimming. After graduating from New York University (NYU), Iris chose a simple, quiet life in Hawai‘i, using geographic distance to protect her personal autonomy from the pressure facing Chinese women in their 20s to settle down, marry, and have children. Halfway across the world, Jessica is confronting the same expectations from within China. After studying in Shanghai and Europe and working at an international organization in New York, where a mentor once urged her to stop working late and “enjoy the New York night,” Jessica returned to China to finish her master’s thesis and enter the domestic job market. There, she met a second, more intimate pressure: the expectation that she should marry and have children. Rather than quietly accepting it, she confronted the idea directly, over dinner with her mother, asking: “Are you actually happy in your own marriage? What has it genuinely brought you?” Iris and Jessica belong to a highly educated cohort of young Chinese women whose lives are unfolding alongside a demographic problem the state is eager to solve. Facing an aging population, a shrinking workforce, and historically low fertility rates, Beijing introduced the Three-Child Policy in 2021 , allowing Chinese couples to have up to three children. China’s government has since increasingly emphasized marriage and childbearing as social priorities . Yet China’s demographic crisis gained steam during the same decades of modernization that gave women access to more education, higher incomes, and greater mobility. That means women like Iris and Jessica have more reasons, and more means, to delay or reconsider marriage and motherhood. Research on China’s education expansion by Jiwei Chen and Jiangying Guo of Nanjing Agricultural University found that increased female education can delay entry into marriage and childbirth and reduce fertility, in part by raising the opportunity costs of childrearing. The modernization that expanded women’s choices has made the traditional sequence of adulthood – marry, have children, settle near family – less inevitable. Jessica confronts this tension directly, pressing her own mother on whether marriage delivered what it promised and treating parenthood as a choice to question rather than a milestone to check off. Iris resists more obliquely: rather than arguing with the assumption that a good daughter eventually settles down close to home, she puts enough distance (first New York, then Hawai‘i) between herself and the people who would enforce the traditional path, letting their expectations fade into background noise instead of demands she has to answer. Neither is rejecting family, marriage, or children outright. Both are refusing to treat any of these options as the default for a Chinese woman. Jessica: Deconstructing the Script Upon returning to China to finish her thesis, Jessica found the job hunt less a search for a career than a reckoning with what kind of life she was willing to accept. In Europe and New York, she’d grown used to a workplace culture defined by what she calls “松弛感”: ease, dignity, being treated first as a person. One night, working late in New York, her mentor stopped her: “You are in New York. You should go enjoy the night.” The line stuck with her. The anecdote formed a sharp contrast with Jessica’s internship at a major Chinese internet company, where a hyper-competitive, results-only culture left people passing their anxiety down the hierarchy. She posted a comparison of the two experiences on Xiaohongshu and it sparked a fight in the comments: some dismissed it as a naive “student mindset”; others agreed with a Chinese woman writing from Europe, who argued that Western employers need their workers enough to treat them decently, while Chinese managers can simply replace anyone who underperforms. For Jessica, the real question was how much room there was for personal choice to override social norms. That questioning carried over from professional pressures straight into marriage. Years abroad had sharpened her sense of independence, but her father still pictured a conventional future for her, and relatives kept the pressure alive by mentioning which of her peers had already married. Jessica pushed back on the premise itself, arguing that a mother-daughter bond can matter as much as a marital one. She half-jokingly tells relatives that if marriage is unavoidable, it’s better to get in and out of it quickly than drag out something broken. The same skepticism shapes how she thinks about children. She’s fond of them but treats parenthood as a serious undertaking that shouldn’t simply follow marriage on a fixed timeline. She has watched enough families to conclude that unhappy marriages, and kids who are under-supported despite material comfort, are more common than the success stories that get celebrated. Teenagers hit adolescence with mental health struggles, some withdrawing from school, often because parents were too consumed by work to be present. Jessica has also watched women of her mother’s generation absorb the burden of family life, reshaping careers around husbands and children. She has no intention of doing the same by default. That came to a head at a family dinner, when marriage came up again and Jessica turned the question back on her mother: was she actually happy in her marriage? What had it given her? It was an invitation to examine whether women’s sacrifices for family are as inevitable as they’re made to seem. “If my pain can never be carried by anyone else,” Jessica told The Diplomat, “then my happiness has to be mine to build, too.” She’s stopped ruling out partners by age, and increasingly by nationality; a good match is rare enough without narrowing the field further. Her mother has softened too, no longer pressing on timelines. None of this makes her anti-marriage or anti-motherhood. But Jessica insists on the right to decide what place they hold in her life, rather than letting either define her adulthood before she’s had the chance to define it herself. Iris: Exiting the Room Growing up in Zhejiang, Iris Liu’s school breaks were a rotation of enrichment classes: Olympiad math, swimming, roller skating, dance, painting, piano. As an only child, she absorbed her mother’s conviction that giving her every possible advantage was simply what good parenting looked like. Before Iris had even reached middle school, her mother was already telling her she needed to learn to swim: American Ivy League universities, she’d heard, liked students who could swim. The plan was always aimed outward, toward a future far from home. Years later, Iris would indeed leave China. She just wouldn’t use that mobility the way her mother had imagined. The first crack came early, almost by accident. A two-week middle-school trip to Los Angeles was supposed to preview the life her mother was preparing her for. Instead, Iris came home unimpressed: a suburban campus, cafeteria pizza, none of the excitement she’d expected. Her disappointment rippled into her mother’s plans: the pressure around swimming eased, and the push toward an international high-school track quietly faded. Still, the broader trajectory held. Iris went on to NYU, and after graduation had the kind of options her education was supposed to produce: interviews for corporate jobs with six-figure salaries. She did not end up in any of these. She chose instead a job in Hawai‘i. Her parents had a particular idea of success. When Iris told them about interviews with major firms with salaries over $100,000 a year, they barely reacted. Her father countered instead with a story about a colleague’s child who’d quit an investment-banking job after three years, burned out. It was mea

https://thediplomat.com/2026/10/the-less.body: A Taliban checkpoint in Balkh province, Afghanistan. Credit: Agnieszka Pikulicka Subscribe for ads-free reading In the female section of an upscale restaurant in Kabul’s Shar-e Naw, a waiter brings me a menu and a form. Only two lines are filled in: one bears an Italian name, the other a local one. The waiter explains that guests are required to fill it in at the request of the Ministry of Interior. It is for the guests’ own safety, he emphasizes, slightly uneasy. It is hard to tell if he believes it. I look at the form. It asks for the guest’s name, date of birth, passport number, address in Kabul, as well as when they visited the restaurant. “It is for your security,” the waiter repeats. I give him the blank form back. “I feel secure without it,” I say. He doesn’t insist. He takes my order and disappears. Five years after the withdrawal of NATO troops from Afghanistan, and into the rule of the Taliban, the group’s control over the country is stable. While the Taliban might not have access to the newest surveillance technologies, their infiltration of local communities is high. They had learned their lesson from their first period of rule, the emirate that ended in 2001 with the U.S. invasion, a United Nations official tells me. “You can say that fundamentally, ideologically, they haven’t really changed. But in terms of control, consolidation, management, messaging, they are far more sophisticated now,” he says. “The first emirate was a brand new experiment. The second emirate is still an experiment, but they have learned a lot of lessons. They are smart.” Kabul still reminds me of its former self, as if time had stopped. The streets are bustling with life; street vendors cover the pavements, selling products ranging from food and cigarettes to clothes and electronics. The new regime is seen in the details: fewer women walk the streets, less rubbish lies scattered across the city center – a lasting feature of the corrupt rule back in the Republic days – and the streets seem less chaotic. But at first glance, the changes are small, sometimes imperceptible. A Taliban checkpoint in Balkh province, Afghanistan. Photo by Agnieszka Pikulicka. Everyone I speak with says that the country has become safer. Twenty years of war and decades of fighting have taken their toll on people. The Taliban, while brutal and devoted to anti-modern ideas, has nevertheless brought peace. The paradox is that the Taliban were the main perpetrators of violence during the Republic days. It was due to their attacks on cars that traveling between provinces used to be dangerous and caution was advised. Since they took power, traveling between different regions of Afghanistan has suddenly become possible. Now, Taliban checkpoints cover the whole country. Some of them are stricter, with soldiers standing under the white flag bearing the Shahada, the Islamic declaration of faith, and the Taliban symbol, checking travel permits meticulously. Other checkpoints are more relaxed, and it is enough to slow down and let the Taliban gaze into the car. There are few roads that the group does not control. To leave their place of residence, drivers need special permits, and so do tourists. A letter from “Afghan Tour,” a unit responsible for travelers, is required to travel and stay in another province. It is unclear what its purpose is, other than surveillance. In Kabul, the “Afghan Tour” official says that getting a travel letter requires paying for an expensive tour. But it is possible to get it in Bamyan, another province, for a small fee. Most other regions also issue such letters in exchange for booking an inexpensive “tour” with an official guide. It is unclear if its price is official or simply a bribe paid for obtaining the letter. It is also hard to call it a tour. As part of the “tour” I book to stay in Mazar-i-Sharif, the local guide shows me into the Blue Mosque, the shrine of Imam Ali, first built in the 12th century before Genghis Khan leveled the original building to the ground. But the tour included little in terms of a history lesson. The guide complained about his low earnings, suggesting I pay extra for his time. Then he demanded that I share my local contacts with him. For my own safety, of course. Today the new Taliban administration is stable. Ministries work, and courts solve disputes without the need to pay bribes, I am told. 96 percent of the poppy fields have been eradicated and hundreds of addicts who formerly squatted on Kabul’s streets and under bridges have been forced into rehabs. This is the kind of “stability” I know all too well from Central Asia’s autocracies, Afghanistan’s neighbors: they are brutal and relentless, but the pavements are clean. According to a recent report from Human Rights Watch , censorship of local media outlets and restrictions on freedom of expression have intensified, while journalists, activists, academics and other regime critics have faced repression, torture, and arbitrary arrests. “The Taliban always accuse us of being spies, it’s hard to work these days,” one local photojournalist told me. The Blue Mosque, the shrine of Imam Ali, in Mazar-i-Sharif. Photo by Agnieszka Pikulicka. Women have been denied basic rights, such as the right to education beyond sixth grade. A woman visiting her parental home who does not return to her husband can be deemed a criminal. That includes survivors of domestic violence. A woman accused of touching, shaking hands with, or hugging a man who is not her mahram, a close male relative with whom marriage is prohibited, can spend a year in prison. Two months if a girl or a boy is seen dancing. A new “Preachers’ law” defines Muslims as followers of the Hanafi school of Islam. Local Hazaras, or Ismaili minority groups, are now officially deemed heretics. “Many Ismailis now hide their faith,” one man from the community tells me. He lost his job in a school in Badakhshan due to his faith. All that in the name of the “peaceful and clear sky above us,” as Uzbekistan’s late President Islam Karimov used to say in justifying his own repressive rule. Except that this is not the reality for most Afghans. While the war might be over – except for skirmishes in Badakhshan province and regular attacks from Pakistan – Afghanistan is hardly facing a post-war recovery. The withdrawal of U.S. and NATO troops and the coming to power of the Taliban, a government recognized only by Russia, meant that the United Nations mandate became much more restricted in scope. Cooperation with the de facto Taliban authorities has focused mostly on securing people’s very basic needs. Most international non-governmental and governmental organizations, and media, have left, and with them hundreds of local jobs disappeared. The biggest difference is noticeable in large cities: Kabul, Herat, or Mazar-i-Sharif, where previously educated, English-speaking men and women could find employment and develop careers. As another local journalist told me, during the Republic days he could support his family working as a photographer and videographer. Now, work is scarce. He has not had any projects for several months. “The situation seems to get worse every day and every year. Unemployment has reached a very high level, especially for people like me who work in the arts and creative fields,” he says. “People of Afghanistan are facing many other serious problems, including unemployment, untreated illnesses, hunger, poverty, and lack of adequate shelter. I do not see a clear government plan to address unemployment at its roots.” According to the United Nations , more than 17 million people, or 40 per cent of Afghanistan’s population, are projected to face acute food insecurity. And the situation is worsening. While following the U.S. withdrawal, thousands of Afghans left the country in search of a better life, this trend is now reversing – though not voluntarily.
