https://novastan.org/fr/kazakhstan/au-ka.body: 2 octobre 2026 Rédigé par : Eléa Muresan Tags Armée Astana Bizutages Défense Jeunesse Service militaire Violences Un paramilitaire kazakh lors d'exercices militaire en 2000 (illustration). Crédit : Wikicommons Au Kazakhstan, l’automne marque le retour de la conscription. Si certains jeunes hommes considèrent le service militaire comme un devoir envers leur pays, d’autres cherchent par tous les moyens à y échapper. À Astana, les récits de recrutements forcés dans les lieux publics et de violences dans les casernes nourrissent une défiance persistante envers l’armée. Au Kazakhstan, le mois de septembre a marqué l’ouverture de la campagne automnale de recrutement de jeunes, dans le cadre de la conscription. Le gouvernement kazakh prévoit le recrutement de 23 000 hommes , âgés de 18 à 25 ans, d’ici fin décembre. Faites un don à Novastan Héritage de l’ère soviétique, le service militaire représente au Kazakhstan un fait de société important, car il concerne l’ensemble des jeunes hommes. En principe, tous sont soumis à l’obligation de servir l’armée pendant une année entière, à travers une formation physique et théorique permettant de se familiariser avec l’univers militaire et sa discipline. Mais dans la pratique, de nombreux jeunes cherchent à y échapper, mettant en place un volet de stratégies pour obtenir des dispenses. Associée à une réputation sulfureuse, l’armée peine à recruter, malgré le caractère obligatoire de la conscription. Des méthodes de recrutement plus offensives que la simple convocation se sont développées depuis quelques années, parmi lesquelles des formes d’enlèvement de jeunes orchestrés par la police dans des espaces publics. Violence et controverses dans l’armée Novastan est allé à la rencontre des habitants d’Astana, la capitale kazakhe, afin de comprendre leurs représentations et expériences relatives au service militaire. La majorité de ces échanges laissent entendre que le service militaire ne jouit pas d’une bonne réputation auprès des habitants de la capitale kazakhe. « Moi je n’irai pas. Chaque année il y a des centaines de garçons qui reviennent blessés . Certains meurent, d’autres qui se suicident, c’est hyper violent. Le Kazakhstan n’est même pas un pays en guerre, ça n’a aucun sens « , raconte Jordan, jeune informaticien âgé de 23 ans. Lire aussi sur Novastan : Dans les rangs de l’armée kazakhe, une violence inouïe : « Mes reins se sont déplacés à cause des coups » La conscription suscite effectivement de l’inquiétude auprès de nombreux kazakhs. Des drames survenant chaque année ont forgé une réputation de violence dans l’imaginaire collectif autour du service militaire : morts, blessures, harcèlement, suicides. Parmi les scandales les plus viraux des dernières années, le cas de Moukhtar Yerebatan, jeune homme de 18 ans, victime d’une commotion cérébrale dans le cadre de son service, avait également suscité l’indignation dans tout le pays. Après un coma de deux ans, la mort du jeune homme le 23 juin dernier avait relancé la polémique sur les violences au sein de l’armée. D’après les sources officielles, il se serait blessé à la tête en tombant dans les toilettes par accident, mais cette version est contestée par ses proches qui suspectent des violences intentionnelles. La semaine passée, la mort d’une dizaine de jeunes conscrits lors d’un accident dans la mer Caspienne a intensifié la colère et les inquiétudes des parents concernant le service militaire, ne croyant plus en la capacité de l’armée à assurer la sécurité de leurs enfants. Lire aussi sur Novastan : Dans les rangs de l’armée kazakhe, une violence inouïe : « Mes reins se sont déplacés à cause des coups » « Les nouvelles sont terrifiantes. Si j’avais un fils, en aucun cas je le laisserais rejoindre l’armée « , confie Samal, hôtesse de l’air et mère de famille à Astana. Nombreux sont les jeunes qui mettent en place des stratégies pour échapper à la conscription, souvent avec le soutien de leurs parents et de leur réseau. Ces méthodes peuvent se baser sur des dispositifs légaux, mais aussi sur des formes de corruption. Sont notamment exemptées les personnes déclarées inaptes lors de la visite médicale, et les inscrits à l’université. Timur, 22 ans, ancien étudiant en économie et commerce, raconte que beaucoup d’étudiants à l’université sont uniquement inscrits pour échapper à l’armée. Il explique les raisons pour lesquelles lui-même s’est soustrait au service militaire : « Je pense que c’est pas pour moi. J’ai pas envie de perdre un an de ma vie, c’est pas le bon moment, j’ai des projets personnels, je compte acheter un appart, voyager... « Rouslan, 26 ans, créateur de contenu, a suivi de longues études et obtenu un doctorat en anthropologie, un choix motivé à la fois par son intérêt pour la discipline et par la possibilité temporaire d’échapper au service obligatoire. « Après 25 ans, si on n’a pas encore servi, on peut être exempté en passant une formation militaire de 40 jours. C’est payant, mais les conditions sont beaucoup moins rudes, on est mieux traités que pour le service d’un an. « « Rapts » et « Kidnapping » Faute de parvenir à recruter un nombre de jeunes correspondant aux effectifs prévus annuellement, le ministère de la Défense met en place des mesures offensives. En particulier, ce que les locaux nomment des “rapts” ou “kidnappings” de jeunes, des formes de mobilisation forcées menées par la police et les militaires dans des lieux publics, sans être toujours justifiées légalement. Timour raconte que pendant les périodes de recrutement, à l’image de celle qui a débuté le 1er septembre, de nombreux jeunes évitent au maximum de fréquenter des lieux publics, par peur de se faire convoquer de force : « La police vient dans des endroits comme ça, par exemple dans le jardin botanique, où y’a beaucoup de jeunes, potentiellement ceux qui n’ont pas servi. Ça peut être un club, un billard, ou des salles de jeux vidéo, ce type d’endroits, où les mecs traînent souvent. » Lire aussi sur Novastan : Avec de nouveaux blindés, le Kazakhstan fait évoluer son armement pour une diversification prudente Un système de solidarité entre usagers s’est d’ailleurs développé sur l’application 2GIS, l’équivalent de Google Maps au Kazakhstan, pour s’entraider à éviter les lieux. Les utilisateurs peuvent se notifier entre eux et écrire des messages à propos de plusieurs lieux publics. Sur l’image, un utilisateur notifie « Police présente pour conscription, ils sont avec des camions « . Contrairement à ses amis qui réduisent leurs sorties pendant les périodes de recrutement, Timur a fait le choix de garder son mode de vie inchangé malgré le risque. « C ‘est impossible de surveiller partout où ils pourraient me trouver. Un ami est allé au magasin près de chez lui, et quand il est sorti, ils l’ont attrapé, embarqué dans une voiture et envoyé direct au bureau militaire. On peut se faire prendre n’importe où, mais je n’ai pas envie de rester enfermé chez moi constamment. J’ai peut-être de la chance « , sourit-il. Pourtant, au cours des deux dernières années, Timour a été embarqué par la police à plusieurs reprises, depuis qu’il a interrompu ses études. Pour s’en sortir, il compte surtout sur le soutien de son réseau. “ J’ai des amis, certains dans des organes d’État. Disons qu’ils ont des ressources administratives. Quand je les appelais, on me libérait directement ” explique Timour. Il relate le cas d’un ami qui a échappé de justesse à l’armée. Après avoir été embarqué par la police, il aurait été aidé par son père pour s’inscrire in extremis dans une université afin d’obtenir un sursis. D’autres, moins chanceux, ne disposent pas assez de ressources sociales et financières pour se tirer d’affaires. Si les bourses au mérite existent pour entrer dans l’enseignement supérieur, les places sont rares et la stratégie de l’inscription à l’université reste souvent coûteuse. « J’ai progressé dans tout » Malgré les controverses et les appréhensions de nombreux citoyens kazakhs, certains ayant

https://novastan.org/fr/kirghizstan/eau-.body: 16 septembre 2026 Rédigé par : Mathieu Lemoine Tags Accès abonné Asie centrale Changement climatique Kirghizstan Ouzbékistan Tadjikistan Syr-Daria à Baïkonour, Kazakhstan. Photo : Ninaras / Wikimedia Commons, CC BY 4.0. Souvent présentée comme une source potentielle de conflits en Asie centrale, l'eau est aussi au cœur d'une coopération régionale ancienne et en pleine évolution. Après vingt-cinq années passées à travailler dans la région, dont près de vingt sur les questions d'eau et d'assainissement, Olivier Normand observe une transformation profonde des relations entre les États d'Asie centrale. Des héritages soviétiques au rapprochement récent entre le Kirghizstan, le Tadjikistan et l'Ouzbékistan, la gestion de l'eau raconte une autre histoire de la région. Lorsqu'Olivier Normand arrive pour la première fois en Asie centrale, en juin 2000, la région ne ressemble guère à celle d'aujourd'hui. Son premier contact avec l'Ouzbékistan est presque fortuit : une rencontre avec un Ouzbek à Moscou le conduit à participer à un projet consacré à de nouvelles techniques agricoles. Il traverse alors le pays, de Namangan à Ourguentch, en passant par Boukhara, Samarcande, Termez et Tachkent. À partir de 2003, il dirige depuis Termez un projet d'appui au ministère du Travail, avant de travailler sur différents projets sociaux. Depuis 2007, ses activités sont principalement consacrées à l'eau et à l'assainissement, notamment dans le bassin du Syr-Daria et la vallée de Ferghana. Ce qui l'a retenu en Asie centrale ? « Le sentiment d'être au centre du monde et d'assister à l'Histoire en marche », répond-il. Vingt-cinq ans plus tard, cette histoire a considérablement changé. Parmi les transformations qu'il aurait difficilement imaginées au début des années 2000, Normand cite l'ouverture des frontières, une plus grande liberté de circulation à l'intérieur de l'Ouzbékistan, la simplification du système bancaire et des taux de change, le développement d'Internet, la modernisation des infrastructures et la transformation des villes. Mais il insiste surtout sur le rapprochement entre les pays d'Asie centrale, et notamment entre ceux qui se partagent la vallée de Ferghana. Le 31 mars 2025, les présidents du Kirghizstan, du Tadjikistan et de l'Ouzbékistan se sont retrouvés à Khodjent, au Tadjikistan, pour signer un traité fixant le point de jonction de leurs trois frontières ainsi que la Déclaration de Khodjent sur l'amitié éternelle. Cette rencontre venait consacrer le règlement de différends frontaliers qui avaient longtemps empoisonné les relations régionales. Elle a également ouvert de nouvelles perspectives de coopération dans des domaines allant des transports et du commerce à l'énergie, l'environnement et l'eau. Pour Normand, le 31 mars 2025 constitue ainsi moins un accord spécifiquement consacré à l'eau qu'un symbole d'une évolution beaucoup plus large : la région apprend progressivement à gérer collectivement . . . https://novastan.org/en/kazakhstan/kazak.body: 2 October 2026 Daniyar Sadvakasov Edited by: Mathieu Lemoine Tags Artificial intelligence Electricity Infrastructure Kazakhstan A sign for the Data Center Valley project in Ekibastuz, where Kazakhstan plans to develop a major cluster of AI and data centre infrastructure. Support Novastan, the European Central Asia magazine By supporting Novastan, you are supporting the only English, French and German-language media specialising in Central Asia. We’re independent and we need your help to stay that way! Support Novastan Kazakhstan has begun building a major data centre cluster in the industrial city of Ekibastuz. Its first phase will require around 50 MW of power, but the government’s longer-term ambition is to expand the site to as much as 1 GW. As the country seeks to position itself as a regional hub for artificial intelligence and computing, questions remain over whether its electricity and water infrastructure can keep pace In early 2026, Kazakhstan launched construction of its Data Center Valley project in Ekibastuz, in the northern Pavlodar region, following instructions from President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev. The first facility in the planned cluster is expected to have an energy capacity of around 50 MW. Depending on investor demand, however, the campus could eventually expand to as much as 1 GW and occupy up to 1,300 hectares. Ekibastuz was not chosen by accident. The city is one of Kazakhstan’s main energy centres and is home to the Ekibastuz GRES-1 and GRES-2 coal-fired power stations. Yet the scale of the project raises questions over whether Kazakhstan can generate enough electricity for such a large new consumer, how the data centres will be supplied with water, and what environmental pressures the development could create. What is Kazakhstan planning to build? According to the Pavlodar regional administration, the precise distribution of land between individual data centres, energy facilities and other infrastructure will be determined as project documentation is developed. The first stage includes data centre facilities, energy and engineering infrastructure, administrative buildings and AI computing infrastructure. Work is currently under way on site preparation, foundations, administrative facilities, checkpoints and the necessary engineering infrastructure. Kazakh Prime Minister Olzhas Bektenov inspects progress on the Data Center Valley project in Ekibastuz. Photo: Prime Minister of Kazakhstan’s official website. The authorities say the initial stage will require around 50 MW, with capacity subsequently increasing in phases. Additional land has been reserved to allow the campus to expand if demand from investors and technology companies materialises. Kazakhtelecom, one of the operators involved in the Data Center Valley project, told Novastan that the project envisages a hybrid cooling system combining precision air conditioning with closed liquid-cooling circuits using non-freezing liquid solutions. Construction has already begun, but public hearings with local residents have not yet taken place. The Pavlodar regional administration said hearings would be held after the necessary project documentation had been completed and the procedures required for environmental assessment had been carried out. The biggest question: electricity Connecting a new consumer with an eventual capacity of 1 GW would be unrealistic under Kazakhstan’s current energy conditions if such capacity were required all at once, according to Yerkebulan Kozhmambet, a member of the Public Council on Fuel and Energy Issues under Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Energy. “If we are being honest, today this looks unrealistic, particularly given that the average age of our generating capacity is more than 65 years,” Kozhmambet said. A phased project would be possible, he added, provided new generation and grid infrastructure were developed at the same time. The first launch complex is expected to require 50 MW and is scheduled to enter operation in June 2027, while 1 GW represents a longer-term target rather than capacity the power system is expected to provide immediately. The scale is nevertheless considerable. According to Kozhmambet, a continuous 1 GW load would consume around 8.76 billion kWh of electricity annually. Kazakhstan’s total annual electricity consumption is approximately 110-115 billion kWh, meaning the completed Data Center Valley could theoretically account for around 7-8 percent of current national consumption. “No region today has a free reserve of this scale,” he said. The project also comes as Kazakhstan’s electricity system has faced shortages and imports, particularly from Russia during peak periods. Kozhmambet warned that if the full 1 GW capacity were introduced before Kazakhstan achieves a sustainable electricity surplus, the new data centres could absorb that additional generation and push the system back into deficit. Energy expert Asset Nauryzbayev takes a less pessimistic view. He argues that 1 GW would not necessarily pose a major problem for Ekibastuz if the development of the data centres is synchronised with new generating capacity. “If I understand the government’s intention correctly, it is based on the Soviet project to build four 4 GW power stations in Ekibastuz,” Nauryzbayev said. “In today’s conditions, the units would be 660 MW rather than 500 MW. An eight-unit station would therefore generate 5.8 GW. In those circumstances, 1 GW of consumption is absolutely not a large amount.” He also pointed to planned new gas generation in southern Kazakhstan, which he expects to reduce the country’s electricity deficit. But there is an environmental price. “This will undoubtedly create an enormous carbon footprint,” Nauryzbayev said, although he believes the price of carbon offsets is unlikely to fundamentally affect the economics of the project. Read more on Novastan : Carbon neutral by 2060? Kazakhstan’s green pledge faces a reality check There is another potential risk if data centres are completed before the generation intended to supply them. “Data centres will undoubtedly be able to pay more than ordinary consumers,” he said. “That could strongly affect the market if there is no direct link to newly built power stations. Data centres built quickly will take electricity away from ordinary consumers.” Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Energy says the government plans to add more than 26.3 GW of generating capacity by 2035 through modernisation, new conventional generation, renewable energy projects and nuclear power. Of this, 13.3 GW is planned through 2029. The ministry expects the country to be able to cover domestic electricity demand from 2027 onwards and subsequently develop a surplus sufficient to accommodate energy-intensive AI infrastructure and large data centres. Whether those projects are delivered on schedule will therefore be crucial to Data Center Valley’s longer-term expansion. Could water become the bigger constraint? Electricity may not be the only – or even the most difficult – resource question facing the project. Kazakhstan’s Ministry of Water Resources and Irrigation told Novastan that it has not yet received an application to establish a water-use limit for Data Center Valley. No specific limit has therefore been set. The ministry said that the appropriate volume would be assessed once an application and supporting documents were submitted. Citing information from the Ministry of Artificial Intelligence and Digital Development, it also said planned AI data centres in Kazakhstan would use immersion cooling with specialised liquids, which should not require large volumes of water or restrict supplies to existing users. This description differs from Kazakhtelecom’s statement that Data Center Valley will use a hybrid system combining precision air conditioning and closed liquid-cooling circuits. Support Novastan, the European Central Asia magazine By supporting Novastan, you are supporting the only English, French and German-language media specialising in Central Asia. We’re independent and we need your help to stay that way! Support Novastan Following a small river from the mountains into the Kazakh steppe, filmmaker Kristina Mikhailova set out to imagine its dreams. Five years later, the journey had become a portrait of Kazakhstan told through the voices of its women – and an intensely personal exploration of freedom, identity and belonging. A small river runs for 130 kilometres through Kazakhstan, beginning among mountain peaks and glaciers before gradually disappearing into the vast landscape below. When filmmaker Kristina Mikhailova first decided to follow the Aksay from beginning to end, she imagined making a film about the river’s dreams. Five years later, that idea had become something much larger. Along the river, Kristina interviewed around 100 women, asking each an unusual question: if you were a river, what kind of river would you be? Fifteen of them eventually became part of River Dreams , a 98-minute film in which the Aksay serves simultaneously as landscape, witness and metaphor. What emerged is not simply a portrait of a river. Through women’s stories of freedom, violence, dignity and belonging, the film became what its director describes as “a political portrait of Kazakhstan through a female perspective”. The film has since travelled internationally, receiving around 30 festival invitations and and winning the Prize of the Ecumenical Jury in the Forum section at the 2026 Berlinale . It has also drawn enthusiastic audiences closer to home, including three sold-out screenings in Kazakhstan and a packed morning screening in Kyrgyzstan, where it won Best Feature-Length Documentary Film at the UmutDoc International Documentary Film Festival in Bishkek. Yet bringing the film to a wider audience in Kazakhstan itself has proved much more difficult. Kristina says censorship has prevented River Dreams from securing the domestic release she wants. For Novastan, Kristina Mikhailova spoke with Novastan Editor-in-Chief Mathieu Lemoine about the “sisterhood of rivers”, the women she met along the Aksay, her Ukrainian grandmother’s memories, female agency and violence, her identity as a Russian Kazakhstani, and the painful experience of feeling deeply attached to a country that she sometimes feels is pushing her away. Kristina Mikhailova, director of River Dreams. Photo: Bauyrzhan Bismildin. A sisterhood of rivers Novastan: The film began with the idea of following the Aksay River for its entire 130-kilometre course. What were you looking for when you first set out? Kristina Mikhailova: When I started filming, I was very young. This was the idea for my first feature-length film: I wanted to follow the river all the way, 130 kilometres from beginning to end, and imagine what it might dream about – to film those dreams as I saw them. But after walking the entire river alone, I saw how much it changed along the way. I wanted to capture those changes and see reality through the river’s eyes, to personify it. I was working with a post-humanist approach and looking for a way to give the river a voice. That is how I came up with the idea of asking the girls who lived along the river what kind of rivers they would be. A still from River Dreams. Photo: Amir Zarubekov / River Dreams. That question immediately helped me understand the person in front of me and shape the conversation in a way that allowed her to share something very important to her. In the Kazakhstani context, very little space is often given to women’s perspectives. It mattered to me that, as a woman, I was creating such a space, and that through the film other women could have that space too. Gradually, what emerged was a political portrait of Kazakhstan through a female perspective. Why did you choose the Aksay in particular? Aksay, or Aksaika, is a very small, modest river. I wanted to film precisely this kind of inconspicuous river, because we have so many of them. Its journey is typical of many mountain rivers in Central Asia: they begin among mountain peaks and glaciers and then disappear somewhere in the steppe or flow into lakes, never reaching the ocean. By filming Aksay, I was also filming all these other rivers. I called it a “sisterhood of rivers”. It is funny because I once heard someone say that the film shows some of the negative aspects of women’s lives in Kazakhstan because I had chosen the “wrong” river – one that was too insignificant. Apparently, if I had chosen some great, “proper” river, the story would have turned out differently. I doubt it. Making female agency visible You interviewed around 100 women during the making of the film, with 15 eventually appearing in the final version. What did these encounters teach you? First and foremost, I learned about myself. Recently, I started thinking about how I changed over the five years it took to make the film. Of course, I established myself as a filmmaker, my name became known and new opportunities opened up. But something much more personal happened too: I discovered myself as a woman of Kazakhstan. I saw who I was. Through meeting other women, I realised how different we are and how many pains we share. I came to understand relationships between men and women better – and men themselves, too. For me, it was a genuine step up in my understanding of myself. One film led to so many personal discoveries. Freedom seems to be one of the central themes of the film. Did making it change the way you understood freedom and the restrictions women face? I am glad you noticed the theme of freedom because, for me, it was one of the key themes on a human level. While making the film, I realised how many layers restrictions can have. Some are so deeply embedded and so difficult even to recognise that overcoming them can sometimes seem utopian. But if we are talking about empowerment, then yes, absolutely. And women expand these possibilities for themselves. I think every one of the 100 girls I interviewed, and each of the 15 who eventually appeared in the film, helped create a safe space through her story and her willingness to share her vulnerability – a safe space for all of us within those 98 minutes. It is a space that women throughout Kazakhstan can enter. That is why I am trying so hard to secure a wide release for the film in Kazakhstan. I want every Kazakhstani woman to be able to see it. Its distribution title is Qyz Republic . The film deals with difficult experiences, including violence, but the women are never reduced to victims. Was challenging stereotypical representations of women something you consciously set out to do? I did not explicitly set out to move away from stereotypical representations of women. I had a different objective: to make female agency visible. That sounds slightly paradoxical, but there is a need for it. Above all, I wanted my girls to feel strong. I think both men and women can connect with that experience. But for girls in particular, the film creates a place where they can recognise themselves, feel seen and feel strong – where they can see themselves as capable of preserving their dignity despite everything. The culmination of this, of course, comes in the final scenes involving violence. At that point, the conflict becomes completely explicit – almost black and white. But in my view, not one of my girls looks like a victim. The river as witness The landscape itself seems to function almost like another character. How did you want the river and its surroundings to appear on screen? The landscape is definitely my silent witness – the ghost of Hamlet’s father. https://novastan.org/en/kazakhstan/the-l.body: 29 January 2025 Julian Postulart Edited by: Anna Wilhelmi Tags decolonisation Identity Kazakhstan Language A selection of clothes from Qazaq Republic, a popular fashion brand that owes much of its success to the ongoing identity debate in Kazakhstan. Photo by Julian Postulart. Over thirty years after the Soviet Union’s collapse, colonial influences persist in Kazakhstan. Russian remains widely spoken and serves as the primary language for interethnic communication. As language is a vital symbol of national identity, the enduring linguistic prominence of Russian poses a significant challenge to fully decolonising Kazakh identity. However, the invasion of Ukraine has spurred a young, urban middle class to confront these imperial remnants by reclaiming their native language. Russia’s colonial war against Ukraine has sent shockwaves throughout Central Asia. Moscow’s emphasis on historical, cultural and linguistic connections makes other former Soviet republics feel increasingly uncomfortable. Especially in Kazakhstan, home to a sizable ethnic Russian population, many fear that their country could be next on the Kremlin’s list. These concerns are not unfounded. Since the start of the war in Ukraine, Russian propagandists have repeatedly voiced thin-veiled threats about annexing parts of their southern neighbour. Moreover, after partial mobilisation was announced in Russia in September 2022, hundreds of thousands of predominantly young men fled across the border into Kazakhstan. Their arrival has exacerbated existing concerns, and magnified domestic tensions between social groups that identify themselves differently. Although over the past three decades, Kazakhstan’s government has attempted to forge a new national identity, Russian influence remains. Since the conquest of the Kazakh steppe in the 19th century by tsarist forces, the lands and the people inhabiting the territory of modern-day Kazakhstan were shaped by imperial rule. First by the Russian Empire, then by the Soviet Union. In the 20th century, forced collectivisation uprooted traditional lifestyles and led to famine. Countless people flocked to towns and cities in a desperate search for food and work, places which themselves were colonial spaces, dominated by imperial infrastructure and buildings. Rapid urbanisation and industrialisation have scarred the landscape and still cause pollution and environmental and health problems to this very day. The whole of Central Asia in your inbox Subscribe to our free weekly newsletter Register Click here for the latest issue Russia’s linguistic legacy But apart from these more abstract, postcolonial realities , there is the pertinent yet controversial issue of language. In the wake of Russia’s invasion of Ukraine, many have grown painfully aware of the influence Russia still exerts over Kazakhstan through language. Over thirty years after independence, Russian remains the country’s main interethnic language. Political scientist Dossym Satpayev, in a piece for Chatham House, writes that Russification policies in the colonial era suppressed the Kazakh language so thoroughly that most forgot how to speak their native tongue. As the de facto official language of the USSR, speaking Russian was key to social mobility . After the collapse of the Soviet Union, the benefits of learning the Kazakh language remained negligible. Although Kazakh is the state language, and Russian a mere ‘official’ language, in reality , Russian-speakers still enjoyed significant privileges and advantages. Until recently, insufficient knowledge of spoken Kazakh was hardly considered a problem, as Russian proficiency was enough to live a comfortable life, especially in the north and in the cities, where most of Kazakhstan’s Russian-speaking population is concentrated. In education, Russian has been more advantageous for increasing the possibilities to study at renowned schools and universities in Russia, partly because of the availability of a broader range of academic resources. Similarly, career-wise, Russian speakers have traditionally had more job opportunities. By contrast, Kazakh was viewed as backward and inferior, as sociologist Azamat Junisbai remembers how, while growing up, he associated the Kazakh language exclusively as rural, uncultured and of low status. Read more on Novastan: “Alaqan” – Aida Adilbek’s decolonial documentary cinema Fear for antagonising Moscow Initially, Kazakhstan’s government made little effort to support the elevation of the Kazakh language. Policymakers were concerned that such a stance would feed into rising Kazakh nationalism, which in turn could endanger the country’s inter-ethnic stability. So, from the 1990s onwards, it chose to counter early national-patriotic movements by prioritising the development of a Kazakhstani civic identity . This civic identity, epitomised by the slogan ‘unity in diversity,’ sought to rally all people of Kazakhstan around the flag of the newly independent republic, regardless of ethnicity. However, the main threat to inter-ethnic stability did not emanate from Kazakh nationalism, nor from the country’s sizable Russian minority. As a matter of fact, Astana’s stance on the issue was long guided by the fear that, should it have followed a more ethno-national course, Kazakhstan would have risked antagonising its northern neighbour. Demographics driving change Meanwhile, it was increasingly difficult for the government to balance the national interest against grassroots calls for the strengthening of Kazakh ethnic identity. After independence, millions of Russians left Kazakhstan, dramatically changing the country’s demographic make-up. Kazakhs now form a clear majority. They are the country’s fastest – growing ethnic group, and their proportion of the total population is only expected to increase. Satpayev, in his contribution for Chatham House, argues that the strengthening of national-patriotic sentiments and movements is occurring organically. Based on demographic trends, support for a Kazakh ethnic identity will continue to grow, while the use of the Russian language is expected to decline. The Russian invasion of Ukraine catalysed societal developments resulting from these demographic developments, which are shaping current and future political preferences. Not so long ago, the debate on national identity was quite marginal , predominantly talked about among small-circles of Kazakh-speaking intellectual elites. The war has caused this discussion to spillover into public domain, with an ever-increasing number of people rediscovering what it means to be Kazakh in the context of persistent colonial legacies. Language as a decolonial tool Language possibly is the most enduring bastion of Russian influence in Kazakhstan. In an episode of RFE/RL’s Majlis Podcast, sociologist Junisbai discusses how older generations primarily engage with Russian media, which makes them more susceptible to Russian propaganda. Consequently, the idea of so-called benevolent colonialism still is widespread among the elderly. Many believe that Kazakhstan owes much to foreign rule, such as industrialisation and modernisation. Read more on Novastan: Pressure from Russia increases on Central Asian media outlets This sentiment is not shared with younger generations. They have no living memory of the Soviet Union, and seek to undo the final vestiges of Russian and Soviet colonialism in pursuit of a new Kazakh identity. For them, language is a tool for decolonisation. On the streets, for example, this is reflected in the growing popularity of fashion brand Qazaq Republic. This company, famous for its trendy clothing and other merchandise with patriotic Kazakh and English language slogans, owes much of its success to ongoing societal developments. https://novastan.org/en/politics/night-t.body: 6 June 2024 Julian Postulart Tags Regional politics Tajikistan Trains Uzbekistan A truck driving on a dusty road between Jizzakh and Samarkand, Uzbekistan. Photographed from the Tashkent-Dushanbe night train. Picture by Julian Postulart. For many years, relations between Tajikistan and Uzbekistan have been fraught with tension. Some analysts even dubbed the ties between the two countries a Central Asian ‘cold war’. But luckily, things are slowly improving. The return of the Tashkent-Dushanbe night train is a testament to this bilateral thaw. The new rail service connecting both capitals is, in many ways, a miniature of the past, present, and future of Uzbek-Tajik relations. “Your phone, please”, one officer demands. As the only man in the kupe , a train compartment, the border guards summoned me into the corridor. Reluctantly I let the officer scroll through the pictures I took during my brief visit to Uzbekistan. Pornography, photos of government buildings, military installations – whatever he is looking for, the man finds none. As he returns my phone, some of his colleagues enter the train to look for contraband and other prohibited items. Luggage is thoroughly searched, as well as the train’s interior. Some ceiling panels are removed and part of the flooring is opened up to examine if anything is hidden underneath. Despite Uzbek authorities having relaxed customs procedures over the past years, the border crossings with Tajikistan remain an uncomfortable exception. But relations between the two countries have improved significantly over the past few years. Travelling aboard the direct Tashkent-Dushanbe night train shows the slow fruition of this regional detente . The whole of Central Asia in your inbox Subscribe to our free weekly newsletter Register Click here for the latest issue 15:47 – Tashkent Some thirteen hours earlier, my travel companion and I boarded the train at Tashkent’s central station. It was mid-May and with temperatures well over thirty degrees Celsius, our kupe was unbearably hot. Although the ticket agent had promised us air-conditioning, the one in our wagon was not working this afternoon. With sweat dripping down my back, a young Tajik mother asked if I could help her store her large suitcase. Nodira and her toddler son would be our cabin companions for the night, travellig to Dushanbe for a family visit. Although Tajik by birth, Nodira often pendles between Uzbekistan and Tajikistan. Her husband owns a suitcase shop in Tashkent, yet she prefers the tranquil mountains of native Tajikistan over the hustle and bustle of the Uzbek capital. For a time, Nodira thought of running her own business as a professional make-up artist on Instagram, though it was no longer acceptable after becoming a married woman, she tells us. Ever since, Nodira has embraced a more conservative lifestyle, focusing on religion, her three children, and running the household. Tajik society is deeply patriarchal and gender roles remain traditional. However, for Nodira, social media has an important emancipatory function. It helps her learn a little English and connect with the outside world through her followers, mostly in Russian. In fact, she has become quite the influencer since our meeting on the sweltering night train. Thousands of people watch her videos in which she prepares classic Central Asian recipes in her kitchen. 20:40 – Samarkand Just after sunset, we made a brief call at Samarkand. The city’s magnificent architecture still reflects its historical significance as a leading centre of Persian civilisation. But Samarkand’s legacy is also highly contentious. For centuries, the Tajik language – a variety of modern Persian – has been Samarkand’s lingua franca. However, this position has come under increasing pressure since Uzbekistan’s independence. Eurasianet writes that former President Islam Karimov seemed intent on erasing the city’s Tajik roots. Many in Tajikistan, however, still see Samarkand as inextricably linked to their ethnic and cultural identity. The issue of Samarkand dates back to the 1920s when the city was made part of the Uzbek SSR under the Soviets’ policy of national delimitation. In 2009, Tajik President Imomali Rahmon told journalists that in a brawl with Karimov, he had threatened to take back Samarkand by force. Interestingly, a significant number of Tajik speakers in Uzbekistan hold more nuanced views about their ethnicity. Research about this topic found that “ many people speak a language as their vernacular language while identifying themselves with the ‘other’ ethnic group in daily life. ” In the same study, Persian-speaking respondents from Samarkand primarily see themselves as Samarkandi, rather than Tajik. On the other hand, for people like Nodira who are multilingual and have mixed families, local, national, and ethnic identities overlap. The new rail connection also has a significant symbolic function as a token of regional interconnectedness. In many ways, the hard border between Uzbekistan and Tajikistan was a historical anomaly, in that it divided a continuous cultural and linguistic space. 05:53 – Border After the Uzbek border guard returns my phone and the customs officials exit the train, we ride into no-man’s land. As we accelerate, I notice that at some point during the night, we have traded our silent, electric locomotive for a noisy diesel enginge. A gust of black smoke occasionally enters through the open windows – an unfortunate tradeoff for ventilation against the heat. As the train pulls out of the Uzbek customs zone, we pass high walls and concrete barriers, manned guard towers, and barbed wire. Suddenly, this militarised border zone gives way to green fields, off-roading Ladas, and even some rice paddies. Despite the early hour, whole families are out working the land. Some wave to the passing train. Indeed, a passenger train on these tracks remains a rare sight. Since independence, ordinary Uzbeks and Tajiks have been caught in the crosshairs of bilateral tensions. Lengthy examinations and searches, considerable red tape and frequent border closures had a significant impact on travel and trade. Relations between the two countries were mired in suspicion and distrust. Uzbekistan even had parts of the border area mined, allegedly to prevent militant Islamist groups from entering the country. Hundreds of people, mostly local farmers, were killed or injured in landmine explosions. After Shavkat Mirziyoyev succeeded Karimov in 2016 as president of Uzbekistan, clearing the minefields was a top priority in his pursuit of better ties with Tajikistan. Read more on Novastan: Moscow attacks highlight Tajikistan’s radicalisation problem With most of the obstacles removed, the task remains to rebuild the political, economic, and cultural ties that were virtually destroyed over the past 30 years. The return of the Tashkent-Dushanbe night train, as the first passenger rail connection between the two capitals since the collapse of the Soviet Union, is a testament to this ambition. 09:41 – Dushanbe On April 18 this year, Mirziyoyev and Rahmon signed a ‘Treaty on Allied Relations’ in Dushanbe. The treaty consists of 28 documents covering various areas of cooperation, ranging from cross-border trade to food safety, and from fostering intercultural exchange to transport and communication. In a statement, the President of Uzbekistan declared that bilateral relations between the countries had “risen to an unprecedented level” . Uzbek news website Darya.uz wrote that developing new transit corridors was among the leaders’ priorities. The Diplomat previously reported that, since coming to power, Mirziyoyev has pushed for new rail projects to bolster regional integration. Read more on Novastan: Railway between Tajikistan and Uzbekistan to be electrified But it might take some time before this treaty will bear fruit. For now, Dushanbe is all but a regional transport hub. The railway station of Tajikistan’s capital city ha

https://novastan.org/en/kazakhstan/kazak.body: 4 July 2023 cbabakoulov ascripka Translated by Abby Scripka Tags climate water shortage Since May 2023, the capital of Kazakhstan is suffering from a severe water crisis, as a result residents are now facing a shortage of drinking water. According to the government, across the country there are more than 600,000 Kazakhstanis that do not have access to drinking water. By 2050 the Republic of Kazakhstan may join the category of countries “ in dire need of water. ” President Kassym-Jomart Tokayev has proposed holding an anti-crisis summit in Kazakhstan under the backing of the UN to solve the water problem. According to the monitoring group “Energyprom” – migration influx, rapid population growth and large-scale construction in the capital of Kazakhstan has exceeded the available capacity of the pumping stations. Therefore, on March 28, 2023, the city water supply service “ Astana Su Arnasy ” resorted to introducing an hourly water schedule to citizens. On May 23, residents of a residential complex expressed their dissatisfaction due to the lack of water by blocking the road. On June 10 the situation was resolved and authorities assured that the problem would be solved by the 30 of June as they are launching a new pumping and filtering system. Meanwhile the publication “KazTAG” reported that the water source for Astana is designed for only 500,000 people while the city has 1.3 million inhabitants. The mayor of Astana has connected the water shortage with the population growth and the active irrigation of agricultural land. The whole of Central Asia in your inbox Subscribe to our free weekly newsletter Register Click here for the latest issue Aset Kaliyev, Directory of the Water Security Centre at the international scientific complex “Astana,” told “Inbusiness.kz,” that one of the causes of the water shortage in the capital was the failure of developers to follow the general plan for city construction, “ Having departed from the general plan, in Astana, with the approval of officials, densification and infill construction began. In turn, the infill developments began to cut into existing neighbourhoods, which already had their own load on the engineering networks. Since then, everything went “crooked and tangled”. According to Nursultan Kerimkulov, head of the Water Supply and Sanitation Department, the lack of water will affect the development of construction in the city, but the quality of drinking water will not be affected. Read more on Novastan: The recession of the Tian Shan glaciers and other recent studies On April 19, 2023, at a meeting on socio-economic development of the country President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev noted , that by 2050 Kazakhstan may enter the category of countries in dire need of water. The President said that the infrastructure of large cities is not able to meet the increasing demand each year. “Even in Astana itself, there has begun to be a shortage of water. One of the main reasons is the increase in construction. If we are not frugal, we will not be able to eliminate the deficit, even if we launch new facilities that provide clean water, ” Kassym-Jomart Tokayev was quoted by the Kazakhstani news outlet “Tengrinews.” Read more on Novastan: A disappearing river: the fate of the Ural The problem of water shortages in Astana is not only related to the lack of design capacity of networks and pumping stations, but also to the direct shortage of water sources. Apart from the Astana reservoir, there are no alternative water supply options. Currently, the Ministry of Ecology of Kazakhstan is considering several options to solve the problem: construction of facilities to replenish the reservoir, laying a water pipeline and taking water from the Irtysh-Karaganda water canal. The crisis of water scarcity in the cities and provinces of Kazakhstan will only get worse According to the deputy director of public utilities of Kazakhstan, the provision of centralized water supply in Kazakhstan in 2022 was 96.8%. At the same time, more than 600,000 people, meaning the remaining 3.2%, are in need of drinking water. Experts draw attention to bureaucratic complications that arise between government agencies at different levels and hinder the timely resolution of problems. For example, the government’s Geology Committee is responsible for water resources in Kazakhstan, while the Water Resources Committee controls pipeline infrastructure. Other local executive bodies manage network design and construction. However, not every region does the necessary work without delays. Marat Karabayev, Minister of Industry and Infrastructure Development of Kazakhstan, made a statement at a recent government meeting. Read more on Novastan: Climate change could lead to ever more fluctuated temperatures in Central Asia The water sector also faces significant problems of deterioration of main pipelines and urban water pipelines. Overall, the degree of wear and tear on the country’s water supply networks is 43% . However, this figure does not reflect the scale of problematic networks in all regions. The highest level of infrastructure wear is seen in Almaty (58%), East Kazakhstan (54%), Akmola (52%), Abay (51%) regions and Almaty region (57%). In contrast, Atyrau region boasts the lowest level of pipeline wear and tear – 29%. In 2023, a significant budget of 544 million Euros was allocated by the authorities for the construction and reconstruction of water supply and sewerage systems throughout Kazakhstan. The government of Kazakhstan plans to provide water to 1,395 villages and 25 cities that do not have full access to water by 2025. Summit in Kazakhstan with back from the UN to solve the water problems On June 8 and 9, 2023, the Astana International Forum was held in the capital, which was attended by the President of Kazakhstan Kassym-Jomart Tokayev and the heads of several other states, including the Emir of Qatar Sheikh Tamim bin Hamad Al-Thani and President of Kyrgyzstan Sadyr Japarov. At the meeting, the President of Kazakhstan proposed to hold a regional climate summit in Kazakhstan in 2026, under the supervision of the UN and other international organizations. “Our country offers tremendous opportunities for a green economy and become a centre for renewable energy. However, time is not on our side. To decarbonize and create a green economy at the necessary speed, we need resources and partnerships ,” the official website of the head of state “Akorda” quotes Tokayev’s proposal. Read more on Novastan: Kazakhstan: replenishing the Aral Sea’s fish stocks To prevent an environmental catastrophe in the region, the country is calling for increased international support for the Aral Sea Rescue Fund. “The problem of water and climate change are closely linked. Central Asia is a region where water security can only be achieved through close cooperation and effectively selected joint measures,” concluded the President. https://novastan.org/en/culture-sports/s.body: 13 June 2024 Florian Coppenrath Edited by: Julian Postulart Translated by Anna Wilhelmi Original Tags Bishkek Music Postpunk Review "Swinaja Poputka" cover of the third album by Vtoroi Ka Bishkek musical duo Vtoroi Ka has recently dropped its third album: carnivalesque postpunk in a world where nothing is as serious as it seems. Novastan’s review. “ These post-Soviet cities have already seen quite some nonsense/ But after seeing our Kyrgyz squad up close/ the lockdown has been abruptly enacted for some reason “, says the chorus of the single “Vstrechyaite Govnyukov” (“Welcome the shitheads”) , released in February 2023. The retro-aesthetic video shows an exuberant wedding party stirring up the Kyrgyz capital Bishkek. The audience has been warned: the “shitheads” are coming to cause a lot of trouble. The whole of Central Asia in your inbox Subscribe to our free weekly newsletter Register Click here for the latest issue “Shitheads” – Govnyuki in Russian – is what Sultan and Ilya of the duo Vtoroi Ka, currently one of the most exciting music groups in Central Asia, call themselves. They adopted the term from a video blogger who mocked them with it and turned it into something positive. As Sultan says in a long interview with the online magazine SRSLY: “ [We are] two shitheads. We’re explorers. The kind that aren’t afraid to try things and are constantly on an artistic quest .” At the beginning of May, Vtoroi Ka released their third album, Svinaya Poputka, a mysterious title that could literally be translated as “ piggy ride ” – a not entirely inaccurate description of the listening experience. It opens with the inviting bass line of “ Teni ot pal’m ” (“ Palm Shadow “): “ Come take me quickly to where the palm shadows are...” A cheerful Joy Division The song, which was released in June 2022 together with a music video filmed in Bishkek and on Lake Issyk-Kul, is the duo’s most successful hit to date. A total of six of the eleven tracks on the album had previously been released as singles, all with funny and colourful videos. Die-hard fans of the group will therefore recognize some of the songs, but in any case Svinaya Poputka offers a musically delightful half hour. https://youtube.com/watch?v=qyTjfhJpEAI%3Fsi%3D-nAQ6fToq_MT9v7e “Palm Shadow” Since their debut album “ Den’ Zavisimosti ” ( “Dependence Day” , 2020), which was still clearly a rap album, Vtoroi Ka seem to be moving further and further back into the musical past. The second album, “Serial” (2022), features excursions into the alternative teen rock of the 2000s, and the most recent tracks are full of allusions to the post-punk of the 1970s and 1980s. However, the characteristic sound of bass, drum computer and synthesiser, which according to one critic is sometimes even reminiscent of the late Soviet cult band Kino around Viktor Tsoi , does not underpin a dark soundscape as is so often the case. “ Vtoroi Ka play post-punk, but their music doesn’t have the depressive vibe so typical for the genre, ” emphasises hip-hop magazine The Flow. On the contrary: Svinaya Poputka is full of colourful irony – a kind of cheerful Joy Division, as those who grew up with English-language music might say (especially as Sultan’s bass voice is not so dissimilar to that of Ian Curtis). Read also at Novastan: Inside Bishkek’s Metal Boom: Portrait of a Music Pioneer in Kyrgyzstan Musical references and quotations can be found in abundance, whether in the lyrics themselves (“ An old cassette, vernissage in the loudspeakers “) or in the musical elements. The reels that Sultan and Ilya use to promote their music on social media are like building instructions. For example, for Dura (dummy), their latest single: “ Oh, try singing like Zhanna Aguzarova “ , an eccentric Russian-speaking singer who was particularly successful in the late 80s. Sex, drugs and gangster romance While Svinaya Poputka takes listeners back to the 80s musically, its content primarily relates to the first decade of independence after the end of the Soviet Union. In the words of another reviewer: “ The main characters in these songs are bandits and shitheads from the times of the wild 90s, such country road romantics”. This is symbolised by the “ Tonirovannyi Kaban ” ( “Tinted Boar” ), which is enthroned on the album cover with Bishkek’s skyscrapers and a “ Kosh Kelingizder ” sign (Kyrg. for “Welcome” ) in the background. On closer inspection, you can also recognise a “ pig duck ” on the sign, the signature of graffiti artist Cherv1, which adorns many a wall in Bishkek. Kaban – Russian for wild boar – is the popular name for the Mercedes W-140 , a status symbol particularly popular among the nouveau riche and mafia of the post-Soviet 1990s. However, the bonnet is emblazoned with a pig’s snout instead of the usual star. The single of the same name, in which Sultan and Ilya stage themselves as music dealers, is also dedicated to the “ Tonirovannyi Kaban “: Bakai Kolchaev, director of the Bishkek music label Infinity Music , which also distributes the music of Vtoroi Ka, plays the role of a mob leader in the music video. “Tinted Boar” But unlike the Russian cult series Brigada , which definitively associated the “ Kaban ” with the criminal 90s, Svinaya Poputka is not so serious. “ We don’t want to be taken seriously – like Skryptonite . We want to be simpler, with irony. Sometimes serious, but with a bit of fun, ” says Ilya, summarizing the group’s approach. Through music, colourful imagery and witty language the actually serious references turn into carnivalesque. A typical example for this is the music video “Dura” (“Dummy”) , whose bizarre characters seem to come from Alice’s Wonderland. At the same time, the piece is peppered with allusions to the world of erotic webcams, an equally l ucrative and dodgy business in Kyrgyzstan, and a recurring motiv in Vtoroi Ka’s work. Dura ‘s text speaks of “her” admirers (“ Ukhazhory “), who “ give her money wholeheartedly and so earnestly “, while she repeatedly goes “on air”. The same applies to the extremely danceable “ Ona sovsem odna ” ( “She is all alone” ): “ Her body is a glossy comic for adults “, and further: “ All admirers are wild, with brisk movements, unarmed/ In the chat, uncles over 40 are frolicking “. “Dummy” The underworld of Vtoroi Ka with its very likeable characters, always on the lookout for the next “Dvizh” , the next adventure, is romantic. In “ Boomerang”, a couple hides from unclear dangers in cosy togetherness in anticipation of the next Dvizh : “ Here we are an easy target/ Let’s leave these rooftops “, whether meant metaphorically or literally. “ We don’t have to die ye t”, it says, as in “Teni ot Pal’m”, which tells of a girl who has become a “ great shooter “, probably not without allusion to Luc Besson’s Leon – The Professional. Obviously, if you die, you can’t have fun anymore. Intoxication and artificial paradises run through the album like another leitmotiv. The place of longing, where the palm trees stand, is one “ where a kilo of junk for the nose costs a thousand “. Or “ Pomyat “( “Crumpled” ), a wild piece about the state “ when there is nothing to recharge yourself with “. “Bong” stands out in particular with its rock’n’roll rhythm – and is, unsurprisingly, dedicated to the water pipe, which, according to the lyrics, should definitely feature in Vtoroi Ka’s Stage Riders (or that of their fictional characters?). Flawless craftsmanship Svinaya Poputka impresses no less with its detailed and flawless production, all handcrafted by Sultan and Ilya, who, by their own admission, like to control “ everything from start to finish ” when it comes to their songs. Without overloading their songs, they manage to surprise you – even on the hundredth listen – with a noise in the background, an imaginative rhyme or a particularly successful transition. The tracks are entertaining, all around two and a half minutes long, with snappy intros – and therefore fit perfectly into the streaming

Photo by Aidan Turumbekova. Support Novastan, the European Central Asia magazine By supporting Novastan, you are supporting the only English, French and German-language media specialising in Central Asia. We’re independent and we need your help to stay that way! Support Novastan A four-day expedition to Kyrgyzstan’s Adygene glacier brought seven women into the field with glaciologist Gulbara Omorova. For filmmaker Tynymgul Eshieva, the journey is part of a larger effort to document both the rapid transformation of Kyrgyzstan’s glaciers and the women working to understand them. In August, seven women set out into Kyrgyzstan’s Ala-Archa gorge for a four-day expedition. Some were experienced hikers; others had never undertaken a high-altitude trek of this kind. Their destination was the Adygene scientific station, around 11 kilometres into the mountains. They were not going simply to see a glacier. From 16 to 19 August, the participants worked alongside Kyrgyz glaciologist Gulbara Omorova, installing ablation stakes to measure melting, recording glacier movement with GPS and carrying out bathymetric measurements on lakes below the ice. Behind the expedition was documentary filmmaker and producer Tynymgul Eshieva. She is developing The Voice of the Glaciers ( Мөңгүлөрдүн үнү ), a feature-length documentary centred on Omorova and her work in Kyrgyzstan’s mountains. The film is still in development and is currently expected to be completed in 2028. But Eshieva has already been filming a landscape that is changing fast enough for those returning to it to see the difference with their own eyes. “We filmed the teaser in June last year, and then we went back for the expedition in August this year,” Eshieva told Novastan Editor-in-Chief Mathieu Lemoine. “The glacier looked completely different. You don’t need instruments to see it. You can see with your own eyes how rapidly it’s disappearing.” A glacier changing within a lifetime The measurements reinforce what the eye can see. During the expedition, around 1.4 metres of surface lowering was recorded near the glacier terminus over approximately one month. Over an entire ablation season, melting in the lower sections can amount to several metres. A field briefing during the expedition in Ala-Archa. Photo by Aidan Turumbekova. Omorova’s longer-term research paints an even starker picture. The Adygene glacier system comprises three glaciers – Bolshoy Adygene, Panfilov and 30-let VLKSM. Bolshoy Adygene has decreased in area from approximately 3.5 square kilometres in 1962 to 2.8 square kilometres in 2025, a loss of around 20 percent. More strikingly, the annual rate of area loss has accelerated from 0.006 to 0.033 square kilometres per year. The smaller glaciers are retreating too. Between 1977 and 2024, Panfilov lost around 20 percent of its area and 30-let VLKSM around 29 percent. For Eshieva, however, seeing the process at close range changed the meaning of such figures. “It’s completely different to see it with your own eyes,” she said. “You can read the news, follow websites, see the numbers online. But when you go there, when you stand on the glacier and feel it, it’s something else.” What struck her just as strongly was the work required to produce those numbers. “She carries heavy equipment up the mountain. She takes the measurements again and again, with total commitment,” Eshieva said of Omorova. “It’s slow, repetitive work, sometimes even boring, but it’s absolutely necessary. Without people like her doing it year after year, we simply wouldn’t know what is happening.” The woman behind the measurements Eshieva has known Omorova since the mid-2000s. Long before either woman imagined making a documentary together, they talked, hiked and even climbed a peak near Bishkek. Expedition participants make their way towards the glacier. Photo by Aidan Turumbekova. Eshieva only began documentary filmmaking in 2023. While editing her first feature documentary, also about a woman activist, she began searching for another project. She hopes to complete that film next year. The catalyst came through social media. The Adygene research station had been robbed and scientific equipment stolen. Omorova appealed publicly for help. People who had never visited a glacier responded, crowdfunding enough money to replace what had been lost. “That was the moment I thought: this could be a film,” Eshieva recalled. “Here is a woman who fights for her science, for the environment, for justice, and she doesn’t wait for anyone to do it for her. And ordinary people answered her call.” She began filming. Omorova’s route into glaciology itself began far from the ice. Trained in sociology, she travelled to villages to interview residents about social issues. During a visit to Batken, farmers told her about shortages of water. Already an experienced mountaineer with training in alpinism, she began asking why. That question eventually took her towards glaciology and the Adygene station. It also illustrates one of the central realities of glacier retreat: what happens high in Kyrgyzstan’s mountains does not remain there. Read more on Novastan : The recession of the Tian Shan glaciers and other recent studies From the glacier to the valley As glaciers retreat, they transform not only water availability but the landscape around them. Omorova’s monitoring has identified 16 new moraine-glacial lakes in the Adygene complex since observations began in 1977. Some glacial lakes can become unstable, making continuous observation essential. During the August expedition, the participants went out by boat to conduct bathymetric measurements using an echo sounder. By measuring water depth at different points, researchers can map the lake and track how it changes. Monitoring can also involve automatic loggers recording water levels and temperatures, water-column profiling and examination of the moraine dams holding back the lakes. Read more on Novastan : Life by the river: the Naryn in Kyrgyzstan The relationship between melting ice and downstream risk is complex. A lake that appears stable today may change as the glacier, surrounding terrain and permafrost evolve. The purpose of monitoring is therefore not to predict an outburst from a single measurement, but to observe the glacier-lake system continuously and identify changes that may eventually become warning signs. Expedition participants rest beside a mountain stream in Ala-Archa. Photo by Aidan Turumbekova. Eshieva did not originally set out to make a film about the relationship between glaciers and water. “When I started, my idea wasn’t to connect what happens up on the glacier with what happens down below,” she said. “But the more I filmed, the more I saw that they are deeply connected.” Whether that relationship ultimately becomes central to the documentary remains open. “People often ask me at pitching forums: is this a film about water? For now, it isn’t,” she said. “Documentary is a long process. You follow a person’s life, sometimes for two or three years, sometimes ten. I don’t know yet where it will go.” Seven women on the ice The August expedition itself emerged partly from necessity. Eshieva had initially envisaged a camp for aspiring ecologists, selected through an open call and led by Omorova. But by August, funding for the film had not materialised and the summer field season was slipping away. “I felt I had to do something,” she said. She changed the plan, crowdfunded an expedition and invited women interested in learning about glaciers to join. There was no competitive selection process. Participants simply had to be willing and able to commit to four days in the mountains. Seven ultimately went. Their backgrounds and levels of mountain experience differed. Two already knew Omorova from pre

Growing up German in Kazakhstan. Photo courtesy of Lena Wolf. Support Novastan, the European Central Asia magazine By supporting Novastan, you are supporting the only English, French and German-language media specialising in Central Asia. We’re independent and we need your help to stay that way! Support Novastan Born in Latvia and raised in Kazakhstan, Lena Wolf grew up with fragments of a history that Soviet society rarely discussed openly. In her graphic memoir, she retraces the deportation of her German family to Kazakhstan, their struggle to preserve language and identity, and her own journey from Aktobe to Germany. For our readers in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan: Lena Wolf’s e-book is now available at reduced regional prices on Google Play Books in Kazakhstan, Kyrgyzstan and Uzbekistan. Available in English and Russian . For much of her childhood, Lena Wolf believed that all Germans came from Kazakhstan. Aktobe was home. Her grandmother cooked German dishes alongside baursaki and manti, organised clandestine religious gatherings and spoke German to her grandchildren, even when they answered her in Russian. Around them lived families whose own histories had been shaped by deportation, repression and displacement. Yet Wolf also learned early that being German could set her apart. “I don’t think I really understood what being German meant to other people until I was called a fascist for the first time,” she recalls. “I was probably about six.” Decades later, Wolf began piecing together the family history that had reached her in fragments behind closed doors. The result was a graphic memoir illustrated by Christoph Heuer, tracing almost two centuries of migration, persecution and repeated attempts to build a home. Migration of German communities to the Russian Empire from the eighteenth to the nineteenth century. Her grandmother Emilia was 25 when she was deported to Kazakhstan in 1941 with two young children. Like many Soviet Germans, the family initially believed the displacement might be temporary. “They left behind their houses, land, animals – everything – still hoping they would return,” Wolf says. They never did. Forced deportation routes of Soviet Germans in 1941, including destinations in Kazakhstan and Siberia. Even after Stalin-era special-settlement restrictions were lifted in 1955, Soviet Germans were not allowed to return to the areas from which they had been deported. Emilia eventually built a new life in Aktobe. “Kazakhstan did become home for her, partly because she knew she could never return to her village in Ukraine,” Wolf says. “She found her people there and had her family around her.” The contradiction would become central to Wolf’s understanding of her family history: Kazakhstan was both a place of forced exile and the country in which several generations of the family made their lives. “Somewhere along the way, she too became a German from Kazakhstan.” German communities in the Soviet Union and its successor states after 1945. Growing up German in Soviet Kazakhstan For Wolf herself, Kazakhstan carried no such ambiguity during childhood. “For me, Kazakhstan was simply home. I didn’t know anything else,” she says. “In fact, when I was very little, I thought all Germans came from Kazakhstan.” Read more on Novastan : Beyond any borders: a new multicultural generation in Kazakhstan Her family’s German identity nevertheless remained clearly marked in Soviet society. Official documents continued to identify Soviet Germans as nemets or nemka , even as German-language education, religious life and much of the community’s institutional culture had been suppressed. “You were expected to stop being German, but you were never allowed to forget that you were German,” Wolf says. In her family, survival meant avoiding attention. Her father’s advice was encapsulated in the Russian expression тише воды, ниже травы – “quieter than water, lower than grass.” “Don’t attract attention. Don’t stand out. That was how you survived.” Wolf remembers the word “German” being routinely associated with “fascist”, decades after the Second World War. Soviet Germans’ own experience of deportation and repression was largely absent from the history taught in schools. “When you don’t know the history, you fill the gaps with your own explanations,” she says. “So people assumed that because we had been deported, we must have been guilty. The deportation itself became proof of our guilt.” As a child, she even changed her surname when helping an elderly Soviet woman whose husband and son had died during the war. “I invented another name for myself: Volkova instead of Wolf.” The Russian name, she says, became a form of protection. When Russian became the common language Language is another thread running through Wolf’s memoir. Her grandmother spoke German to her; Wolf usually answered in Russian. She later recognised almost exactly the same pattern among Kazakh families: grandparents speaking Kazakh while younger generations responded in Russian. “When that happens, it isn’t only language that gets lost,” Wolf says. “Stories, traditions and knowledge can no longer be passed on in the same way.” She remembers receiving some Kazakh-language teaching at school but says it was far too limited for children to become proficient. Russian, meanwhile, dominated education, television and popular culture. “You didn’t necessarily have to force children to speak Russian,” she says. “Education, television, culture and opportunities were in Russian, while Kazakh was often seen as old-fashioned or backward. Of course children were going to choose Russian.” Read more on Novastan : The Lexicon of Kazakh Decolonisation Looking back, she says she is glad to see the Kazakh language gaining greater prominence today. A garden as survival – and as home One image reappears throughout Wolf’s family history: the garden. Her ancestors had originally migrated eastward to work the land. After deportation, a garden helped her grandmother and a neighbour survive wartime shortages. Decades later, during Wolf’s own childhood in Kazakhstan, home-grown food helped sustain the family when Soviet shops were empty. But the garden came to represent more than food. Wolf recounts the story of her father, whose mother was sentenced to the Gulag after attempting to leave the deportation zone and return to Ukraine. He was sent to an orphanage in Zaporizhzhia shortly after the war. One teacher once invited him to her home for dinner. While she cooked, he played in the garden with her son. “He remembers standing there among the flowers and plants and realising, for the first time, that the world was beautiful,” Wolf says. The memory remained with him throughout his life. Now 91, he can no longer maintain a large garden but still cares for flowers on his balcony in Offenbach, Germany. “Perhaps that is what a garden means in our family,” Wolf says. “It feeds you when there is nothing to eat, but it also gives you beauty when there isn’t much beauty around you. And wherever you end up, you can plant something and make that place your own.” A ‘return’ to a country they did not know In 1989, Wolf and her family left Kazakhstan for Germany. Officially, such migration was often presented as a return to an ancestral homeland. In practice, Wolf discovered that Germany was another unfamiliar country. “What surprised me most was that in Germany I wasn’t seen as German,” she says. “After everything our families had gone through in the Soviet Union because they were German – persecution, discrimination and sometimes literally fighting for survival – we arrived in Germany and suddenly we were foreigners.” At 17, Wolf initially tried to assimilate as completely as possible. She stopped speaking Russian, avoided food associated with her Soviet childhood and even began using the name Helene. I

Oktober 2026 jschupp Schlagwörter Azamat Omarov Pressefreiheit Satire Azamat Omarov hatte in der Vergangenheit wiederholt Witze über die kasachstanische Regierung gemacht. Im September verurteilte ihn ein Gericht in Astana zu dreieinhalb Jahren Haft auf Bewährung. Photo: Instagram/Collage. Wer in Kasachstan Witze über die Regierung reißt, kann wegen „ Anstiftung zur Zwietracht” vor Gericht landen. So wie der Satiriker Azamat Omarov. „Ich sehe, dass euch die Witze über Toqaev gefallen haben, also kommt hier der nächste:” , sagt der kasachische Satiriker Azamat Omarov in die Handykamera, er läuft unter kahlen Baumreihen entlang. „Treffen sich die einheitliche Zeitzone, das neue Steuergesetzbuch und die neue Verfassung – und zack wird scharf geschossen!” Omarov stellt hier – für Kasach:innen offensichtlich – die jüngsten Reformen der Regierung ihrer brutalen Handhabung der Proteste von 2022 gegenüber. Es sind Witze wie dieser, veröffentlicht auf seinem YouTube-Kanal Akhual Segodnya [die heutige Lage, Anm. der Redaktion], die den Satiriker ins Visier der Behörden gebracht haben. Unterstützt Novastan – das europäische Zentralasien-Magazin Als vereinsgetragene, unabhängige Plattform lebt Novastan vom Enthusiasmus seiner ehrenamtlichen Mitarbeiter:innen – und von eurer Unterstützung! Novastan unterstützen Am 18. Juli 2026 nehmen Polizeikräfte Omarov in Astana fest und durchsuchen seine Wohnung. Nach zwei Monaten Untersuchungshaft kommt es zum Prozess. Omarovs Satire, so die Anklage, habe „soziale, nationale, stammesbezogene, rassistische, klassenbezogene oder religiöse Zwietracht“ gesät, strafbar unter Artikel 174 des kasachstanischen Strafgesetzbuches. Konkret hatte sich die Anklage laut dem Kazakhstan International Bureau for Human Rights and Rule of Law auf ein Video vom Januar 2026 berufen, in dem Omarov die Führung des Landes kritisiert hatte. Lest auch auf Novastan: Verurteilt wegen lustig – Fünf Jahre Haft für Temirlan Ensebek Durch eine Verfahrensvereinbarung kommt Omarov Mitte September schließlich frei. Die Einigung: Omarov bekennt sich schuldig und entgeht so einer Haftstrafe, die nun über dreieinhalb Jahre zur Bewährung ausgesetzt wird. Fünf Jahre darf er keine neuen Inhalte mehr verbreiten, sich nicht politisch oder sozioökonomisch engagieren. Nur um der Haft zu entgehen, habe Omarov sich schuldig bekannt, sagte sein Anwalt Tölegen Şaıkov nach dem Prozess. „Durch diesen Artikel (174) landen viele Leute im Gefängnis. So absurd es ist, er existiert und funktioniert.” Man könne nicht genug betonen, wie ungerecht dieses Urteil sei, schrieb Mihra Rittmann, Senior Advisor bei der NGO Human Rights Watch , Mitte September in einem Beitrag über den Fall. Kasachstanische Behörden nutzten die vage Formulierung von Artikel 174 schon lange, um unliebsame Stimmen zum Schweigen zu bringen. Erst 2025 hatte ein Gericht in Almaty den Satireblogger Temirlan Ensebek unter eben jenem Artikel der „Anstiftung zur Zwietracht” schuldig befunden. Amnesty International stufte seine Strafverfolgung als politisch motiviert ein. Lest auch auf Novastan: Internationale Resonanz zum Fall Temirlan Ensebek Um die Pressefreiheit ist es in Kasachstan schlecht bestellt. 2026 belegt das Land im World Press Freedom Index Platz 149 von 180. Der Index wird von der NGO Reporter ohne Grenzen erstellt. Sie begründen ihre Einstufung damit, dass die Regierung alle verfügbaren Mittel nutze, um unliebsame Berichterstattung einzuschränken. Das scheint insbesondere für die sensible Mischform der Satire zu gelten, für die sich Artikel 174 als probates Gegenmittel etabliert hat. Der Zeitpunkt von Azamat Omarovs Festnahme – etwa ein Monat vor den ersten Wahlen des neuen kasachstanischen Parlaments – fällt zudem in ein breiteres Muster. Zwischen Juni und August 2026 wurden gegen mindestens drei weitere unabhängige Journalist:innen Strafverfahren eingeleitet, eine von ihnen wurde verurteilt. Im Gespräch mit der Menschenrechtsorganisation CIVICUS sagte die kasachstanische Journalistin Nazira Därimbet, dass Behörden insbesondere vor großen politischen Ereignissen wie der Kurultai-Wahl darauf aus seien, unbequeme und unabhängige Stimmen zum Schweigen zu bringen. Auf YouTube ist der Kanal Akhual Segodnya nicht mehr zu finden, Omarovs Satire ist gelöscht. Dass irgendwo in Kasachstan jedoch weiterhin Witze über die Regierung von Qasym-Jomart Toqaev gemacht werden, lässt sich nicht verhindern. Doch autokratische Regime wie das Kasachstanische setzen für ihre Machterhaltung auf Kontrolle: Der politische Diskurs soll in staatlich geregelten Bahnen verlaufen. Auf Satire wie die von Omarov reagiert der Staat repressiv: Es soll verhindert werden, dass der Diskurs seine Bahn verlässt – und potenziell die Legitimationsgrundlage des Regimes unterminiert. Artikel 174, in all seiner Vagheit, hat sich dabei als probates Mittel erwiesen. Für Zentralasien direkt in eurer Mailbox könnt ihr euch auch zu unserem wöchentlichen Newsletter anmelden .
